size_legend.L: <6000 lines or a new solver/format, 1-2 weeks
size_legend.XL: new subsystem, GPU path or >6000 lines

rows.capability: Schema-derived contract (XSD/Schematron tables drive validation and typing)
rows.description: build.rs reads the vendored XSD and Schematron at build time and emits simple/complex type tables, a typed model and an assert catalogue, so a schema change reaches validator, model and explain in one build. The generator aborts on any XSD construct outside the subset the schema uses.
rust_evidence: README.md Document model: The contract is generated from the schema
python_evidence: scenerender/schema.py:35-95 (Schema parses scene-render-1.1.xsd with lxml at runtime)
rows.divergence: Rust generates static tables and structs at build time and fails the build on unsupported XSD constructs. Python reads the XSD at runtime and uses libxml2's XMLSchema for the structural check, plus a hand-written type_of_path / base_kind collapse (_BUILTIN_KIND/_NAMED_KIND) for attribute parsing. The mechanism differs, and Python has no assert catalogue (the Schematron is run opaquely through lxml.isoschematron). Both are schema-driven, so a schema update is mostly a data change in Python, but only for the 1.1 contract.
rows.notes: Parity here is mostly satisfied by replacing the XSD/SCH files; the only extra piece is a code/assert catalogue (see DOC-15).

rows.capability: Typed, fully resolved document model (struct per complex type, defaults applied, shared enums for node/animation groups)
rows.description: After validation the Rust engine builds a ~20k-line typed model: 134 enums for enumerations, one struct per complex type with defaults applied, and shared enums (Node, Animation, NodeBehaviour, BodyBehaviour) for the model groups. It is Serialize-able (inspect --json) and carries source Loc on each element.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-model/src/element.rs (Element trait: element_name, loc, element_id, get_attr, visit)
rows.searched: grep for dataclass/NamedTuple models of scene elements, 'class Scene', 'Node(' and 'to_json/asdict' in scenerender/*.py and nodes/; found only document.py Document (lxml tree + dicts) and schema.py TypeInfo/AttrInfo. Python evaluates directly off the lxml tree, resolving defaults lazily via schema.type_info (evaluator.py ev.num/ev.str), which gives equivalent defaults but no typed objects, no enum types and no JSON serialisation.
rows.notes: Functionally replaced by the lxml tree plus schema-driven lazy typing. Parity matters only if Python must expose a typed API or JSON dump (see DOC-16). No pixel/behaviour consequence.

rows.capability: Checked numeric newtypes and enum-valued attributes at model level
rows.description: 18 checked newtypes enforce XSD numeric restrictions at construction (UnitDecimal::new(1.5) fails), and enumerations become Rust enums, so an out-of-range value cannot reach the evaluator.
python_evidence: scenerender/document.py:153-186 (XSD validator checks facets: enumeration, pattern, bounds)
rows.divergence: Both reject out-of-range values at validation through the XSD facets (Python through libxml2). Python has no construction-time guard: with --lenient, values violating the facets still reach the evaluator and the parse helpers silently fall back to defaults (values.py parse_float/parse_length return default on bad input).

rows.capability: Name-based dynamic attribute access (get/set by name, declares, walk) for overrides, binds, variants and animate
rows.description: Element trait exposes AttrValue (Num/Bool/Str/Length/Color/Paint/Point/Numbers/Tokens) by attribute name, with set_attr parsing the lexical form by declared type and errors for unknown or invalid attributes. Templating and animate use it.
python_evidence: scenerender/schema.py:96-200 (attr type resolved per element path)
rows.notes: Python operates by string attributes on lxml elements and types them on read through the schema. The result is equivalent for overrides and binds. Unknown-attribute errors on override are not typed (SetAttrError equivalent): unverified.

rows.capability: Vendored schema provenance and version record (schema/UPSTREAM: tag + SHA-256 per file)
rows.description: The schema is vendored unchanged from sr-core with the tag and SHA-256 of each file recorded in schema/UPSTREAM, plus a list of local pending additions (SREPs 9-11, 13, cinematic 1.3). A new release replaces both files.
rust_evidence: README.md: The schema is vendored from sr-core
python_evidence: scenerender/schema/scene-v1.PROVENANCE.md (only the 1.0 reference xsd has a hash and commit)
rows.divergence: Python records provenance (commit and SHA-256) only for the 1.0 scene-v1.xsd. Its 1.1 xsd/sch carry no tag or hash record, and the Python 1.1 files are older than sr-core 1.1.3: the Schematron has 87 assert ids vs 185 in Rust, and V6 and V7 (part of 1.1.3 per README) are absent. Python also has no UPSTREAM-style list of local additions.
rows.notes: Prerequisite for every schema_gated row: sync the XSD/SCH to the Rust vendored files, including the 1.2 and 1.3 local additions.

rows.capability: Schema version enumeration and gating 1.0 / 1.1 / 1.2 / 1.3 (scene@version)
rows.description: scene@version accepts 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3. The crate reports SCHEMA_VERSION 1.3. Version is exposed as doc.version(). New attributes and enum values are accepted in every version, while new elements and asset kinds need the version that introduced them.
rows.divergence: Python rejects version="1.2" and "1.3" documents at the XSD stage (verified: validate of a version=1.2 file reports 'The value 1.2 is not an element of the set {1.0, 1.1}'). There is no version accessor object, so code branches on the string.
rows.notes: Needed for every 1.2/1.3 feature to be loadable at all.

rows.capability: Version gates V1-V4, V6, V7 for version="1.0" documents
rows.description: The Schematron p1 pattern rejects 1.1-only sections (V1), more than one output (V2), 1.1 node/animation elements (V3), 1.1 asset kinds (V4), 1.1 elements such as simulation nodes, geo and map assets, clay blobs, audio buses and effects, output posters, camera shake, representations, text spans and effect params (V6), and 1.1 object3D primitives capsule/clay/cone/cylinder/extrude/text/torus (V7).
rows.divergence: Python has V1-V4 and its test covers V1/V3/V4. V6 and V7 are missing from its Schematron, so a version="1.0" document using object3D primitive="capsule" or similar, or a 1.1-only element, is accepted. The exact element lists are in rules.rs and are not copied into Python.

items.name: V6
items.note: not in Python .sch (grep id="V6")

items.name: V7
items.note: not in Python .sch

rows.notes: Rule text is part of the validation parity work; this row only records the gate structure. Fixed by syncing the Schematron. [review] Confirmed: the Python .sch has asserts V1-V4 only (87 sch:assert in total; Rust has 185). object3D exists in the Python XSD (object3DType, primitive enum includes capsule/cylinder/cone/torus/text/extrude), so V7 is a real gap. Not run as a probe against a version=1.0 document.

rows.capability: Version gates V5 (1.2) and V8 (1.3)
rows.description: V5 requires version>=1.2 for tiles assets, basemap, object3D/rigidBody, primitive map/globe, and output segment/audioTrack/captionTrack. V8 requires version=1.3 for volume assets, medium, pyro, object3D primitive=volume or @volume. New attributes and enumeration values are accepted in every version.
rows.searched: grep -n 'V5\|V8\|"1.2"\|"1.3"' over scenerender/ and the shipped .sch/.xsd; only 1.0/1.1 exist, and the sch ids end at V4
rows.notes: Validation: see schema parity work. Listed because these are the gates that make 1.2/1.3 element families loadable in the right versions.

rows.capability: Four-stage loading over one parse (Structure, Rules, Assets, Model), every stage reporting all problems, model built only if no error
rows.description: Structure and rules always both run, so one pass reports every problem. Assets run when verify_assets is set. The typed model is built only if the report has no errors, and M01 reports an internal model-construction error. The warning list is retained on the Document.
rust_evidence: README.md: Loading runs four stages over one parse
python_evidence: scenerender/document.py:153-186 (load: XSD validate, normalise attrs, then Schematron, then _prepare)
rows.divergence: Python also runs XSD and Schematron and lists every problem in strict mode (raising SceneError with the whole list). But it parses once for each validator (lxml tree validated twice) and has no asset stage. Prepare (includes/params/binds/repeat) runs even on invalid trees under --lenient, which Rust does not offer: Rust never builds a model from an invalid document. Python has an opt-in lenient mode (--lenient) that Rust lacks. Errors are plain strings (see DOC-12).

rows.capability: Structure stage diagnostics S01-S12 and XML (stable codes, parse-error position)
rows.description: XSD structure errors have stable codes: S01 root, S02 element not allowed, S03 missing child, S04 undeclared attribute, S05 missing attribute, S06 value violates type, S07 text in element-only content, S08 bad text content, S09 duplicate ID, S10 unresolved IDREF, S11 foreign namespace, S12 nesting over 256. XML is a malformed-file error with line and column.
python_evidence: scenerender/document.py:162 (etree.parse(..., huge_tree=True) lifts libxml2's depth limit)
rows.divergence: The same classes of error are detected through libxml2, but with libxml2's free-text messages and no code. Verified: unknown attribute, missing required attribute, bad pattern and duplicate ID are all reported with 'line N: <libxml2 message>'. Not matched: (a) malformed XML raises a bare lxml XMLSyntaxError that load() does not wrap in SceneError; (b) huge_tree=True removes the depth limit (no S12 equivalent); (c) the README says libxml2 does not resolve xs:IDREF values (S10), and Python adds no check beyond the Schematron R rules such as R1, so a dangling IDREF is caught only where an R-rule exists (not enumerated); (d) rejecting whitespace-only xs:IDREFS or '1e' as xs:double (stricter than libxml2, per README) is not replicated.

(a) Malformed XML: cli validate prints a raw lxml.etree.XMLSyntaxError traceback, because cmd_validate catches only SceneError and load() calls etree.parse unguarded (document.py:162-163). (b) A dangling layer@asset gives only the Schematron R1 and a duplicate id gives the libxml2 xs:ID message; no generic IDREF check exists, since the xsd has about 55 xs:IDREF attributes and libxml2 does not resolve them. (c) huge_tree=True lifts the depth limit, so there is no S12.

rows.capability: Non-finite numeric guard (W01)
rows.description: A numeric attribute holding INF, -INF, NaN or a number overflowing a double (1e400), also inside lengths and number lists, is flagged W01 because the schema accepts them but the renderer needs finite values.
python_evidence: Probe: validate of <layer x="INF">, x="1e400" and x="5" all print 'valid scene-render 1.1'. No isfinite/W01 handling in document.py, schema.py or values.py.
rows.searched: grep -rn 'isfinite\|INF\|W01\|inf' scenerender/document.py scenerender/schema.py scenerender/values.py; probe: validate of <layer x="INF"> and x="1e400" reports no error (verified by running scenerender validate on a scratch doc).

rows.capability: Renderer-safety limit rules P01-P05 and loader limits
rows.description: Rules stage checks limits no schema can express: P01 soft-body stiffness needing over 4096 substeps, P02 counts that multiply into nodes or particles (repeater copies, star points, burst count, instances), P03 symbols containing themselves, P04 expression nesting beyond 62 levels, P05 cyclic matte dependencies (including after composition expansion). hardening.rs also tests 64 non-ASCII digit bytes as a digest, bounded frame placeholder width, and unexpanded all-integer sequences.
rows.divergence: Python has no validation-time limit rules. It guards a few of the same hazards at render time instead: include cycles (hard error), property-evaluation recursion (warning) and timing cycles (warn_once). No equivalent of P01/P02/P03/P04/P05 as pre-render diagnostics. A self-containing symbol or an enormous repeat count is found only when rendering.
rows.notes: Validation: see schema parity work for the Schematron-expressible overlap; P rules are native Rust code, not Schematron.

rows.capability: Diagnostic record format: severity, stable code, message, line/column/offset, XPath-like element path, help text
rows.description: Diagnostic{severity, code, message, loc{line, column, byte offset}, path /scene/composition/layer[2], optional help} is Serialize-able. Loc columns count characters. Reports are sorted by offset, deduplicated and counted, with codes() listing the distinct ones.
rows.divergence: Python has no structured record: validation_errors is list[str]. XSD errors carry a line number but no column or offset. Schematron errors carry an absolute XPath ('/scene/composition/layer', with [n] indices only when libxslt adds them) and the assert id, but no line. The CLI prints the XPath under the label 'line', which mislabels it (verified by running validate). No severity (everything is an error; warnings are logging), no help text, no stable code except the Schematron assert id embedded in the string.

rows.capability: validate command: multi-file, human and JSON output, --deny-warnings, --quiet, --no-assets, --base-dir, exit statuses
rows.description: scene-render validate FILE... prints human diagnostics with source excerpts and a per-file summary, or one JSON document (valid, files[], diagnostics) with --format json. --no-assets skips file checks and --base-dir sets the URI base. --deny-warnings turns warnings into failure, and --quiet prints only summaries. Exit status is 0 valid, 1 invalid, 2 I/O error.
python_evidence: scenerender/cli.py:55-69 (cmd_validate: one file, --max-errors, exit 3 on invalid)
rows.divergence: Python validates one file only. cmd_validate always loads with strict=False, so it also prints a log WARNING per run, and prints errors as 'line <str>', which mislabels the Schematron XPath as a line. It has no JSON output, --deny-warnings, --quiet, --no-assets or --base-dir. Exit codes are 0 or 3 (cli.py:73-86); Rust uses 0/1/2. A malformed XML file crashes with a traceback (see DOC-10).

rows.capability: Source-excerpt diagnostic rendering with colour
rows.description: Human output shows the file path, line and column, the offending source line with a caret/underline, the message and help, with colour decided by --color auto/always/never and NO_COLOR/SCENE_RENDER_COLOR.
rows.searched: grep -n 'excerpt\|caret\|line_text\|NO_COLOR\|colorama\|ansi' scenerender/cli.py scenerender/document.py; no source-line rendering exists.

rows.capability: explain command and diagnostic code catalogue
rows.description: scene-render explain lists every code (fixed S/A/P/W/M/XML codes, plus all Schematron asserts with id, rule context, XPath test and message, generated from the .sch at build time) and explains one on request, case-insensitively. Evaluator codes are listed alongside under stage 'eval'. Exit 2 on unknown code.
rows.searched: grep -rn 'explain' scenerender/cli.py scenerender/*.py; sub-commands in cli.py are still, render, check, validate, coverage only. Searched for 'catalog', 'codes' and 'lookup' modules; none exist. 'coverage' (coverage.py) lists renderer feature support, which is different.

rows.capability: inspect command: model summary and full typed-model JSON
rows.description: scene-render inspect FILE loads the document (printing diagnostics and exiting 1 if invalid) and prints version, frame size and fps, duration and frame count, background, colour space and linear-light flag, asset counts by kind, composition node count and depth, symbols, effects, outputs (path and codec) and id count. --json dumps the whole typed model.
rows.searched: grep -rn 'inspect' scenerender/cli.py; checked 'coverage' command (coverage.py report) which lists unsupported or supported features, not the document summary; and scenerender-vpkg inspect, which moved to sr-core.
rows.notes: A summary is cheap off the lxml tree; --json dump of a full model depends on DOC-02 or a generic tree-to-JSON export.

rows.capability: ID index by kind (asset/paint/material/symbol/effect/light/marker/param/layout/output/node...) and lookups
rows.description: Index maps every id to a Target (Asset, Paint, TextStyle, Material, Symbol, Marker, Effect, Light, TrackData, Param, DataSource, Variant, Layout, SafeArea, Output, AudioTrack, Bus, CaptionTrack, Node(path), or any other Element) and every style-token name to its token. Document offers doc.asset("logo"), paint, material, symbol, node, node_at(NodePath), token, composition_nodes() and similar lookups returning the right kind or None.
python_evidence: scenerender/document.py:227-232 (_index: ids = first element per @id, flat dict)
rows.divergence: Python keeps one flat dict id -> lxml element (setdefault, first wins) and rebuilds it after include/repeat expansion. The kind comes from the element tag, so callers do their own 'is this an asset?' checks, and there is no wrong-kind-returns-None lookup. Style tokens are kept in doc.tokens (a separate dict). There is no NodePath addressing.

rows.capability: ID uniqueness and reference integrity (xs:ID / xs:IDREF / IDREFS, id-by-kind rules)
rows.description: xs:ID uniqueness is enforced (S09) and xs:IDREF resolved (S10). The Schematron R-rules additionally require references to name the right kind (for example a layer asset must name an element of assets). Rust is stricter than libxml2 in three places: IDREF resolution, whitespace-only IDREFS, and '1e' as a double.
rust_evidence: README.md: Conformance is measured against lxml
python_evidence: scenerender/document.py:97-122 (id remap for include namespaces and repeat copies)
rows.divergence: xs:ID uniqueness and kind rules R1.. are checked via libxml2/libxslt (verified: dangling asset gives R1, duplicate id gives xs:ID error). A generic S10 check for every xs:IDREF/IDREFS attribute is not added on top of libxml2 (README says libxml2 does not resolve IDREF), so dangling references on attributes that no R-rule covers go unreported. R26-R41 are absent from the Python .sch. Rule parity: see validation parity work.

rows.capability: Style-token and paint resolution (var(--name), url(#id), resolve_color / resolve_paint)
rows.description: A Color is an Rgba or Token; resolve_color follows var(--token) chains to at most 8 levels and returns None if the token is missing, cyclic or not a colour. Paint is a colour or a PaintRef url(#id), and resolve_paint returns a solid colour or the paints element.
rows.divergence: Same semantics for valid input. Minor differences: Python resolves up to depth 16 and leaves an unresolved or cyclic var(--x) in the string, giving the default colour (transparent black) rather than None; Python accepts #RGB/#RGBA shorthand and clamps out-of-range comma components, whereas Rust accepts only 6/8-digit hex and rejects out-of-range channels. XSD pattern checking (colorType) rejects those at validation, so only lenient mode can see them.

rows.capability: Lengths with units (px, %, vw, vh, vmin, vmax) and resolve against parent and frame
rows.description: Length{value, unit} with units Px, Percent (of the parent box on the same axis), Vw, Vh, Vmin, Vmax. resolve(parent, frame_w, frame_h) returns pixels. A bad string is a ValueError.
rows.divergence: Resolution formulas are the same (percent of parent, v-units percent of frame). Python is lenient: an unparsable string falls back to float(s) and then default 0.0, while Rust returns an error. Python returns a float, not a typed Length, so the unit is lost.

rows.capability: Rational frame rates and exact frame arithmetic (Fps: frame_time, frame_at, frame_count, nominal)
rows.description: Fps is a u32/u32 ratio such as 24000/1001. frame_time(i) is computed exactly from the ratio. frame_at(t) floors t*fps with a 1e-9*fps guard so decimal times just below a boundary land in the next frame. frame_count(duration) rounds to the nearest frame when within 1e-9*fps and otherwise rounds up. nominal() gives the integer rate used by timecode.
rows.divergence: Python has at least three different time-to-frame rules, none matching Rust frame_at (floor(t*fps + 1e-9*fps)). output.py:405 uses round(t*fps). output.py:1047 uses ceil(n - 1e-9) for the frame count. assets/video.py:418 frame_index uses floor(t*fps + 1e-6), and its source-clip count uses floor(duration*fps + 1e-3). Rust frame_count rounds to nearest within 1e-9*fps and otherwise rounds up. There is no Document.frame_count().
rows.notes: Behaviour-affecting: the last frame count of a render and which frame a time belongs to. Verify against Rust corpus values.

rows.capability: Timecode with drop-frame (HH:MM:SS:FF and HH:MM:SS;FF) to frame/seconds
rows.description: Timecode{h,m,s,f,drop_frame}. to_frame(fps) validates the frame field against the nominal rate, rejects non-existent drop-frame labels (0..n at every minute except each tenth), requires a 29.97/59.94-family rate for drop-frame, and subtracts drop*(minutes - minutes/10). Display round-trips with ':' or ';'.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/video.py:755-780 (source_timecode: nominal-rate drop-frame from @timecodeStart); scenerender/values.py:108-110 (parse_timecode, unused and wrong)
rows.divergence: Python has no typed Timecode and no validation. Nothing checks the frame field against the nominal rate, nothing rejects non-existent drop labels (00:01:00;00/01), and nothing requires a 29.97/59.94-family rate for ';'. The only consumer, video.source_timecode, uses the nominal rate and applies the drop-frame correction, but it silently returns None on a malformed value. values.parse_timecode is an unused, incorrect helper (it ignores ';' and divides by the fractional fps).

rows.capability: Points, aspect ratios, SHA-256 digests and language tags as typed values
rows.description: Point2 (x,y), Aspect (W:H, both non-zero, ratio()), Sha256 (exactly 64 ASCII hex digits, to_hex lowercase) and LanguageTag (primary subtag lower-cased) are parsed with errors, round-trip through Display, and serialise.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-model/tests/hardening.rs:27 (64 non-ASCII bytes is an error)
python_evidence: scenerender/values.py:63-70 (parse_point: raises on one-component input, no 2-number check); XSD sha256Type pattern (scene-render-1.1.xsd:77); tracking.py:1623, video.py:212 and physics.py:1875 compare digests with .lower()
rows.divergence: Points exist. Digests are validated by the XSD pattern [0-9a-f]{64}, so uppercase digests are rejected at validation, while tracking.py and captions.py compare case-insensitively (inconsistent with the schema). Aspect ratio and language tag have no typed helper: 'aspect' only appears in unrelated renderer maths (output.py:1058 etc.) and consumers read the raw strings (grep for aspectType and languageTag found nothing).

rows.capability: Numeric list and token-list value types (numberListType, IDREFS/NMTOKENS) with XSD whitespace normalisation
rows.description: Vec<f64> and Vec<String> parse space-separated lists with XSD collapse semantics. Lexical forms follow the XSD whitespace facet of each type before parsing, and doubles follow xs:double (INF/NaN accepted lexically, with W01 on top).
rows.notes: Python parse_numbers splits on commas as well as whitespace, a lenient superset.

rows.capability: Asset check A01: existence of every input URI (file:/relative/absolute, percent-decoding, proxy as warning, physics cache A06)
rows.description: Every attribute that names an input (src, cache, proxy and so on, via input_uri_attributes()) on any element is resolved against the base dir (percent-decoding, file: URIs, absolute paths). Missing files are A01 errors, a missing proxy is an A01 warning, a missing physics cache is A06 (a warning, since it is recomputed), a directory or unreadable file is A05. generated/captionTrack/tiles caches get a help message pointing at `scene-render resolve`.
python_evidence: scenerender/document.py:90-95 (resolve_path: file:, scheme passthrough, base join)
rows.divergence: The row says URI resolution is equivalent. It is not quite. Rust resolve() percent-decodes every URI, including relative and absolute paths, and also accepts file://localhost. Python Document.resolve_path (document.py:90-95) calls unquote only for 'file:' URIs, so a relative src such as 'my%20clip.mp4' stays literal in Python and is decoded in Rust. Otherwise the original divergence stands: there is no validation-stage file check, and missing images only warn_once at draw time.

items.name: A01 missing input file
items.note: render-time only

rows.notes: Which attributes count as inputs must follow the Rust set (including the 1.2/1.3 elements: tiles, volume, meshSequence).

rows.capability: Asset check A02: SHA-256 verification of @sha256 / @cacheSha256
rows.description: Every @sha256 on a src and @cacheSha256 on a cache is checked by hashing each distinct file once, in parallel. A mismatch is an A02 error that shows expected and found digests and a help message (regenerate or update; `scene-render resolve` for generated/captionTrack/tiles). It also covers srvseq volume bakes. All of it runs at validation.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/video.py:196-218 (provenance_src: @sha256 on video, lottie and vector svg, and on a selected <representation>, warn_once, file still used); scenerender/physics.py:1870-1908 (physics @cacheSha256: log.error and re-simulate on mismatch; warns if the written cache differs); plus the cited document.py, assets/__init__.py, tracking.py and captions.py sites
rows.divergence: Python verifies digests at use time, with three failure modes: hard SceneError (include, data, generated cache), logged error and fallback (trackData and captionTrack skipped, physics cache re-simulated), and warn-once while still using the file (video/lottie/svg/representation @sha256). Plain image, audio and font src digests are not checked. Nothing runs at validation, so `validate` cannot detect drift and there is no expected/found/help diagnostic.

rows.capability: Asset check A04: image/mesh/volume sequence frame completeness
rows.description: For imageSequence, meshSequence and numbered volume, it expands the %0Nd, %d or #### placeholder (bounded width) over first..last by step, checks each frame exists in parallel, and reports missing runs compactly (for example 3-9, 14). It reports an error when missingFrame=error (or, for mesh/volume, hold with a missing first frame) and a warning otherwise. last < first, no placeholder, more than the max frame count and remote sequences each have their own case.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/image.py:60-90 (missingFrame handling per frame at render time)
rows.divergence: Python applies the missingFrame policy (error draws nothing with a warning; black and so on) only when the frame is drawn, one frame at a time, so there is no pre-render completeness check, compact missing-run report, last<first or missing-placeholder diagnostic. Whether Python's 'error' policy aborts the render, where Rust's A04 error makes validation fail, is unverified: the code only warns and draws nothing. meshSequence and volume sequences do not exist (see the other areas).

rows.capability: Asset check A03: remote inputs reported as unverified offline
rows.description: An input whose scheme is http, https, s3 and so on is not fetched. The validator emits an A03 warning ('was not verified offline'), also for remote image sequences.
rows.searched: grep -rn 'A03\|not verified\|urlsplit.*scheme' scenerender/; found urlsplit only in document.resolve_path (passes non-file schemes through unchanged), and no validation-time check or warning.

rows.capability: Asset check A07: declared image width/height versus the local file header, EXIF-orientation-aware
rows.description: For each local <image src> with declared width and height, the engine reads the file header once per distinct file without decoding pixels (format guessed by content, not extension) and compares it with the declared size, swapping dimensions for EXIF orientations 5-8. A mismatch is an A07 warning at the width attribute, with help to set the asset size and use boxWidth/boxHeight/fit. Remote sources, proxies and formats without a native header reader are skipped. Layout still uses the declared size.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-model/tests/image_dimensions.rs (5 tests: EXIF, mismatch warning, matching and proxy, missing, content-identified headers)
python_evidence: Searched: grep -i 'exif|exif_transpose|getexif' over scenerender finds nothing; only image_io.py:92-101 reads TIFF page Orientation. No declared-vs-file size comparison exists.
rows.searched: grep -rn 'A07\|declared\|Image.open\|exif\|Orientation' scenerender/assets/image*.py scenerender/document.py. Python takes asset dimensions as declared (assets/image.py:31-37) without comparing them with the file. image_io.py:49 uses PIL without ImageOps.exif_transpose, and its Orientation handling (image_io.py:92-101) is TIFF-only, so JPEG EXIF-rotated photos are possibly not upright (unverified outside this area).
rows.notes: Declared-size layout semantics already match Rust; only the warning and EXIF-aware dimension probe are missing. Pillow's Image.open reads headers without decoding.

rows.capability: Load options: verify_assets, base_dir, per-file base resolution, LoadError (Io vs Invalid report)
rows.description: LoadOptions{verify_assets, base_dir} controls asset checks and the URI base, which defaults to the file's directory (cwd for strings). load_file/load_str/validate_file/validate_str return a Document or a LoadError (read/UTF-8 failure vs Invalid(Report)). Non-UTF-8 files are I/O errors.
rows.divergence: Python has base override and strict/lenient, but no validate-only API returning a report object (validation errors are stored on Document.validation_errors, and strict raises SceneError with a joined string), no in-memory string loader (load takes a path), and no distinction between I/O and invalid errors. The lenient mode has no Rust counterpart.

rows.capability: Timeline accessors on the loaded document (fps, duration, frame_count, frame_size, version, warnings)
rows.description: Document exposes version(), base_dir(), warnings(), fps(), duration(), frame_count() and frame_size() resolved from project.
python_evidence: scenerender/document.py:46-80 (Document.fps set in _project at :238; project property)
rows.divergence: Python exposes doc.fps (Fraction), width/height through project/_project and the root version string, but has no duration() or frame_count() on the document. Frame counts are computed per output in output.py:1047 (see DOC-22 for the rounding differences).

rows.capability: Rules stage (Schematron assert evaluation with libxml2-compatible XPath 1.0 semantics) and the 56-pattern coverage
rows.description: The 56 Schematron patterns are evaluated natively in Rust with XPath 1.0 semantics, and number() follows libxml2 (2.4e1 equals 24), because the .sch names libxslt as its engine. Rule families: V1-V8, C1-C59, R1-R41 with R24/R25/R30/R31 attribute families, plus the 1.3 families CRT, FRX, GEO, MSQ, OCN, P3D, PYRO, VOL.
rust_evidence: README.md: Conformance is measured against lxml
rows.divergence: Python runs the identical engine the Rust side uses as its oracle (libxslt), so the 87 rules it has should give the same verdicts for shared asserts. It lacks the 98 assert ids that exist only in the Rust file (C45-C59, R26-R41 plus the R30/R31 families, V5-V8, CRT/FRX/GEO/MSQ/OCN/P3D/PYRO/VOL, from comm of the two .sch id sets). Rule-by-rule status: see schema parity work.
rows.notes: Syncing the .sch gives the rules for free because lxml evaluates them, and the cost is runtime (DOC-35). [review] The Rust README says 140 Schematron asserts while the inventory counts 185 ids in the .sch (id families, such as the R24/R25/R30/R31 attribute families, are enumerated separately). Python has 87 asserts across 41 patterns (82 open/close sch:pattern lines). The 98-id difference holds only under the 185-id count; the README's 56 patterns versus Python's 41 is the safer comparison.

rows.capability: Validation and load performance budget (10,000 nodes / 40,000 elements in ~100 ms; 200 ms test; stages example)
rows.description: A 10,000-node composition (2.1 MiB) parses, validates and loads in about 100 ms in release. perf.rs asserts 200 ms and the `stages` example times each stage.
python_evidence: scenerender/schema.py:60-75 (Schematron results cached by SHA-256 of the tree and rules in ~/.cache/scenerender/schematron.json; comment 'checking a large document costs about a second')
rows.divergence: Python's libxslt Schematron costs about a second on a large document (per its own comment) and is mitigated with an on-disk cache keyed by digest. Cache misses stay slow, and the cache write is skipped on a read-only home. No performance test exists for validation. An exact figure for 10,000 nodes was not measured.
rows.notes: Only a native rule engine would close the gap, which is expensive and low-impact; the cache is a reasonable substitute.

rows.capability: Conformance corpus and differential fuzzing against lxml (tests/corpus, oracle.py, oracle_diff.py)
rows.description: tools/build_corpus.py writes 179 documents: a kitchen sink, one mutation per Schematron assert (all ids) and one per structural and asset code, with the oracle's verdict. cargo test requires exactly the manifest's codes. tools/oracle_diff.py mutates randomly, comparing XSD verdicts and (assert id, line) multisets; seeds 1-4 (7,000 mutants) give zero disagreements. Evidence is in tools/evidence/*.json.
python_evidence: tests/test_semantic_validation.py (a few parametrised rule mutations, V1/V3/V4)
rows.divergence: Python uses lxml itself as its validator, so it needs no oracle. But it has no per-assert mutation corpus, no kitchen-sink fixture and no coverage check that every assert and code is exercised. Only a handful of rules are tested. The Rust corpus (179 documents plus manifest) could be reused directly as a shared conformance suite for the Python validator once the schema is synced.
rows.notes: Cheap win: run Python validation over the Rust tests/corpus and compare against its manifest (code mapping needed, see DOC-10).

rows.capability: Include/import with namespaced ids, parameters, variants, data binding and overrides in the document stage
rows.description: Documents compose through include (src plus optional symbol, sha256, override) with id namespacing and rebased paths, and parametrise through param/variant/data/bind with type checking. Where Rust does this (sr-eval or sr-model) was not located within this area's reading: element.rs only shows the name-based set_attr substrate and Index records Param, DataSource and Variant targets.
rows.divergence: Python's behaviour is extensive (include/repeat/binds/layout/variant substitution). Semantic equality with the Rust evaluator on these features was not compared here; it belongs to the templating/evaluation area.
rows.notes: Listed so the document stages are not lost; status is PRESENT for existence only.

rows.capability: Compile-once Program and pure-function FrameGraph evaluation (order-independent, deterministic)
rows.description: sr-eval compiles a validated document once per variant/layout into a Program (nodes, slots, channels, expression bytecode, links, transitions) and Evaluator::evaluate(t) returns a FrameGraph: active nodes in paint order with local/world transforms, own and accumulated opacity, timeline/local/source times, resolved text, matte links, per-property values, active transitions with eased progress, active camera and animated state of non-node elements. The same (document, options, t) gives the same bits in any evaluation order.
python_evidence: scenerender/evaluator.py::Evaluator (lazy per-property get() on the lxml tree, caches _keys/_statics/_builtin_memo)
rows.divergence: Rust: separate compile step then a pure evaluate(t) that yields an inspectable FrameGraph value. Python: templating is prepared once at load, but all timing, animation, expression and layout evaluation happens lazily per frame inside the compositor, with mutable caches (_keys, _statics, _builtin_memo, sequence/duration caches) and no FrameGraph or Program object. Determinism holds in practice (tests render backward seeks, test_particle_evaluation) but order-independence is not asserted as a contract or tested as such.
rows.notes: A FrameGraph is mainly tooling/diff-testing value; pixel parity does not need it. Python also lacks 'accumulated opacity' and 'source times' as first-class outputs.

rows.capability: Evaluation CLI: eval (FrameGraph dump), --bench, explain Exxx, --row
rows.description: `scene-render eval FILE [--bench]` prints or benchmarks the FrameGraph and `scene-render explain E03` describes any evaluation code. crates/sr-eval/tests/perf.rs asserts a 2 ms/frame budget for 5,000 keyframed properties across 1,020 nodes plus 500 expressions.
rows.searched: scenerender/cli.py subparsers (still, render, check, validate, coverage only); grep -rn 'explain\|--bench\|--row\|FrameGraph' scenerender tests docs; only unrelated hit tests/test_perf_color.py bench-explainer fixture
rows.notes: Python has --param/--variant/--layout on still/render but no eval/explain subcommands and no evaluation-only benchmark.

rows.capability: Parameter value precedence: @default, variant set, data row, --param
rows.description: Parameter values resolve in order default, then the selected variant's <set>, then the selected data row (--row), then --param; the later source wins. --param naming an undeclared parameter is an E07 error with a did-you-mean hint. Declared defaults are checked like any other value.
rows.divergence: Python implements default, then variant set, then --param (same order for those three). There is no data-row layer (see EVAL-04). An undeclared --param only logs a warning and is still stored (document.py:284-286) instead of failing with E07. Declared defaults that violate their own constraints only warn (document.py:333) where Rust errors. Unknown variant raises SceneError with no code or suggestion.
rows.notes: Python also merges included documents' <parameters> (namespaced), so --param inc/p works there; Rust templates an include with default options only.

rows.capability: Data sources (json/csv/tsv, inline or src) and --row selection for batch rendering
rows.description: <data> sources load JSON (array of records/values or {"rows": [...]}), CSV or TSV (RFC 4180 quoting, header required, ragged rows are errors, numeric cells become numbers). --row [source:]index overlays the chosen record's fields onto declared parameters; missing source or row is E09. Data sources are also exposed to repeat/@over as lists.
rows.divergence: Python loads json/csv/tsv with src or inline text and verifies sha256, and uses them for repeat/@over, but has no way to select a row into parameters (no --row, no EvalOptions.row equivalent). Differences in parsing: Python csv.DictReader keeps every cell a string (Rust makes numeric cells numbers), a non-list JSON object becomes a single row (Rust accepts only an array or an object with a 'rows' array, else E09), ragged CSV rows are tolerated, errors are raw exceptions without E09.
rows.notes: --row is the batch/personalisation entry point (one render per data row).
rows.searched: grep -n 'row' scenerender/cli.py document.py; grep -rn '"--row' scenerender

rows.description: Each resolved value is converted by declared type (string, enum, color, asset, number, boolean, time as seconds or HH:MM:SS:FF timecode, list as JSON array or comma list) and checked: number/time min and max, string/enum maxLength and anchored regex pattern, enum options, color parse, asset id exists, required means a value must come from default/variant/row/CLI (E08). Violations are E07.

rows.capability: Binds (with map), variant overrides and layout overrides: order, id lookup, typed set, E05/E06
rows.description: After parameters resolve, binds (param to target.property, optional 'a=b;c=d' map) are applied first, then the variant's overrides, then the selected layout's overrides; later wins. Overrides go through a generated name-based Element interface on every model type: an unknown id is E05, an undeclared attribute or a value its type rejects is E06.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-eval/src/program.rs::template (binds, variant override, layout override order), ::apply_override (lines 769-794)
rows.divergence: Order is reversed: Python applies layout overrides first (inside _project), then variant overrides, then binds, so a bind beats a variant and a layout; Rust applies binds, then variant, then layout, so the layout wins. Python sets the raw string with el.set() with no type check (no E06) and an unknown target only logs 'override target not found' (no E05). Bind map: Python does not trim around '=' / ';' and matches exact text; Rust trims.
rows.notes: Validation of values against the schema type on set is the part needing a typed attribute setter (Python has schema.type_info/base_kind to build one).

rows.capability: {{id}} / {{item.field}} placeholders in text-bearing attributes, E16 warning
rows.description: {{param}} and {{param.field}} resolve once at templating in the text/data/tex/value/label/prompt attributes of text, object3D, code, formula, meta and word elements and in span text; {{index}}, {{count}} and {{var.field}} resolve per repeat copy on text asset layers. Unknown names are left unchanged with an E16 warning.
rows.divergence: Python substitutes only the 'text' attribute and span text of <text> assets (assets.iter('text')); code, formula, meta, word and object3D text attributes and value/label/prompt/data/tex are not templated. Per-copy {{index}}/{{item.x}} for text layers is implemented (clone of the asset per copy, also {{item.0}} array indexing which Rust lacks). No E16 warning: unknown names stay silently.
rows.notes: code/formula/meta/word asset elements may be absent from the 1.1 schema in places; check before extending.

rows.capability: Repeat expansion: count/over, from/step, offset/rotation/scale/opacity/time steps, scoped copy ids, per-copy bindings
rows.description: A repeat expands into one scoped copy per item (ids 'list[2]/label') with cumulative offsetX/offsetY, rotationStep, scaleStep^k, opacity 1-k*opacityStep (floored at 0) and timeStep stagger on the copy's clock. count generates numbers from + k*step; over iterates a list parameter or data source (skipping 'from', every 'step'), binding the item to @var; index/count/item are visible to expressions, param(var.field) and text. E10 if over names a non-list.
rows.divergence: Transform/opacity/time stepping and index/count/item/var bindings behave the same (tested). Differences: copy ids are 'r#i' with children 'child#i' (flattened), Rust uses 'r[i]' with children 'r[i]/child'; references from outside a repeat to 'r[2]/l' (prop(), link, matte, @parent) therefore do not resolve in Python. With @over, Python ignores from/step and uses all items (index = from+i*step only for count); Rust skips 'from' items and steps. Python does not raise E10 when over names a non-list (silently empty/param_list). No E18 cap on count (see EVAL-11). Python expands at load (static), so animated count/over are not representable (neither in Rust).
rows.notes: Fixing the id syntax touches Document.ids, resolve_id references maps, scheduling caches and every ref() resolver; the largest part of the cost.

rows.capability: Symbol instances: scoped ids, overrides applied inside the instance, own clock, validation
rows.description: An instance clones its symbol with ids scoped 'instance/inner', applies its <override> children inside that scope only (E05 unknown target, E06 bad value), and runs the symbol on its own clock (speed, clipIn, loop, reverse, timeRemap, ends with the symbol unless @end). Box is the symbol's width/height.
rows.divergence: Semantics are equivalent but implemented as runtime override scopes (ctx.scope.overrides keyed by (target id, property), outermost wins) instead of cloned scoped nodes; scoped ids 'inst/inner' resolve through Evaluator.reference. No E05/E06 for bad override targets/values (they are silently ignored). Python additionally honours clipOut and fit on instances; sr-eval's instance() ignores clipOut/fit (unverified whether sr-gpu applies them).
rows.notes: Only the error reporting is missing.

rows.capability: Includes: other document under a namespace, symbol or composition, overrides, own clock and lifetime
rows.description: <include src symbol?> loads another document, templates it with default options, namespaces its assets and ids ('inc/logo', 'inc/mark'), applies the include's overrides inside that namespace, and runs the included composition/symbol on the same clock rules as an instance (it lasts the library's duration; speed/loop default). Missing file, invalid document or missing symbol is E12.
rows.divergence: Namespacing, relative-path rebasing, token/asset/paint reference remapping, overrides, include cycle detection and sha256 verification are implemented (and stronger than Rust: tokens, parameters, markers, styles are merged). But an include becomes a plain group (document.py:491-500) with no media clock: it does not end at the included composition/symbol duration and does not take the symbol's own clock. Strict mode raises SceneError instead of E12; lenient mode skips a missing include.
rows.notes: Rust documents 'Animated elements of included documents outside their composition are not evaluated' as a limitation.

rows.capability: Expansion guards: self-instantiation (E13) and node cap 2^19 (E18)
rows.description: Instance/include recursion (a symbol that instantiates itself, directly or via other instances, or an include cycle, depth > 16) is rejected with E13; a composition whose repeats, object3D @instances and nested instances expand past 2^19 nodes is E18 (counted before allocation, saturating arithmetic for huge from/step).
rows.divergence: Python detects include-file cycles only. A symbol instantiating itself, and nested repeat counts that multiply, are not checked and would recurse or exhaust memory.
rows.notes: Validation: see schema parity work for the P02 count rule.
rows.searched: grep -rn 'itself\|too many nodes\|MAX_NODES\|2 \*\* 19\|RecursionError' scenerender; only expr.py RecursionError handling and the include-cycle check

rows.capability: object3D @instances: one evaluated node per copy with index/count, copy ids and seeds
rows.description: object3D @instances expands into N nodes evaluated with their own index and count; copy 0 keeps the id and copy k is 'id[k]'; each copy gets its own seed when no @seed is authored.
rows.divergence: Python evaluates index/count per copy (and vectorises expressions via vexpr), so transforms match. Copies are not separate addressable nodes: no 'id[k]' ids for prop()/links, and no per-copy derived seed.
rows.notes: 3D rendering detail belongs to the 3D area.
rows.searched: grep -rn '\[k\]\|instances' scenerender/three scenerender/evaluator.py

rows.capability: Node windows: start/end and startMarker/endMarker
rows.description: Each node's window is placed once before the first frame: @start plus the marker time when @startMarker is given, @end (or marker time plus @end for endMarker); a layer of video or image sequence ends with its media unless @end is set.
rows.divergence: Rust adds: start = @start + marker time; end = marker time + @end. Python lets the marker replace @start/@end (markers.get(startMarker, start)). Python's layer media_time returns None (draws nothing) once media runs out even when an explicit @end is later (nodes/core.py:175-176), so a layer with @end beyond its media disappears at media end; Rust keeps it visible until @end (holding the last frame). Python additionally supports animated/expression-driven start/end/speed/clip windows solved by fixed point (scheduling._fixed_timing, docs/TIMING.md); Rust windows are static.
rows.notes: Python's dynamic-timing machinery is a superset; keep it when aligning marker semantics.

rows.capability: Sequence placement: end-to-end with timeGap, child start offsets, marker-pinned children
rows.description: A sequence places children end to end: each child starts at cursor + its own @start, the next cursor is the child's end plus timeGap (negative overlaps); a child with startMarker stays on its marker; contents of groups and nested sequences move with their container, instances run on their own clock.
python_evidence: tests/test_sequence_scheduling.py (nested sequences, group scale, timeGap, normalized windows)
rows.divergence: Core cursor+gap+own-start placement matches (test_sequence_scheduling). Differences: (1) a child with startMarker is placed at cursor + marker time in Python (marker replaces @start and is then offset by the cursor), but at the absolute marker time in Rust. (2) Python computes the natural duration of nested groups/sequences from their content (and from timeRemap, clip, speed, timeStretch, loop); Rust only knows an intrinsic length from explicit @end or media, so a group without @end makes the following child start at infinity (Rust limitation).
rows.notes: Marker-pinned children need an authoritative decision on the intended semantics.

rows.capability: Transitions: auto-transitions at junctions, explicit transitions, alignment, cut point, handle extension
rows.description: A sequence with @transition gets a transition at every junction without an explicit one (cut = outgoing child's end, window centred by duration, ease-in-out); explicit <transition> windows use center/start/end alignment around the cut (from's end, else to's start); both members stay visible across the window (handle extension).

rows.capability: Group timeOffset/timeScale and repeat stagger clocks
rows.description: A group's children run on child = origin + (t - origin - timeOffset) * timeScale where origin is the group's start; repeat copies stagger by k*timeStep through the same affine clock; the clock chain composes through ancestors.
rows.notes: Same formula; Python additionally evaluates timeScale/timeOffset as animatable properties.

rows.capability: Media clock of layers and instances: speed, timeStretch, clipIn/clipOut, reverse, loop, freezeAt, timeRemap
rows.description: Local time maps to source time: rate = speed/timeStretch (negative speed plays backwards), clipIn offset, source length after clipIn/clipOut, loop counts extra plays then holds the end, reverse flips within the length, freezeAt holds one source frame for the node's whole window (frozen layers do not end with media), timeRemap keys give source seconds.

items.note: rate = speed/timeStretch for layers; instances have speed only (as in Rust)

items.name: negative speed plays backwards
items.note: Python media_time does not take abs(rate) or flip reverse; negative speed gives negative source time

items.name: loop (extra plays then hold)
items.note: Python also treats loop<0 as infinite (not in schema type nonNegativeInteger)

items.name: reverse
items.note: u = span - u

items.name: freezeAt
items.note: frozen layers do not end with media

items.name: timeRemap
items.note: anim.sample of keys at local time, hold extrapolation

items.note: Python draws nothing past media end even with a later @end (Rust holds)

rows.notes: sr-eval ignores instance clipOut (Rust side) so instance parity target for clipOut is Python's behaviour.

rows.capability: Paint order: static z (stable), 3D exemption, animated z restacking every frame
rows.description: Siblings are sorted once at compile time by static z, stably in document order; object3D, particles3D, ocean and camera nodes are exempt (z is a scene-unit depth, they sort as 0). A node with animated z (keys, expression or link) marks its siblings for per-frame restacking by current value, stably in document order; the animated value is integer-rounded.

items.name: static z, stable sort
items.note: sorted(kids, key=z) is stable

items.name: object3D/camera z exempt
items.note: key 0

items.name: particles3D/ocean exempt
items.note: Rust-only nodes (schema-gated)

items.name: animated z restack per frame
items.note: z evaluated per frame unless authored static; cache bypassed when animated

items.name: integer rounding of animated z
items.note: Python sorts by float; Rust truncates with `as i32` (README says rounds)

rows.divergence: Rust animated z IS rounded: eval.rs:946 reads the z slot value, which value.rs clamps with the integer kind (clamp(2.6)=3), then `as i32` only converts an already-rounded number. Static z is xs:int in the 1.1 XSD (line 1504), so it has no fraction. The README ('rounds') is therefore accurate and the inventory's 'Rust truncates' oddity is wrong. The remaining difference is Python: child_order sorts by the unrounded float of an animated z, so 0.4 and 0.6 order as 0.4<0.6 where Rust gives 0 and 1 (same order here, but ties/ordering differ for e.g. 0.6 vs 1.4 -> 1 vs 1 tie in Rust).
rows.notes: Schema gated only for the particles3D/ocean exemption. [review] Drop the claim that Rust truncates z or that README and code disagree. Fix on the Python side is to round animated z before sorting (one line in child_order).

The box comes from boxWidth/boxHeight, parent box or the asset size; the cropped region is what is fitted.

rows.capability: Group flex layout: row, column, stack, grid with gap, padding, six justify modes, alignItems incl. stretch
rows.description: Groups (and sequences) with @layout arrange children as row, column, stack (all children overlaid) or grid (gridColumns), with gap and padding; justify start/center/end/space-between/space-around/space-evenly on the main axis; alignItems start/center/end/stretch/baseline on the cross axis; a child's own x/y offset it from its slot. Grid columns are as wide as their widest child and rows as tall as their tallest child.

rows.capability: Responsive alignment: alignX/alignY to parent, frame or safe area with margin and stretch

rows.capability: cubic-bezier (@bezier and After Effects influence/speed handles) and spring segment semantics
rows.description: cubic-bezier uses @bezier x1,y1,x2,y2 (x1,x2 must be in [0,1], else E04) or AE temporal handles: x = influence, y = influence*speed with defaults influence 1/3 and speed 1 and influence clamped to [0,1]. Spring runs in seconds (stiffness, damping, mass) with the underdamped, critical and overdamped solutions, and its residual 1-spring(duration) is spread linearly so the value lands exactly on the next key.
rows.divergence: Defaults: with no @bezier and no easeOut/easeIn Python uses speed 0.0 (handles (1/3,0),(2/3,1) -> ease-in-out-like; executed: f(0.25)=0.15625) while Rust uses speed 1.0 (handles (1/3,1/3),(2/3,2/3) -> linear). No @bezier validation or influence clamp in Python; solver tolerance 1e-6 vs 1e-12. Spring: Python 1-x(t*duration) does not land on the next key (executed: spring(100,10,1,0.5)(1.0)=1.0746, a jump at the next key) and its zeta>1 branch reuses the critically damped formula (executed: overdamped value 0.264 vs correct 0.132 at t=0.1); Rust has the exact overdamped solution and exact landing.
rows.notes: AE-handle animation exported from other tools is affected by the default-speed difference.

rows.capability: Non-uniform Catmull-Rom and Kochanek-Bartels splines through neighbouring keys
rows.description: Catmull-Rom (t=c=b=0) and TCB (tension, continuity, bias on the keys) interpolate in value space with Hermite tangents scaled for non-uniform key spacing (Kochanek and Bartels 1984 eq. 9: factor 2*dt_next/(dt_prev+dt_next)); end keys use the single available difference.
rows.divergence: By code reading (not executed against Rust): uniform spacing and c=0 agree. Python scales per-second velocities by the segment dt (tangent_out = a*dp*dt_next/dt_prev + b*dn), Rust multiplies the mixed difference by 2*dt_next/(dt_prev+dt_next); these differ for non-uniform keys. The continuity sign is also opposite: Rust weights the previous difference by (1-c) outgoing, Python (standard KB) by (1+c). Rust uses the TCB parameters of this key for both tangents of a segment's end keys.
rows.notes: Low impact: used by few documents.

rows.capability: Spatial Bezier tangents with arc-length parameterisation and roving keys
rows.description: spatialIn/spatialOut tangents turn a pair of 2D px keys into a cubic Bezier path that the temporal ease travels by arc length; roving keys between two fixed keys are retimed in proportion to value-space distance for constant speed; first and last keys never rove.
rows.divergence: Minor: Python generalises to N-component vectors (Rust: pixel pairs only), uses a 64-segment chord table, and measures roving distance along the spatial curve when tangents exist (Rust uses chord distance because roving is retimed before spatial tables are built). Overshooting eases extrapolate the Bezier polynomial in Python and the chord in Rust.
rows.notes: Marked PRESENT: normal use gives the same motion; edge cases differ.

rows.capability: Seeded randomness primitives: splitmix64, lattice hash, 53-bit uniform, packing, Box-Muller, Fisher-Yates, CRC-32 element seeds

rows.capability: Bit-identical transcendental functions across platforms (libm)
rows.description: Every transcendental function in curves, expressions, noise and layout comes from the portable libm crate so results are bit-identical on every machine.
rows.searched: grep -rn 'libm' scenerender; math.sin/cos/exp/pow and numpy ufuncs used throughout curves.py, expr.py, noise.py (host libm / numpy SIMD), no portable math layer

rows.capability: Element seed derivation for nodes, copies and simulations
rows.description: Each instantiated node gets a seed (its @seed, else hash_str(id): FNV-1a of the scoped id mixed by splitmix64); repeat copies and object3D copies derive theirs from the copy id; emitters seed as hash_str(id) ^ project seed unless @seed is set. (The README's CRC-32 'project:id:@seed:purpose' rule is used for text-animator order, wiggly selectors, scramble letters and effects.)
rows.divergence: Python derives every per-element seed from the CRC-32 rule; Rust's node/emitter/simulation seeds use FNV-1a of the id (and ^ project seed), a different hash, so particle and simulation draws differ for the same document even though the underlying counter-based generator is identical.
rows.notes: Needs a decision on the canonical seed rule per feature; belongs with the particles/simulation parity work, listed here because determinism claims cross areas.

rows.capability: Markers and beat grid: beat.N / bar.N generated markers, marker times
rows.description: markers resolve by id; a beatGrid (bpm, offset, beatsPerBar) generates beat.N = offset + N*60/bpm and bar.N = offset + N*beat*beatsPerBar for any N (0-based: bar.1 is one bar after the offset); the first grid is used by beat(), which prefers detected audio beats when available.
rows.divergence: Python numbers beats and bars from 1 with beat.1 = offset and bar.1 = offset (document.py:421-425 comment: 'the schema leaves it open'); Rust has beat.0 = offset and bar.1 = offset + one bar. Every beat.N/bar.N reference is therefore one beat/bar apart. Python only generates ids up to the project duration (Rust computes any N on demand) and ignores detected beats.
rows.notes: One-line off-by-one plus on-demand lookup.

rows.description: Instances and includes always, and groups that are isolate=true, masked, clipped, matted, carry effects, or have a non-normal blend, render their children into an offscreen that composites as one layer. Everything else passes children straight through. Opacity<1 and threeD are NOT isolation triggers.
rows.divergence: Rust isolated(): instance|include, isolate, effects, mask child, clip, matte, blend!=normal. Python is_isolated(): the same list PLUS opacity<1 and threeD=true. So a group with opacity 0.5 composites as a flattened layer in Python (children overlap invisibly) but in Rust each child is drawn at world opacity (overlaps show through). Python has an _isolation_redundant optimisation that only skips isolation when opacity==1.
rows.notes: Python include is expanded at load time (nodes/core.py:21) and instance always renders to its own Buf, so those two match. Changing the opacity rule changes pixels of existing documents, so it needs a conformance decision before porting.

rows.capability: Group pass-through with opacity multiplied down; 2.5D children share the frame camera
rows.description: A non-isolated group draws each child directly into the parent target with the group's opacity multiplied into the child's, so threeD children of plain groups project through the frame's camera/space rather than a flattened group plane.
python_evidence: scenerender/camera.py:60-68 docstring: threeD node inside threeD group flattens unless collapse=true
rows.divergence: Python passes through only when is_isolated is false (so never for opacity<1 or threeD groups); a threeD group without collapse flattens its children into one projected plane, with collapse=true children share camera space. Rust has no such flatten/collapse distinction for groups in the compositor (groups never isolate for threeD); behaviour of a threeD GROUP node itself in Rust was not traced.
rows.notes: Unverified: whether Rust applies a threeD group's own transform to its children.

rows.capability: All 35 blendType modes with published formulas
rows.description: normal and dissolve use fixed-function premultiplied over; the other 33 modes copy the backdrop under the layer and composite in the shader. W3C Compositing Level 1 formulas for separable and non-separable modes, After Effects definitions for add, subtract, divide, darker/lighter colour, linear/vivid/pin light, hard mix, stencils, silhouettes, alpha-add, behind. A test checks every mode against a CPU reference within f16 precision.
rows.divergence: All 35 formulas exist and agree for inputs in [0,1] (checked line by line: soft-light, vivid/pin/linear-light, hard-mix, divide, dodge/burn, hue/sat/color/luminosity, stencil/silhouette, alpha-add, behind). Differences: add/linear-dodge clamp the premultiplied sum to 1 in Python (Rust only plus-lighter clamps); inputs are not clamped in Python (see COMP-04); only normal and behind run on the GPU path in Python, the rest are numpy.

rows.capability: Blend input clamping and HDR behaviour
rows.description: Every mode except add, multiply and difference takes backdrop and source colours clamped to [0,1] before B(cb,cs); add/multiply/difference pass HDR values through. Working buffers are float so values above 1 survive the other operators.
rust_evidence: README GPU compositor: 'takes its inputs clamped to [0, 1]'
rows.divergence: Python never clamps cb/cs: screen of cb=2, cs=0.5 gives 1.5 in Python and 1.0 in Rust; divide, burn, soft-light sqrt etc. see unclamped HDR. Add family clamps the sum to 1 in Python but not in Rust. Identical for SDR content.
rows.notes: One np.clip in _separable plus an exemption set; the add family needs the unclamped form.

rows.capability: Luminance weights 0.3/0.59/0.11 for non-separable and darker/lighter colour; Rec.709 luma elsewhere
rows.description: Hue, saturation, color, luminosity, darker-color, lighter-color use W3C Lum = 0.3R+0.59G+0.11B. Stencil/silhouette luma, luma mattes and generators use Rec.709 0.2126/0.7152/0.0722.
rows.notes: Same ClipColor/SetLum/SetSat; zero-range SetSat returns black in both.

rows.capability: General compositing model, backdrop copy and whole-target stencils
rows.description: Non-normal modes use the W3C general formula on premultiplied colour: (1-ab)*s + (1-as)*b + as*ab*B, alpha as+ab(1-as). Stencil and silhouette modes act on the whole target (everything outside the layer is cut away) within the isolated parent.
rows.notes: Python composes tile-wise (expand_to) rather than copying the backdrop; results agree.

rows.capability: Dissolve: seeded per-pixel hash threshold
rows.description: A pixel is kept at full strength when a hash of its position and project seed is below the layer alpha: h = seed ^ x*0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 ^ y*0xC2B2AE3D27D4EB4F, MurmurHash3 64-bit finaliser, top 24 bits / 2^24.
rows.divergence: Identical hash and threshold. Coordinate origin differs for nested offscreens: Rust hashes the pixel within the current render target, Python the frame coordinate of the tile (origin=(x0,y0)). At the root target they agree.
rows.notes: Not verified numerically against Rust output.

rows.capability: Project background composited last, beneath everything (destination-over)
rows.description: The composition composites on transparency and the project background is drawn beneath everything at the end, so behind, subtract, stencils and silhouettes act on layers only.
rows.notes: For solid colour backgrounds only; see COMP-09 for paints.

rows.capability: Project background as a gradient or pattern paint (background="url(#id)")
rows.description: The project background may reference any paint (linear/radial/conic/mesh gradient or image pattern) over the document frame; it is drawn beneath everything last.
rows.searched: grep 'background' in scenerender/*.py and nodes/*.py: render.py:66-71 returns None for paint_ref(bg) and graded_background substitutes (0,0,0,1). Rendered a 64x32 scene with background=url(#bg) red->blue linear gradient via 'scenerender still': pixels (2,2) and (60,2) both (0,0,0). The 1.1 schema already types project/@background as paintType (xsd l.2845), so no schema gate.
rows.notes: Needs the paint rasterised over the frame beneath the finished frame, including in alpha outputs (frame_rgba omits the background).

rows.capability: Mask primitive shapes as signed distance fields: rect, ellipse, rounded-rect
rows.description: Rectangles, ellipses and rounded rectangles are SDFs in the node's local space with analytic antialiasing (coverage = clamp(0.5 - d/aa)); mask x/y/width/height default to the node box; radius applies to rounded-rect only.

items.name: rect
items.note: Python promotes type=rect with a radius to rounded-rect (masks.py:18); Rust kind 0 ignores radius

rows.divergence: Python rasterises the mask path with cairo (8-bit A8 coverage, in frame pixels under matrix M); Rust evaluates analytic float coverage per pixel in local space. Equivalent geometry, different quantisation (Python coverage is 8-bit).
rows.notes: Rust clamps rounded-rect radius to half the smaller side.

rows.capability: Polygon, star and SVG path masks: winding/even-odd, vertex placement, innerRadius
rows.description: Polygons, stars and SVG paths (flattened to within 1/4 px) use nonzero winding or even-odd coverage with distance to the nearest edge. Polygon and star vertices lie on the ellipse inscribed in the mask box, starting at the top and going clockwise; a star's inner vertices lie on that ellipse scaled by innerRadius (a fraction, 0.5 when absent).
python_evidence: scenerender/geometry.py:187 star() first point straight up, clockwise

items.name: polygon
items.note: min points 3 in both

items.name: star
items.note: Python min points 2, Rust 3 (edge case)

items.name: path
items.note: flatten tolerance: cairo 0.1 vs Rust 0.25 px

rows.notes: Python honours outerRoundness/innerRoundness for polygon/star shape nodes; the mask code path does not pass them, matching Rust.

rows.capability: Mask feather as Gaussian blur in local space
rows.description: Feather is a Gaussian blur of standard deviation feather in the node's local units: rectangles integrate exactly, rounded rectangles and ellipses integrate the blurred outline row by row, polygons/paths use the normal CDF of signed distance (exact along straight edges). Masks stay sharp and feather scales with the node transform.
python_evidence: scenerender/masks.py:66-68 effects.gaussian on the rasterised 8-bit coverage
rows.divergence: Python blurs the rasterised frame-space coverage with an isotropic Gaussian of sigma = feather * project scale. Under a node scale or rotation Rust's blur is anisotropic/scaled with the node (local space), Python's is constant in frame pixels. Python coverage is also 8-bit before blurring.
rows.notes: Fix options: rasterise masks in local space then warp, or blur with a per-axis sigma from M. Exact integrals are not needed for pixel parity within tolerance.

rows.capability: Mask expansion, invert and opacity
rows.description: Expansion grows or shrinks the outline by a disc; invert flips coverage; opacity scales it. Applied in local space after feather.
python_evidence: scenerender/masks.py:48-61 round-join stroke for expansion, CLEAR stroke for negative
rows.notes: Python grows with a cairo stroke in user space (local space), equivalent to the SDF offset.

rows.capability: Seven mask combine modes
rows.description: intersect (a*m), add (a+m-a*m), subtract (a*(1-m)), lighten (max), darken (min), difference (|a-m|), none (skipped). The start value is 0 when the first mask is add/lighten/difference, else 1.

items.name: none
items.note: edge case: Rust picks the start value from the first mask even if it is none

rows.capability: Track mattes: alpha, inverted alpha, luma, inverted luma
rows.description: The matte node is rendered into a texture in the target's space; alpha matte uses its alpha, luma matte the Rec.709 luma of its colour (linear), inverted modes use 1-value; the result multiplies the layer's coverage.

items.name: luma
items.note: with linearLight=false Rust decodes to linear before luma, Python weights encoded values

rows.notes: Cyclic matte references: Rust reports an error without aborting (cache_regressions.rs); Python behaviour not checked.

rows.capability: Layer-edge antialiasing by distance to the content rectangle
rows.description: Layer quads are grown ~1.5 px (3 px for 2.5D) and the shader multiplies coverage by the analytic distance to the content rectangle per axis (no MSAA).
rust_evidence: crates/sr-gpu/src/shaders.wgsl shade() flags&8 edge block, fs_texture_edge
rows.notes: Same principle (analytic coverage); pixels not compared. Warped 2.5D edges in Python use a bilinear warp that drops outside samples.

rows.capability: Working colour spaces and primaries conversion with Bradford adaptation
rows.description: Working space from colorManagement/@workingSpace else project/@workingColorSpace, from sRGB to ACEScg; primaries convert through XYZ D65 with Bradford adaptation for DCI and ACES (D60 0.32168,0.33767) whites.

items.note: DCI white 0.314,0.351 Bradford to D65 in both
