rows.capability: Transfer functions for decode/encode
rows.description: Image decode through srgb, bt1886, gamma2.2, gamma2.6, linear, PQ (203 cd/m2 reference white, BT.2408), HLG (scene light, 75% signal = 1.0), ACEScc, ACEScct and the camera logs S-Log3, LogC3, LogC4, V-Log, C-Log3, REDLog3G10, F-Log2, N-Log (each decoding to scene reflectance, 18% grey = 0.18).
rows.divergence: HLG decode: Rust = inverse OETF scene light / hlg_reference() so 75% signal -> 1.0 (scene-linear). Python = inverse_OETF^1.2 * 1000/203 (display-referred at 1000 cd/m2 peak, color.py:344). They agree near reference white (~1% apart) but differ in the curve: for scene light 0.1 Rust gives 0.377, Python 0.311. PQ identical (x10000/203).

items.name: hlg
items.note: see divergence

rows.notes: Camera-log curve constants not compared digit by digit with Rust; Python tests check them against OCIO.

rows.capability: Image decode into premultiplied working space with alpha modes and mip chain
rows.description: Images decode through asset colorSpace, transfer and alpha (straight, premultiplied, none/auto) into premultiplied working-space float values with a full box-filtered mip chain sampled trilinearly.
rows.divergence: Colour/alpha decode matches. Minification differs: Rust samples a continuous trilinear mip chain per pixel; Python picks floor(log2(1/scale)) and lets cairo filter the remainder, so downscaled images are not pixel-identical.
rows.notes: Python also keeps an exponent trick to carry HDR values (>1) through cairo.

rows.capability: Embedded colour profile (ICC matrix/TRC, H.273 CICP) honoured when colorProfile="embedded"
rows.description: With imageAsset/@colorProfile=embedded, the file's own ICC profile (matrix/TRC, mapped to a named space when it equals one) or H.273 code points take precedence over declared colorSpace/transfer; unusable profiles produce a note.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-gpu/src/resources.rs Coding, coding(), named_profile, cicp_space, cicp_transfer l.150-260
rows.searched: grep -i 'icc|cicp|nclx|iccp|colorProfile|icc_profile' in scenerender/ (only usd_materials.py:104 reads a PIL icc_profile for USD textures; nothing in image/video decode); the Python schema has no colorProfile attribute.
rows.notes: Needs the schema attribute, an ICC parser (Pillow ImageCms can supply it) and CICP parsing for PNG/AVIF/video tags.

rows.capability: linearLight="false": composite on encoded values in the working space
rows.description: With linearLight=false blending happens on encoded values (After Effects style); encoding is the working space's own default transfer (sRGB when it is linear). 50% red over blue gives (0.5,0,0.5) encoded.
python_evidence: scenerender/compositor.py:112,122 (working_primaries forced to srgb when not linear)
rows.divergence: Python: linearLight=false always works in sRGB-encoded Rec.709 regardless of workingColorSpace/colorManagement. Rust: encoded with the working space's own transfer (e.g. bt1886 for rec2020, sRGB for acescg) and in that space's primaries. Identical for the default sRGB working space.
rows.notes: Also affects luma-matte weighting (COMP-15).

rows.capability: Colour literals and paint colours into the working space
rows.description: A document colour literal is read as display sRGB (decoded with the sRGB transfer), converted from sRGB primaries to the working space and stored in the compositor's representation, so #808080 displays as 128 in any working space.
python_evidence: scenerender/paint.py (cairo sRGB sources converted via to_working)
rows.notes: The Rust README sentence 'Colour literals are working-space values in that space's own encoding' contradicts color.rs from_literal; the code (and Python) treat them as display sRGB.

rows.capability: Premultiplied RGBA16F working buffers (HDR range) end to end
rows.description: All render targets and offscreens are premultiplied RGBA16F in the working space, so HDR values, vector content, gradients and generated content stay in float through blending.
python_evidence: scenerender/raster.py Canvas.to_buf (cairo ARGB32 8-bit sRGB -> working via table)
rows.divergence: Python's tile buffers are float32 (more precision than f16) but shapes, text, paints/gradients and generator rasters are drawn by cairo in 8-bit sRGB-encoded surfaces and converted, so vector-derived content is quantised to 8 bits and cannot exceed 1.0; float only for image layers, blends, effects. Rust keeps these in f16 end to end.
rows.notes: Closing this means replacing cairo for fills/gradients with a float rasteriser.

rows.capability: Linear gradient: spread modes, units, rotation about the box centre
rows.description: Per-pixel evaluation with pad/reflect/repeat spread; object or userSpace units; rotation turns the gradient about the centre of the painted box in pixels whatever the units. Stops and attributes animate.
rows.notes: Python goes through cairo patterns (8-bit surface, stops subdivided), so values equal only within a few 8-bit levels.

rows.capability: Radial gradient: focal point, focal radius, aspect
rows.description: Focal point fx/fy (default centre), focal radius fr and aspect (x stretch about the centre). t = (len - fr)/(s - fr), where len is the distance from the focal point to the pixel and s the distance from the focal point to the end circle along that ray.
rows.divergence: Python uses cairo's two-circle gradient: circle(t) has centre f+t(c-f) and radius fr+t(r-fr). With fr=0 this equals Rust's ray formulation; with fr>0 and the focal point off-centre the two parametrisations differ (Rust scales the distance along the ray, cairo moves a circle). Focal point outside the end circle is also handled by cairo's cone semantics versus Rust's sqrt clamp.
rows.notes: Aspect and fr=0 / centred focus agree.

rows.capability: Conic gradient
rows.description: Angle measured clockwise from the top (angle attribute offsets), t = fract(angle/360), evaluated per pixel with stops and spread.
rows.notes: Spread is moot for a full turn in both.

rows.capability: Mesh gradient
rows.description: A Catmull-Rom tensor-product surface through the row x col grid for colours (in the interpolation space), edge rows/cols repeated, missing points take the nearest defined colour; positions follow the regular grid (a 2x2 mesh is bilinear in position).
rust_evidence: crates/sr-gpu/src/paint.rs MeshGradient arm (reads only point colours)
rows.divergence: Python additionally honours per-point x/y (Catmull-Rom surface through displaced points) and draws it as 8x8 cairo Coons patches per cell with linear corner colours, so it is C1-approximate; Rust ignores x/y (schema meshPointType has them) and evaluates exactly per pixel. Python's mesh default space is oklab; oklch is treated as srgb in Python and not in Rust's enum.
rows.notes: Python is ahead on point positions; parity either way is low priority.

rows.capability: Stop midpoints, interpolation spaces linear/sRGB/Oklab/OKLCh, stop ordering
rows.description: Stops interpolate premultiplication-free in the requested space (linear = working-space linear light, srgb, oklab, oklch with shorter hue); midpoint m remaps u by u^(ln0.5/ln m); stop offsets that decrease are raised to the previous one.

items.name: linear
items.note: Python linear = linear sRGB; Rust = working-space linear (differs only when working space is not sRGB)

items.name: oklch
items.note: shorter hue in both

items.name: stop ordering / offset range
items.note: Python sorts by offset and clamps to [0,1]; Rust keeps document order, raising decreasing offsets to the previous, no clamp

rows.divergence: Python approximates non-sRGB interpolation by subdividing each interval into 12 cairo stops (a few 8-bit levels of error); Rust evaluates exactly per pixel.

rows.capability: Gradient dither
rows.description: dither=true adds per-pixel noise of about half an 8-bit step (white hash noise, scaled 0.25 in linear light) before quantisation; deterministic.
rows.divergence: Python quantises to 8 bits with an 8x8 Bayer ordered threshold in device space; Rust adds hash noise of +-0.5/255 in working space and leaves quantisation to the later 8-bit conversion. Both deterministic and zero-mean; patterns differ.
rows.notes: Default dither is on in Python (ev.bool default True).

rows.capability: Pattern paint: image tiles with offset, rotation and scale
rows.description: An image tiles over the painted area with tileWidth/tileHeight (default asset size) times scale, rotation and offsetX/offsetY; sampled with mip-aware repeat.
rows.notes: Same transform order (scale, rotate, offset); Python's filter is cairo GOOD rather than trilinear mips, and the source surface is 8-bit.

rows.capability: The ten generator kinds with seeded, animatable parameters
rows.description: solid, gradient, noise, fractal-noise, cells (Worley), checkerboard, grid, stripes, film-grain, light-rays render from paint/paint2, scale, angle, evolution, octaves, contrast and seed; noise kinds mix paint2->paint in display sRGB premultiplied; gradient mixes premultiplied sRGB; patterns centre on the asset, rotate clockwise by angle and scroll by evolution periods.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/generator.py:107 field, :47 perlin3, :78 fbm, :92 worley, :232 _tile_pattern, :262 render_generator
rows.divergence: Noise kinds, cells, film-grain, light-rays use the same formulas as Rust (same octave offsets 17.3/5.1, gain 0.5, Worley jitter 0.4, ray fall-off constants). Rust applies contrast to solid/gradient/checkerboard/grid/stripes (t=clamp((t-0.5)*contrast+0.5)); Python ignores contrast for those kinds. Python draws checker/grid/stripes from an n-pixel cairo tile at output resolution (n=round(scale*eff), capped 256) so squares are rounded to whole pixels; Rust is analytic.

items.name: solid
items.note: contrast!=1 only differs in Rust

items.name: gradient
items.note: contrast ignored in Python

items.name: checkerboard
items.note: contrast ignored; pixel-rounded tile

items.name: grid
items.note: contrast ignored; line width round(0.04*n) px of tile

items.name: stripes
items.note: contrast ignored

items.name: film-grain
items.note: 3-draw average, grain size scale/100 (min 0.25)

rows.notes: Rust test name states its patterns 'follow the python renderer', consistent with this reading.

rows.capability: Generator seeding: CRC-32 seed, D24 permutation and lattices, per-frame grain seed
rows.description: Seed = CRC-32 of project seed, asset id and @seed (+'generator'); Perlin permutation by Fisher-Yates over D24 draws; Worley/grain lattices U(seed,k,pack(i,j)); film grain reseeds per composition frame (seed + frame*7919 + round(evolution*1000)*104729).
rows.notes: GPU uses the top 24 bits of the 64-bit hash; Python uses 53 bits, an invisible difference (<1e-7).

rows.capability: Generator evaluation resolution and where it runs
rows.description: Generators are evaluated per pixel on the GPU at the asset's own resolution (capped at max texture size), then used as a layer texture.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/generator.py:194 _max_spacing, :290-300 sample grid <= 2 samples/px then bilinear draw
rows.divergence: Python samples smooth fields on a coarser grid (spacing up to scale/12, scale/2^(oct-1)/6) and upsamples bilinearly through cairo, in 8-bit; film-grain at full density. Result differs from the exact per-pixel field by interpolation error.
rows.notes: Numba kernels (kernels.fbm) already exist for the CPU path.

rows.capability: 2.5D layer plane: zDepth, rotationX then rotationY about the anchor
rows.description: threeD layers place their quad at zDepth, rotate it about the anchor by rotationX then rotationY (positive rotationX turns the top edge away, positive rotationY the right edge, After Effects convention).
rows.notes: Python gets an exact homography and draws through its projective path; Rust projects the four quad corners with perspective-correct interpolation.

rows.capability: Perspective camera for 2.5D: default 60 degree horizontal fov, active camera position and rotation
rows.description: Layers project through a perspective camera centred on the frame using the active camera's fov (60 degrees horizontal by default), position and rotation, staying registered with 3D objects when the camera moves; texture coordinates interpolate perspective-correctly.
rows.notes: Python additionally supports orthographic, lens distortion and DoF on threeD layers; those were not compared with Rust here.

rows.capability: Behind-camera clipping of 2.5D layers
rows.description: A layer behind the camera is clipped (clip-space w<0 fails the rasteriser's test) rather than magnified.
python_evidence: scenerender/camera.py:50-53 docstring: returns None when the whole plane is behind the camera
scenerender/raster.py:371 'points behind the projection centre dropped'
rows.notes: A straddling plane is clipped at the eye plane in Rust and dropped per pixel in Python's warp; not compared.

rows.capability: Depth sorting of consecutive threeD siblings, back to front
rows.description: Runs of consecutive threeD siblings are drawn farthest first, sorted by their zDepth (larger z first); the sort does not cross group boundaries.
python_evidence: scenerender/compositor.py:244-247 depth_sort hook only when parent collapse=true
scenerender/camera.py:921 depth_sort (key: z attribute, then -camera-space depth)
rows.divergence: Python sorts only inside collapsed threeD groups, by (the element's z attribute, camera-space depth) with 2D nodes keeping their slots; siblings of ordinary groups and of the composition root draw in document order. Rust sorts every run of consecutive threeD siblings by zDepth descending, independent of camera position.
rows.notes: A parity change alters document-order stacking of 3D layers in existing documents.

rows.capability: Content-hash caching of offscreens and mattes
rows.description: Offscreens and mattes are keyed by a hash of node state relative to the target, source time of time-dependent assets and animated paint/generator values; an unchanged subtree reuses last frame's texture; offscreens of sized nodes live in the node's own space so moving, rotating or fading reuses the texture.
rows.divergence: Python caches CPU rasters of static nodes (and runs of consecutive normal-blend siblings) per one-second window, proven static by analysing the node, its references and files; moving placements are bilinearly resampled from a raster drawn 15% oversized (approximate, softens edges; SCENERENDER_RASTER_CACHE=0 renders exactly). Rust hashes content every frame and reuses exactly. Python excludes animated content, expressions and media from the cache entirely.
rows.notes: Behavioural equivalence (same pixels with and without cache) is already a property of Python's exact mode.

rows.capability: Root prefix snapshot
rows.description: At the root the longest run of leading draws unchanged between the last two frames is stored as a snapshot; the next frame restores it with one copy and draws only what follows, bit-identical to a fresh render.
rows.searched: grep -i 'prefix|snapshot' in scenerender/compositor.py, render.py, gpucomp.py: only compositor._snapshot (copy of the backdrop for transmissive 3D refraction) and Python's _rc runs (consecutive static normal-blend siblings cached as one raster, compositor.py:238-290); no previous-frame draw-list diffing.
rows.notes: Python's run cache covers a similar case approximately (static leading siblings) but is window-based and resampling.

rows.capability: GPU compositor architecture: headless wgpu, one command buffer per frame, frames stay on the GPU
rows.description: A FrameGraph is planned on the CPU into one draw list per render target and submitted as a single command buffer on Vulkan/Metal/DX12/GL; masks, paints, generators, blends and edges all run in shaders; Frame stays on the GPU, read() copies back.
rows.divergence: Python is a CPU numpy/cairo compositor; an optional moderngl GL layer holds frames and cache tiles in float textures and accelerates only source-over, behind, warps, 3D layers, single-pass shaders and the 8-bit/yuv conversion. All other blend modes, masks, mattes, paints, generators and effects chains run on the CPU. Documents with adjustment layers keep the frame on the CPU (gpucomp docstring). No wgpu; CUDA/CuPy kernels and Numba stand in for acceleration.
rows.notes: This is an architectural choice rather than a behavioural gap: most rows above are semantic parity on the CPU path.

rows.capability: Golden-frame comparison metrics: PSNR and CIEDE2000
rows.description: sr_gpu::golden compares frames by PSNR and CIEDE2000 (Sharma-Wu-Dalal verified); a frame passes at PSNR >= 50 dB and max dE2000 <= 1.
rows.searched: grep -rniE 'psnr|ciede|delta.?e2000|ssim|golden|bless' over scenerender/ and tests/ (*.py, *.md): no metric implementation; tests assert hand-computed pixel values or CPU-vs-GPU equality within one 8-bit code (tests/test_gpucomp.py:58); CLI sub-commands are still, render, check, validate, coverage.
rows.notes: A ~150 line module plus a CLI/compare helper.

rows.capability: Golden-frame test harness: blessing, provenance, diff output

rows.capability: Bare-render-then-composite model: effects run on the node drawn without opacity/blend/masks/matte; masks and matte cut the EFFECTED image
rows.description: A node with effects renders once 'bare' into an offscreen covering its box plus the effects' reach, the chain runs in document order, then the result composites with the node's opacity, blend, masks and matte. Masks and mattes therefore cut the effected image (a glow is cut by the mask).
rust_evidence: README.md 'Effects, transitions and colour finishing' para 2
README Limitations: 'Masks and mattes apply after a node's effects'
python_evidence: scenerender/compositor.py:1317-1334 finish_node: deform -> DoF -> masks -> effects -> matte
rows.divergence: Rust: effects first, then masks AND matte cut the result. Python: masks are applied to the raster BEFORE the effect stack (so glow/shadow/blur spill beyond the mask edge and effects see a pre-cut input); only the track matte is applied after effects. Opacity/blend are applied after in both.
rows.notes: Reordering is a few lines in finish_node but the raster cache signatures (_render_cached, _effect_signature) and mask-aware crop logic must follow.

rows.capability: Colour grading operations (color-grade, lift-gamma-gain, cdl, levels, curves, white-balance, exposure, hue-saturation, tonemap)
rows.description: Per-pixel ops on straight values. color-grade: encoded sRGB (e-0.5)*contrast+0.5+brightness then linear luma saturation. lift-gamma-gain on encoded values: e*gain + lift*(1-e), then pow(1/gamma). cdl: encoded pow(max(e*slope+offset,0),power) then Rec.709 saturation. levels: encoded in/out black/white + inverse gamma on rgb or one channel. curves: Catmull-Rom through points sampled at 256 entries, alpha channel -> master curve (reported). white-balance: temperature/tint on a -100..100 scale as linear gains (1+0.3t, 1-0.3g, 1-0.3t). exposure: linear x 2^ev. hue-saturation: HSV hue shift, multiplicative HSV saturation (clamped), brightness added to V.

items.name: color-grade
items.note: Python D9: linear exposure(attr) -> 0.18-pivot power contrast -> saturation -> +brightness in working space; Rust: encoded-space linear contrast about 0.5 + brightness, no exposure

items.name: lift-gamma-gain
items.note: Python applies gain AFTER gamma ((e+lift(1-e))^(1/g) * gain); Rust applies gain before gamma ((e*gain + lift(1-e))^(1/g))

items.name: cdl
items.note: Python clamps e*slope+offset to [0,1] before power; Rust only clamps at 0 (values above 1 survive)

items.name: levels
items.note: same in/out/gamma maths; Python adds alpha/luma channels

items.name: curves
items.note: Python piecewise-linear np.interp, alpha channel curves alpha; Rust Catmull-Rom spline into a 256-entry table, alpha curve treated as master

items.name: white-balance
items.note: Python treats temperature as kelvin (CIE daylight/Planckian -> D65 via Bradford, tint on CIE 1960 v); Rust temperature/tint are +-100 style linear channel gains

items.name: exposure
items.note: linear x 2^exposure

items.name: hue-saturation
items.note: Python rotates hue preserving HSV s/v, saturation = luma blend, brightness added to RGB; Rust HSV h/s scaling clamped, brightness added to V

items.name: tonemap
items.note: see FX-13

rows.divergence: see items
rows.notes: Python also fuses lift-gamma-gain through kernels.display_chain; Rust fuses up to four consecutive pointwise ops.

What is absent is only the in-scene 8-deep layer stack and mask/matte commands inside one batched vector scene. The 'no Python equivalent of the six mask modes' wording should be narrowed to 'no in-scene layer stack'.
rows.notes: Pixel parity of shape edges against the Rust golden frames needs a tolerance; a numpy exact-area rasteriser would be the only path to identical coverage and is a new subsystem. Python tests: test_core.py test_svg_path_and_trim_and_sampler, test_assets.py shapes.

rows.capability: Batched vector scene: consecutive simple shape/vector nodes rasterise as one job in target pixel space, cached by hash of the nodes
rows.description: Consecutive shape/vector nodes with normal blend and no mask/matte/clip/3D placement merge into one scene at screen resolution, drawn with one quad, cached by node-hash so still vector art is free after frame 1. Other vector nodes rasterise in local space at on-screen scale and composite like image layers.
python_evidence: scenerender/nodes/core.py:172 render_shape (one cairo canvas per node, rasterised at M)
rows.divergence: Rust merges runs of simple shapes into one tile-encoded job. Python rasterises each shape node into its own cairo tile and composites it; a node-level raster cache exists for static content but there is no cross-node batching, so 2,000 shapes cost 2,000 tile composites. Output is equivalent for normal-blend shapes up to AA differences.
rows.notes: Performance feature, not semantics; matters for the perf_vector scenario (2,000 stroked shapes at 1080p60).

rows.capability: Rect/rounded-rect geometry with per-corner cornerRadii (TL TR BR BL) CSS-style joint scale-down; ellipse; line
rows.description: rect/rounded-rect uses radius or 4-value cornerRadii. When adjacent radii exceed a side, ALL radii are scaled by the smallest f = min(side/(r_i+r_j)) as in CSS. ellipse fills the box; line runs across the middle of its box left to right.
rows.divergence: Rust: radii scaled down together by the CSS rule (e.g. 100x50 box, radii (60,0,0,0): r0 becomes 50 because h/(r3+r0)=0.83 and w/(r0+r1)=1.67). Python: each radius clamped independently to min(r, w/2, h/2) (same case gives 25). Equal for uniform radius that fits and for sums that already fit; differs when a radius exceeds half the shorter side or adjacent radii overflow. cornerRadii accepted with <4 values: Python pads with the last value, Rust ignores the list unless it has exactly 4 entries (falls back to radius). Ellipse and line are identical (verified by running geometry.box_outline).
rows.notes: One-function fix in geometry.box_outline/rounded_rect. [review] Verified both sides by reading code: Rust shapes.rs::rect scales ALL radii by min(w/(r0+r1), h/(r1+r2), w/(r2+r3), h/(r3+r0)) filtered to finite and capped at 1; Python geometry.box_outline clamps each radius independently to min(r, w/2, h/2). Example (100x50, r0=60): Rust 50, Python 25. Rust sr-gpu vector.rs:108 uses cornerRadii only when it has exactly 4 entries. Row stands.

rows.capability: Polygon and star (Lottie polystar geometry): first tip up, roundness tangent length, outerRadius/innerRadius units, inscribed-ellipse in non-square boxes
rows.description: Vertices lie on the ellipse inscribed in the box, or on a circle of outerRadius units; star inner vertices on a circle of innerRadius units (not box-scaled) or the outer figure x0.5. Roundness handles are tangent to the ellipse with length round*TAU/(2n) (star, n = 2*points) or round*TAU/(4n) (polygon) times the radius derivative. points clamped (polygon>=3, star>=2, max 10,000).
rows.divergence: Geometry for roundness 0 matches (first tip up, same vertex placement, default inner = outer/2, non-square box stretches the figure). Roundness differs: Python handle = 4/3*tan(seg/4)*r*roundness with seg = full vertex spacing angle, which is about angle/3 for both polygon and star; Rust uses angle/2 (star) and angle/4 (polygon). So rounded stars are rounder in Rust, rounded polygons less round. When outerRadius is absent and innerRadius is given on a non-square box, Python scales innerRadius by the box stretch (sx, sy) whereas Rust keeps it a circle of innerRadius units. Python has no MAX_POINTS cap.
rows.notes: Both implementations accept the same attribute names; only constants/scaling differ. [review] Verified: Rust handle length k = TAU/(2n_total) for star (n_total = 2*points) and TAU/(4n) for polygon, multiplied by round; Python uses 4/3*tan(seg/4)*r*round with seg = 2pi/count for both. Rust clamps points to [3|2, 10000] (MAX_POINTS), Python has no cap. Row stands.

rows.capability: Path shapes from SVG path data (M L H V C S Q T A Z, relative and absolute, arcs to beziers)
rows.description: shape=path parses @path with every SVG command; quadratics, arcs and smooth continuations; parse errors are reported.
rows.notes: Python silently stops parsing on malformed input (unknown command is skipped / loop ends) instead of returning an error; Python emits quads as cubics, Rust keeps Seg::Quad (no visible difference). Error reporting is validation territory: see schema parity work.

rows.capability: SVG-2 outline start points for closed shapes (ellipse at 3 o'clock, rect at x+radius,y; clockwise on screen) - where trim and dashes begin
rows.description: Closed primitive outlines start where SVG 2 starts them so trim paths and dash phase line up with CSS/SVG expectations.
python_evidence: scenerender/geometry.py:158 box_outline (starts top-left after rounding, clockwise)
scenerender/geometry.py:179 ellipse (starts cx+rx,cy; goes down first)
CONVENTIONS 5.21 cited in the geometry docstring
rows.notes: Rust also has ellipse_top (Lottie ellipse starts at the top) for Lottie; Python delegates Lottie to rlottie.

rows.capability: Stroke geometry: butt/round/square caps, miter (miterLimit)/round/bevel joins, solid winding at sharp turns, non-uniform-scale SVG pen
rows.description: Strokes are built as closed outlines filled nonzero; miter limit per SVG ratio; inner joins pass through the vertex so overlap keeps a solid winding. Used by shapes, vector assets, Lottie and SVG.
rows.notes: Same semantics through cairo's stroker (miter limit is the SVG miter-length/width ratio in both). Outline polygons differ at the sub-pixel level because cairo tessellates round joins/caps differently; classify as the same DIVERGENT-by-design rasteriser difference as VEC-01, not a feature gap. miterLimit default 4 in both.

rows.capability: strokePosition inside/outside (stroke 2x width, keep inside/outside the fill) and paintOrder (fill-stroke | stroke-fill)
rows.description: inside/outside strokes draw twice the width and keep the part inside or outside the fill region (fill rule respected); paintOrder picks fill-first or stroke-first. Applies per repeater/merge item.
python_evidence: scenerender/nodes/core.py:115-170 draw_paths (clip_preserve for inside; push_group + CLEAR fill for outside; order tuple)
rows.notes: Same algorithm (2x width, clip/clear against the fill region). For trimmed open outlines both close the fill region implicitly. fillRule defaults: shape nonzero, vector asset evenodd in both.

rows.capability: Dash patterns: odd-length patterns repeat twice (SVG), dashOffset, zero-length dashes, dash on outline start, over-dense dashes drawn solid
rows.description: dash is a list; an odd count is doubled; dash phase starts at the outline start; patterns with more than 2^20 dashes fall back to solid.
python_evidence: verified by running cairo set_dash([10,5,2]): on/off sequence 10,5,2,10,5,2 = SVG doubling
rows.notes: cairo cycles the array while toggling on/off, which equals SVG's doubled odd pattern. No dash-count safety cap in Python (dash density is cairo's problem). Negative entries clamped to 0 in both.

rows.capability: Trim paths on shapes: trimStart/trimEnd fractions, trimOffset in degrees (360 = full length), wrap seam join
rows.description: Trim cuts the outline before stroking (and before fill): start/end are fractions of length (swapped if start>end), trimOffset is DEGREES (offset/360 of the length) and wraps; a wrapped range on a closed outline joins across the seam.
python_evidence: verified: geometry.trim(rect 100x100, 0, 0.5, 0.25) starts at (100,0) i.e. a quarter of the perimeter
rows.divergence: Rust: trimOffset is in degrees, shape.trimOffset=90 shifts the window by a quarter of the length. Python: trimOffset is in turns, so 90 means 90 laps (wraps to no shift) and 0.25 shifts a quarter; the same document attribute produces different geometry. Also: Python does not swap start>end (empty result), and the wrapped range on a closed outline yields two open pieces (a visible cap seam) rather than one joined piece.
rows.notes: Fix: divide trimOffset by 360 in nodes/core.shape_paths and join the seam. Python's own trim *modifier* already uses degrees (modifiers._trim_range), so the two Python entry points are inconsistent today.

rows.capability: Trim mode on shapes: simultaneous (each subpath) vs sequential (all subpaths as one outline), including trimOffset
rows.description: trimMode=simultaneous (default) trims every subpath by the same fractions; sequential treats all subpaths of all items as one outline in order, offset and wrap applying to the combined length.
rows.divergence: Python's sequential branch of geometry.trim computes start/end against cumulative length but never applies `offset` (and no wrap), so trimOffset is silently ignored when trimMode=sequential. Simultaneous mode applies offset (in turns, see VEC-10).
rows.notes: Default modes agree (simultaneous). [review] Confirmed by reading geometry.trim: the sequential branch computes s/e from start*total and end*total and never adds `offset` or wraps. Also early return at line 341 (end-start>=1) happens before the offset is applied, so a full-length trim with offset is a no-op in both modes (harmless). Rust only trims when ts>0 or te<1, same effect.

rows.capability: Pattern paints fill and stroke shapes
rows.description: Pattern paints (tile of another asset/node) draw through the coverage of the parts that use them. Limitation: pattern-filled parts draw above other paints and ignore the shape's own matte.
python_evidence: scenerender/paint.py:1 (url(#id) patterns), paint.set_source used by draw_paths for fill and stroke (nodes/core.py:115-170)
rows.notes: Python uses a plain cairo SurfacePattern source so it has no 'draws above other paints / ignores matte' limitation; pattern semantics (paint area box, transform) belong to the paint/gradient area and were not compared pixel-wise.

rows.capability: The nine shape modifiers applied in document order (repeater, offset-path, pucker-bloat, zig-zag, twist, round-corners, wiggle-path, merge, trim)
rows.description: Each <shapeModifier type=...> transforms the shape's items in order. Repeater pivots on the box centre; zig-zag/pucker/round-corners work on bezier contours; wiggle displaces along the normal at 'detail' points per 100 px using D24 noise; merge combines by coverage; trim cuts the combined outline.
rows.divergence: All nine exist; pucker-bloat and round-corners agree, the other seven differ (see items). Python additionally keeps per-path opacity (OpPath) and draws each repeater copy as its own group.
rows.notes: A cross-engine document using any of repeater/zig-zag/twist/wiggle/offset-path/trim modifiers will render differently. Rust has caps (MAX_REPEATER_ITEMS 65,536, MAX_RIDGES 1024, MAX_WIGGLE_POINTS 65,536) Python lacks.

items.name: repeater
items.note: Rust pivots on the shape box centre; Python pivots on the shape's anchorX/anchorY (schema default 0 => top-left unless the node sets an anchor). Opacity lerp startOpacity..endOpacity, offset, composite below, copies=floor are the same. scale<=0: Rust clamps to 1e-6, Python 0. (modifiers.py:182)

items.name: offset-path
items.note: Rust offsets each closed contour with a one-sided stroke (join per mode, miter limit 4); open subpaths pass through unchanged. Python builds the nonzero-filled region and uses shapely buffer (exact for self-intersections/vanishing parts) and gives open subpaths a parallel curve (modifiers.py:281). Python is the more exact one; results agree on simple convex contours.

items.name: pucker-bloat
items.note: Vertices move toward the centroid by amount%, tangents the opposite way, same formula (modifiers.py:310). Centroid = mean of vertices; Python uses segment start points (omits the last vertex of open paths).

items.name: zig-zag
items.note: Rust: 2*ridges samples per segment alternating 0 and +size along the normal (one-sided), smooth uses tangent handles of len/(4*ridges). Python: alternating +size/-size (symmetric), ridges per segment, smooth via Catmull-Rom (modifiers.py:333).

items.name: twist
items.note: Rust pivots on the box centre with R = max distance of any point to that centre and subdivides edges to 4 px first. Python pivots on the bbox centre of the flattened path, R = max distance, no subdivision so straight edges stay straight (modifiers.py:363).

items.name: round-corners
items.note: Radius amount clamped to half the adjacent edges, sharp (handle-less) corner vertices only, K=0.5519 (Rust) vs 0.5523 (Python); collinear and curve-adjacent corners skipped in both (modifiers.py:389).

items.name: wiggle-path
items.note: Rust: points = length*detail/100 (detail per 100 px), offset along the normal by size*smooth_noise(d24, 1D value noise, smoothstep). Python: detail = points per original segment, displaces in x and y with 3D quintic value noise (physics.vnoise) and Catmull-Rom smooths the result (modifiers.py:436). Same seed hashing family (D24) but different noise function and point density.

items.name: merge
items.note: See VEC-14: Python returns one boolean region path (shapely); Rust keeps operands and combines by coverage at fill time.

items.name: trim (modifier)
items.note: Rust: amount clamped to 0..100 (negative = no trim), offset degrees, mode attr honoured (sequential unless mode=simultaneous). Python: negative amount trims from the start instead, `mode` ignored (always sequential across paths with wrap) (modifiers.py:502-540).

rows.capability: merge modifier: combine fills by coverage (add/subtract/intersect/exclude); strokes follow each operand's outline
rows.description: merge keeps every path of the shape as an operand with a MaskOp (Add, Subtract, Intersect, Difference=exclude). The fill is rendered as a compound mask stack over the group bounding box; strokes are drawn per operand outline (not around the union).
python_evidence: scenerender/modifiers.py:471 merge_paths (shapely union/difference/intersection/symmetric_difference, returns one path with opposite-winding holes)
rows.divergence: Fill result is the same region. Python replaces all operands by the boolean outline, so strokes outline the merged boundary (and strokes of subtracted operands disappear); Rust strokes each operand's own outline, including parts hidden inside the union. Python needs shapely; Rust has no dependency. Python's first path is the base and later ones fold left, Rust the same.
rows.notes: If strokes on merged shapes matter, Python would need to keep operand outlines for stroking.

rows.capability: SVG import (core): paths, fills, strokes with dashes, linear/radial gradients (sRGB interpolation), paint order, group opacity
rows.description: <vector shape=svg> imports through usvg once per tolerance step into a Scene in SVG user units; colours convert sRGB to working space.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/vector.py:58 _render_rsvg (librsvg through ctypes on the pycairo context)
rows.divergence: Python renders with librsvg (HAVE_RSVG is True in this environment) when PyGObject Rsvg 2.0 is importable; otherwise a minimal fallback draws only path/rect/circle/ellipse/line/poly*/g with solid fill/stroke (no gradients, no dashes, no clip) and the registry level drops to PARTIAL. Rendering is rasterised through cairo at the asset box scale, not imported as a reusable path Scene, so SVGs cannot be deformed point-wise or trimmed as geometry. Both fit the viewBox per preserveAspectRatio.
rows.notes: Environment-dependent: parity holds only where librsvg is installed.

rows.capability: SVG clip paths -> masks in the referencing element's space; <mask> -> luminance or alpha matte
rows.description: clip-path content becomes intersecting masks (nested clip-path: outer clip only, reported); <mask> becomes a luma or alpha matte layer.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/vector.py:58 _render_rsvg (librsvg implements clipPath/mask natively, including nested clips)
fallback subset skips clipPath/mask (vector.py:164 tag list)
rows.notes: Via librsvg only; Python is more complete (nested clip-path honoured).

rows.capability: SVG unsupported-feature policy: text, filters, embedded images, pattern paints, mix-blend-mode reported per node and skipped
rows.description: usvg-based import skips these, and records each skipped feature in Svg.skipped so the evaluator can report it.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/vector.py:58-70 (librsvg draws text, filters, images, patterns, mix-blend-mode)
no skipped-feature reporting anywhere in vector.py
rows.divergence: DIVERGENT-by-design (superset): librsvg renders text, filters, images, patterns and blend modes, so a document using them looks correct in Python and has gaps in Rust. Python never reports skipped features; the fallback subset silently drops everything not in its list. Intentionally not a gap to close in Python except for the reporting of fallback-subset skips.
rows.notes: Searched vector.py for warn_once/skipped; only a missing-file warning exists.

rows.capability: Lottie keyframes: Bezier easing, hold keys, spatial tangents (to/ti)
rows.description: Own evaluator for keyframed numbers/colours/shapes with cubic-bezier easing handles, hold keys and spatial position tangents.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/lottie.py:1-60 (rlottie renders; Python only prepares JSON)
rlottie parseKeyFrame<VPointF, Position> (spatial tangents) in librlottie.so; Python's own lottie_value/_bez_y (lottie.py:168-231) is used for slot/text paths
rows.notes: Delegated to rlottie 1.3.8 (rlottie_python): easing/hold/spatial supported. Not verified pixel-for-pixel against the Rust evaluator.

rows.capability: Lottie transforms: parenting, skew/skew-axis, split position
rows.description: Layer transforms with parent chains, skew (sk/sa) and split-dimension position.
python_evidence: probe with rlottie 1.3.8: parenting honoured, split position honoured, skew (sk/sa) has NO effect (pixels identical to unskewed)
rows.divergence: rlottie ignores layer skew; Rust applies it. Parenting and split position verified working in rlottie.
rows.notes: Closing the skew gap means pre-baking skew into per-frame matrices or replacing rlottie; Python's text-to-shape converter handles sk only for text animators (lottie.py:987).

rows.capability: Lottie precomps: clipped to size, time stretch (sr), time remap (tm)
rows.description: Precomp layers evaluate nested compositions, clipped to the precomp w x h, with layer time stretch and time remap; cycles are drawn once and fan-out is budgeted (65,536).
python_evidence: rlottie probes: precomp animation timing correct, stretch sr=2 correct, clip to precomp w honoured; static time-remap tm=0.5s did NOT hold the nested comp at 0.5s (nested position followed the outer frame)
scenerender/assets/lottie.py:246 scale_time (sub-frame scaling of ip/op/st/t, check whether tm is scaled)
rows.divergence: Time remap is unconfirmed/not honoured by rlottie for a static tm property in my probe; stretch and clip behave as in Rust. No recursion/fan-out budget in Python (rlottie's own behaviour).
rows.notes: Keyframed tm not probed (see unverified).

rows.capability: Lottie shape layers: solids, groups, rect, ellipse, polystar, path; fills, strokes with dashes, linear/radial gradients with opacity stops
rows.description: Shape layer item evaluation, styles applying to shapes above them, gradients with alpha stops and dashes.
python_evidence: rlottie parsers present (parseRectObject, parseEllipseObject, parsePolystarObject, parseGFillObject, parseGStrokeObject, parseDashProperty)
probes: dash (stroke 'd' array) applied; gradient fill alpha stop 0 to 0.5 rendered (alpha 0 at left to ~139 at right); star with is/os roundness changes pixels
rows.notes: Verified existence by rlottie probes; exact polystar-roundness tangent constants not compared to Rust (rlottie follows lottie-web).

rows.capability: Lottie shape operators: trim, repeater, round corners, merge, pucker-bloat, zig-zag, twist, offset path
rows.description: Operators acting across a group (Lottie's shape model), evaluated by the same Modifier code as native shapes.
python_evidence: rlottie 1.3.8 library strings: Trim, Repeater, RoundedCorner parsers only
probes: zz, pb, tw, op, mm items leave pixels identical to the unmodified shape; tm, rp, rd change pixels
rows.divergence: rlottie supports trim, repeater and round corners and silently ignores merge paths, pucker/bloat, zig-zag, twist and offset path; Rust applies all eight. The Python package already has native implementations of those operators for shapes (modifiers.py) but they are not wired into Lottie.
rows.notes: Parity needs either a native Lottie shape evaluator or pre-expanding unsupported operators in the JSON before handing it to rlottie.
