rows.capability: Lottie masks in all modes (add, subtract, intersect, lighten, darken, difference) and track mattes (alpha/luma, inverted)
rows.description: Layer masks with every Lottie mode and opacity/invert, plus the four track-matte types, drawn by the tile rasteriser.
python_evidence: rlottie probes: mask modes a, s, i, f give correct areas (400, 3200, 400, 400); mask modes l (lighten) and d (darken) make the layer disappear (0 coverage)
track matte tt=1..4 (alpha, inverted alpha, luma, inverted luma): 394/3150/394/3150 px - all four work
rows.divergence: Track mattes: present. Masks: add/subtract/intersect/difference present; lighten and darken are not supported by rlottie (layer is not drawn).
rows.notes: Mask feather/expansion not probed. [review] Lottie lighten/darken are MISSING only through rlottie (assets/lottie.py never reads or rewrites masksProperties modes beyond text layers at line 705). Python's native masks.py already supports lighten and darken for node masks, so a Lottie pre-pass could reuse that logic. Not a missing Python capability overall.

items.name: mask lighten
items.note: probe: layer vanishes

items.name: mask darken
items.note: probe: layer vanishes

rows.capability: Lottie markers and "start,end" frame segments; source time drives the frame and holds at the segment end
rows.description: @segment picks a marker (cm, tm, dr) or an explicit frame range; layer source time maps to the frame, held at the end.
rows.notes: Python uses sub-frame scaling (SUBFRAMES=8) for fractional frames; Rust evaluates continuous frames. Unknown segment: Python warns and plays the whole range, Rust segment() returns None (caller decides).

rows.capability: dotLottie archives (choose animation by id)
rows.description: A .lottie zip is read with hardened zip limits; animation attribute selects animations/<id>.json or a/<id>.json.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/lottie.py:96 _read_source (zipfile; manifest activeAnimationId/initial.animation, animations/ and a/, embedded images)
rows.notes: Python reads with stdlib zipfile and has no entry-count/inflated-size caps (zip-bomb hardening is Rust-only). Python additionally honours the manifest's active animation.

rows.capability: Lottie <slot id value> overrides (sid properties): numbers, comma lists, #RRGGBB[AA] colours, JSON property
rows.description: Overrides the property naming the slot through sid; also root "slots" table.
rows.divergence: Python is a superset (named layers/shape items, text documents, image assets, var(--token) colours, 'r,g,b,a' colours) but does not accept a JSON-valued override; a JSON value falls through to parse_color and is dropped. Rust accepts JSON property objects.
rows.notes: Python warns once when a slot matches nothing.

rows.capability: Lottie expressions, images, text, effects: reported and skipped
rows.description: Layer types and features the evaluator does not draw are collected into Lottie.skipped (image layer, text layer, layer effects, expressions with keyframed fallback, layer type N, recursive precomps).
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/lottie.py:778 convert_text_layers (text layers converted to shape layers with Pango, animators, text on path, embedded glyphs)
scenerender/assets/lottie.py:969 warn_once('lottie-expression') only for text-selector expressions
rows.divergence: DIVERGENT-by-design (superset): Python draws images and text layers (a substantial text-animator implementation) that Rust skips. Expressions are not evaluated in either engine, but Python does not report them (only text-selector expression failures) and does not report effects/layer styles that rlottie ignores. Reporting channel (Rust: per-node skipped list) is absent.
rows.notes: Parity target is the report, not the feature: Python could scan the JSON for ty/ef/x keys and warn_once like Rust.

rows.capability: Deform modifiers: application model (vector outlines point-wise after subdivision; raster layers as deformed 32x32 grid mesh; centres default to box centre, radii to half the smaller side)
rows.description: Vector content deforms its flattened outline point-by-point after subdividing long edges; image/video layers draw as a 32x32 grid mesh keeping rest coordinates so masks stay in layer space. An image/video with both a deformer and 2.5D placement draws undeformed.
python_evidence: scenerender/deform.py:862 apply_deform (inverse-map resample of the rendered node tile, GRID=4 px per sample, bilinear)
rows.divergence: DIVERGENT-by-design: Python resamples the already-rasterised tile through the inverse of the composite map for every node kind (so strokes/gradients are resampled rather than re-stroked), Rust deforms geometry for vectors and uses a mesh for raster. Defaults differ: bulge/pinch default radius is min(w,h)/2 in both, but twist/ripple/spherize default to half the diagonal in Python (deform.py:80 _common) and min(w,h)/2 in Rust (ripple: no radius = no falloff).
rows.notes: Interaction with 2.5D (threeD) placement not verified in Python (see unverified).

rows.capability: The 14 deformers (bend, twist, wave, squash, stretch, mesh-warp, puppet, skin, bulge, pinch, spherize, ripple, turbulence, corner-pin)
rows.description: Point maps over the node's local box with amount/axis/frequency/phase/radius/centre attributes; chained in document order.
rows.divergence: All 14 exist, but most use different units/axes/formulas, so one document renders differently in the two engines (details per item). Only corner-pin matches exactly.
rows.notes: Highest-risk conventions to align: squash/stretch/bulge/pinch/spherize amount units (percent vs fraction), bend/wave axis meaning, ripple frequency units, mesh-warp interpolation.

items.name: bend
items.note: Rust: axis=y (default) bends the horizontal centre line (extent = width); Python: axis=y bends the vertical centre line (along = height, deform.py:95). Axis meaning is swapped; sign conventions follow arc radius extent/theta in both.

items.name: twist
items.note: Rust: rotation amount*(1-d/r)^2 inside r, default r = min(w,h)/2. Python: same quadratic falloff but default R = half the box diagonal (deform.py:124).

items.name: wave
items.note: Rust: axis=y (default) displaces y by sin(f*x/w); axis=x displaces x by sin(f*y/h). Python: axis=x displaces y by sin(f*x/w), axis=y displaces x by sin(f*y/h) (deform.py:140): axis labels swapped.

items.name: squash
items.note: Rust: area-preserving scale 1-amount (amount is a fraction); Python: 1-amount/100 (percent) (deform.py:152).

items.name: stretch
items.note: Rust: 1+amount (fraction); Python: 1+amount/100 (percent).

items.name: mesh-warp
items.note: Rust: bicubic Catmull-Rom over the rows x cols control offsets; Python: bilinear (deform.py:248, note says so).

items.name: puppet
items.note: See VEC-30.

items.name: skin
items.note: See VEC-33/VEC-34.

items.name: bulge
items.note: Rust: scale 1+amount*(1-d/R)^2 (amount a fraction); Python: r*(1+a*(1-(r/R)^2)^2) with a=amount/100 (deform.py:180) - different falloff and units.

items.name: pinch
items.note: Same as bulge with the sign inverted in both engines.

items.name: spherize
items.note: Same hemisphere map r -> R*sin(pi/2*r/R) blended by amount; Rust amount clamped to -1..1 (fraction), Python amount/100 (deform.py:193).

items.name: ripple
items.note: Rust: sin(TAU*(d*frequency/100 - phase/360)), linear falloff only when radius is set; Python: frequency = rings per radius, quadratic falloff, default radius half diagonal (deform.py:203).

items.name: turbulence
items.note: Rust: 2D smooth value noise built on D24 1D noise (seed, channel=row); Python: 3-octave fbm (physics.fbm), phase as the z slice. Both amount px, frequency per 100 px, seeded (deform.py:212).

items.name: corner-pin
items.note: Exact homography of the box to the 8 corners in both (deform.py:223).

rows.capability: Puppet deformer: as-rigid-as-possible (Sorkine-Alexa) over a 16-cell grid, 12 fixed iterations from rest; position/bend/starch pins
rows.description: Pins at restX/restY with x/y offset; position pins are soft constraints (weight 1e4), bend pins also fix the rotation of their cell, starch pins stiffen cells within amount cell widths. Result is a pure function of the pins (deterministic).
python_evidence: scenerender/deform.py:435 build_puppet (24 cells across, ARAP_ITERS=32, uniform edge weights, Procrustes initial rotation, bend rotation fixed within 1.5 cells, starch weights x(1+20*amount*gauss(2 cells)))
rows.divergence: Same algorithm family and pin kinds, different constants: grid 16 vs ~24 cells on the long side, 12 vs 32 iterations, Rust starts each solve from the rest pose with identity rotations, Python from a Procrustes/bend-pin initial rotation; starch radius and falloff differ (Rust linear within amount*2 cells, Python Gaussian), Python pin weight is 1e4*amount, Rust a flat 1e4. Pin positions are satisfied in both; the interior deformation differs.
rows.notes: Python is the more rigid for large rotations (more iterations). Matching Rust exactly requires adopting its constants and iteration scheme.

rows.capability: Skeleton nodes: bones with x, y, rotation, length, scaleX/Y relative to the parent bone, any listed order, animated
rows.description: A skeleton is a node whose bones pose each frame; bone local = T(x,y) R(rotation) S(sx,sy) in the parent bone's space; world poses via parent chain; bones may be animated like any element.
python_evidence: scenerender/deform.py:557 skeleton_pose (rest = un-animated, pose = animated + IK)
rows.notes: Python's rest pose is the un-animated attribute values (ev.base); Rust 'rest' likewise. Python only evaluates a skeleton on demand from a skin deformer (no stand-alone skeleton node output).

rows.capability: IK solvers on bone chains: one-bone aim, two-bone analytic with bendPositive, FABRIK for longer chains, zero-length base bones skipped, influence
rows.description: ik solves the chain from the constrained bone up to the root: one bone aims; two bones use the law-of-cosines solution (bendPositive side); more use FABRIK (32 iterations); zero-length bones at the base are skipped; influence blends rotations the short way.
python_evidence: scenerender/deform.py:573 _skeleton_ik (effector via @point, chain = effector + ancestors, else deepest leaf; influence scales the delta angle)
rows.divergence: Same two-bone and FABRIK maths. Differences: Python has no explicit zero-length-base skipping (two_bone returns unchanged when l1 or l2 < 1e-9, so a zero-length first bone disables a 2-joint solve instead of leaving the remaining bone to aim), influence scales the rotation delta linearly (equal to Rust's short-way blend for deltas under 180 deg). Chain definition differs, see VEC-35.
rows.notes: Core solvers are shared by node IK and skeleton IK in Python.

rows.capability: Skin weights from @weights JSON {"points":[[x,y]...],"weights":[{"boneId":w}...]} in skeleton space, nearest-sample lookup
rows.description: Skeleton @weights file gives explicit weights at sample points in skeleton space; each vertex takes the nearest sample's weights. Unreadable file or unknown bone is E17.
python_evidence: scenerender/deform.py:624 load_weights (requires "bones" list + "weights" rows and "vertices" or "grid"; keys 'format','version','space' optional)
rows.divergence: Different file format and interpolation: a Rust file has no "bones" array and uses key "points"; Python raises KeyError -> warn_once 'cannot read skin weights' and falls back to automatic weights. Rust takes the nearest sample (piecewise constant), Python interpolates (grid bilinear or Shepard). Python weights are normalised and negative values clipped; Rust uses weights as given then renormalises by total.
rows.notes: Supporting the Rust format is a small extra branch in load_weights (accept "points" + dict rows, nearest-sample lookup in skeleton space). Failure policy (E17 vs warning): see VEC-44.

rows.capability: Automatic skin weights: inverse fourth power of distance to each rest-pose bone segment, four strongest kept
rows.description: Without @weights, weight_i = 1/(d_i+1)^4 where d_i is the distance to bone i's rest segment; keep the four largest and normalise.
python_evidence: scenerender/deform.py:683 build_skin (auto weights 1/(d^2+12^2)^2, all bones, normalised; 32-cell mesh)
rows.divergence: Rust: 1/(d+1)^4, top 4 bones only. Python: 1/(d^2+144)^2 (a 12 px softening radius), all bones contribute. Far from the skeleton Python weights flatten sooner (12 px core) and nearby weights are less peaked; skinned deformation near bone boundaries differs.
rows.notes: Trivial constant swap; Rust limit of 4 influences also bounds cost.

rows.capability: transformConstraint inside a skeleton: applies to the bone before it, all constraint types
rows.description: Constraints listed inside a skeleton apply to the bone that precedes them in document order (ik uses that bone as the chain end); parent/look-at/copy-*/distance/follow-path/track also work on bones; targets may be nodes, bones or tracking data.
python_evidence: scenerender/deform.py:557-571 skeleton_pose (only ik; other types warn 'skeletons only use ik constraints')
scenerender/deform.py:573 _skeleton_ik (effector chosen by @point = bone id, else deepest leaf)
rows.divergence: Authoring model differs: Rust ik is positional (ends at the preceding bone, @point names the track point of the target); Python reads @point as the effector bone id (or auto-picks a leaf) and ignores position in the document. Non-IK constraints on bones are not supported in Python at all. A Rust document with ik after a bone but no @point drives that bone; Python would pick the deepest leaf instead.
rows.notes: Bone-targeting of constraints (target = a bone id) is missing in Python (constraints.target_point only resolves node anchors).

rows.capability: Transform constraints on nodes: parent, look-at, follow-path, copy-position/rotation/scale/transform, distance
rows.description: Post-pass over the frame in paint order: constrained node's new world transform replaces the old and carries to descendants. parent: target world x node local. look-at: rotates about the anchor. follow-path: node at progress along path in its parent's space, autoOrient to tangent (one continuous track across subpaths). copy-*: world components or local with space=local. distance: clamp min..max.
python_evidence: scenerender/constraints.py:125 apply_constraint (applied while computing the node matrix, compositor.py:662)
rows.divergence: Types and space=world|local exist in both; semantics differ in detail (see items). Python also offers 3D variants (camera.py apply_constraint3d).
rows.notes: Differences matter for documents that combine constraints with parenting/anchors.

items.name: parent
items.note: Rust: new world = target world x node LOCAL (the node's own ancestors are dropped). Python: out = target_world x inv(frame) x M where M is the node's full world matrix, so the node's ancestors still apply (constraints.py:147).

items.name: look-at
items.note: Rotate about the anchor so +x points at target point (+offset, +offsetRotation); same in both.

items.name: follow-path
items.note: Rust: path in the node's parent space, progress clamped, subpaths bridged into one track, offsetRotation only with autoOrient. Python: world-space path in composition px (SP = frame matrix) or parent space with space=local, subpaths not bridged (pg.sample), orot applied also without autoOrient (constraints.py:181).

items.name: copy-position
items.note: Move the node's anchor to the target anchor (+offset) in world or local space.

items.name: copy-rotation
items.note: World rotation (+offsetRotation); local uses target rotation + parent rotation.

items.name: copy-scale
items.note: Scale the world matrix about the anchor so column lengths match the target's.

items.name: copy-transform
items.note: Rust replaces the world transform with the target's (plus offset/offsetRotation about the pivot) so the node's own scale/skew are dropped; Python copies scale, rotation and position separately while preserving skew and anchor (constraints.py:157).

items.name: distance
items.note: Clamp the anchor to [minDistance,maxDistance] of the target point; Python scales limits by the frame-matrix scale.

rows.capability: Constraint evaluation order and influence: post-pass in paint order; targets earlier in paint order read already constrained; influence blends translation, rotation (short way) and scale
rows.description: Constraints run after animation and layout in one pass over the frame in paint order; each constraint's delta is applied to the node and its descendants; influence interpolates the decomposed transform components.
python_evidence: scenerender/constraints.py:125-208 (constraints run in document order per node on the matrix left by the previous one; influence = M + (out-M)*influence, a linear matrix lerp)
rows.divergence: Python applies constraints inline while building each node's matrix (pull-based), Rust post-pass in paint order; a Rust target 'earlier in paint order' is read constrained, while Python reads the target through rc.world_matrix (also constrained, evaluation order dependent on references, not paint order). Influence: Rust blends translation/rotation (short way)/scale; Python lerps matrix entries, which shrinks scale and mis-blends large rotations (constraints.py:208); 3D elements in Python do use slerp.
rows.notes: A cheap fix for influence: decompose and blend components in constraints.apply_constraint.

rows.capability: IK on nodes: rotates the parent about its anchor, then the node, so the node's anchor+offsetX/Y reaches the target
rows.description: A two-joint solve on nodes: parent pivots at its anchor, the node at its own, effector = node anchor + offset.
python_evidence: scenerender/constraints.py:317 _node_chains, :358 _solve_chain, :397 ik_pose (chain = the effector's @parent links up to the first node without @parent; two joints analytic, longer FABRIK; effector keeps its transform and rides along)
scenerender/physics.py:2028-2043 (delivers solved rotations through the physics hook)
rows.divergence: Python generalises to arbitrary chains by following @parent links (FABRIK for >2 joints) and rotates all chain nodes; Rust always solves exactly two joints (the node and its parent). For a parent+node chain the answers agree (law of cosines); with deeper @parent ancestry Python rotates every ancestor, Rust only the direct parent. Offset in Python is in composition pixels (world) or parent space (local).
rows.notes: Python IK is delivered via the keyframe pose (x/y stay keyframed) rather than a post-pass.

rows.capability: track constraint: follow point of tracking data, footage-layer frame space, planar tracks carry rotation and scale
rows.description: track follows point @point (default first track) of trackData @target; in the footage layer's frame space when the data names footage; planar tracks add similarity (rotation+uniform scale) relative to their first frame.
python_evidence: scenerender/constraints.py:210 _track (point, transform-with-anchor, planar corner-pin homography, mask/face centroid)
scenerender/tracking.py:373 Track.sample, :351 Track.channel (name, last path component, index, name:sub)
rows.divergence: Python is a superset and uses different mapping: data coordinates are composition pixels (not mapped through the footage layer's placement; @footage only supplies fps/size), planar tracks without a sub-point corner-pin the node box with a full perspective homography (Rust applies a similarity), anchor-bearing transform data replaces the node's transform, rotation/scale of point tracks supported, @timeOffset on trackData. Rust maps footage pixels into frame space through the layer's fit/transform and similarity only.
rows.notes: Documents that use footage-space tracks on a transformed/fitted layer will place nodes differently.

rows.capability: Tracking data formats: JSON, CSV, Nuke, After Effects/Mocha, ASCII FBX (binary FBX rejected)
rows.description: Six formats parsed into point, planar (4 corner) and camera tracks keyed by name; frames to seconds via fps (default 24 when no rate); tracks sampled by linear interpolation.
python_evidence: scenerender/tracking.py:554 parse_json, :629 parse_csv, :675 parse_nuke, :1000 parse_after_effects, :1107 parse_mocha, :1398 parse_fbx, :1555 sniff_format
rows.divergence: Only the JSON schema is truly incompatible: Rust {"fps", "points":{name:[[frame,x,y]..]}, "planes":{name:[[frame,x0..y3]..]}, "cameras":{..}} versus Python {"tracks": ..., keys with t|frame}; verified: Python parse_json on a Rust JSON raises TrackError 'expected a "tracks" object or list'. Other formats are supersets in Python (Nuke Tracker3/4, Transform, CornerPin2D, .chan; AE keyframe text incl. camera; Mocha; ASCII and binary FBX via ufbx; mask/face tracks; sha256; sniffing).
rows.notes: Python also returns channel dicts rather than point/plane/camera maps, so name resolution is richer (e.g. 'Tracker #1/Track Point #1').

items.name: JSON (fps, points, planes, cameras rows)
items.note: Python expects {tracks:{name:{keys:[...]}}}; searched parse_json for 'points'/'planes'/'cameras' top-level keys - none (only per-key 'points' for mask vertices)

items.name: CSV (frame,track,x,y / x0,y0..x3,y3)
items.note: Python accepts these headers plus many more (delimiter sniffing, scale%, corner aliases)

items.name: Nuke (name {{curve ...}} knobs, to1-to4 corner pins, .chan cameras)
items.note: Python: exact NDK curve evaluation, Tracker3/4, Transform, CornerPin2D (to1..to4 mapped), .chan; y-flip with footage height

items.name: After Effects keyframe data (Units Per Second)
items.note: tracking.py:1000

items.name: Mocha (AE export)
items.note: tracking.py:1107

items.name: ASCII FBX (Lcl Translation / Lcl Rotation)
items.note: Python also reads FBX 7 binary and FBX 6 takes

items.name: binary FBX rejected with a message
items.note: Python parses binary FBX (tracking.py:1131 _fbx_binary); a Rust-invalid file is valid in Python

rows.capability: Tracking time model and file loading: frame numbers at 24 fps without a rate, load once at program build, missing/malformed file is error E17
rows.description: Frame numbers without a rate are 24 fps; tracking files are read once when the program is built and a missing or malformed file (also binary FBX, bad rows, unknown skin bone) is the error E17; trackData footage ties the data to a layer.
python_evidence: scenerender/tracking.py:403-430 Ctx.fps precedence (footage asset fps, file fps, document fps)
searched 'E17' across scenerender/, docs/, tests/: no hits in code
rows.divergence: Failure policy: Rust raises E17 (document does not build); Python logs a warning and the constraint does nothing. Rate: Rust 24 fps default; Python uses footage fps, then the file's own rate, then the document fps. Loading: Rust once at program build; Python lazily with an rc.cache keyed by path/mtime/size and verifies @sha256.
rows.notes: Error-code wiring: see schema parity work for how E-codes are surfaced; E17 content is a runtime load error, not a schema rule.

rows.capability: stabilize: layer correction from tracking data minus its Gaussian-smoothed version (sigma = 2 x stabilizeSmoothness s; 1 locks to first sample); translation for points, similarity for planes
rows.description: A layer whose asset is some trackData's footage is corrected by the difference between the tracked motion and a smoothed version.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/video.py:437-700 (layer_stabilize, stabilize_correction: camera path estimated by coarse-to-fine luma alignment, Gaussian-smoothed by stabilizeSmoothness, similarity correction)
rows.divergence: DIVERGENT-by-design: Python estimates the camera motion from the video pixels (analysis cached on disk) for video/generated video layers and never reads trackData; Rust uses the trackData tied by footage and no pixel analysis. Smoothing windows differ (Rust sigma = 2*smoothness s; Python smoothing of the estimated path, 1 = locked off, 0 = off); Python leaves uncovered edges transparent. Result: stabilize on a layer with tracking data in Rust, an analysed shake path in Python.
rows.notes: A Rust-style trackData-driven stabilize would be a new path next to the existing estimator.

rows.capability: Camera tracks in tracking data: parsed but not applied
rows.description: cameras entries (tx, ty, tz, rx, ry, rz, fov) load and are sampled but nothing drives a camera from them.
python_evidence: scenerender/camera.py:554 _constraint_via_2d (a track constraint on a camera uses only the projected 2D position); no code path binds a camera to a trackData camera channel (grep trackData|load_track in camera.py and three/: none)
rows.notes: Same limitation in both engines (parsed, not applied to the camera).

rows.capability: Constraints on lights (look-at, parent, copy-position, copy-transform, distance, follow-path)
rows.description: Lights follow the 2D constraint set listed (not copy-rotation/copy-scale/ik/track).
python_evidence: scenerender/camera.py:480 apply_constraint3d (3D parent/look-at/copy-*/distance/follow-path on object3D/camera/light, TRS+slerp influence)
rows.notes: Python's 3D semantics are richer (3D copy-rotation/copy-scale) and live in a different space than Rust's 2D light placement; same constraint names accepted.

rows.capability: Seeded determinism of vector noise (wiggle-path, turbulence) via D24 counter-based hashing
rows.description: All seeded functions draw from splitmix64 counter-based (seed, channel, index) hashes; 1D value noise with smoothstep is the wiggle/turbulence basis, so results are order independent.
python_evidence: scenerender/noise.py:1 (D24 splitmix64 hashing and 1D gradient noise)
scenerender/physics.py:145 vnoise (3D quintic value noise on the same hash), fbm
rows.divergence: The hash family is shared, but wiggle-path/turbulence use different noise constructions (Rust 1D smoothstep value noise per channel; Python 3D quintic value noise / fbm), so equal seeds do not give equal wiggles.
rows.notes: Cross-ref VEC-13 (wiggle-path) and VEC-29 (turbulence).

rows.capability: Hardening caps on vector geometry (MAX_REPEATER_ITEMS 65,536; MAX_RIDGES 1024; MAX_WIGGLE_POINTS 65,536; MAX_POINTS 10,000; MAX_DASHES 2^20 solid fallback; MAX_SUBDIVIDE 2^20; MAX_PRECOMPS 65,536; zip limits 4096 entries/256 MB entry/512 MB total; tile MAX_DEPTH 8)
rows.description: Rust bounds every user-controlled geometry expansion so a hostile or buggy document cannot exhaust memory or time: repeater copies, zig-zag ridges, wiggle samples, polygon/star points, dash count (over-dense becomes solid), subdivision count, Lottie precomp fan-out, and dotLottie zip size and entry count.
rows.searched: grep for MAX_/65536/10000 in modifiers.py, geometry.py, nodes/core.py, assets/lottie.py, assets/vector.py: only _MAX_SIDE=8192 (raster size) in lottie.py
rows.notes: [added by review] Individual caps were mentioned in notes of VEC-09, VEC-13, VEC-20, VEC-25 but never tracked as a feature.

rows.capability: Soft-body lattice deformation of a node through the deform mesh
rows.description: A node with a soft body deforms through the same grid mesh warp as images (sr-gpu vector.rs deformers handles n.soft with the simulated lattice).
python_evidence: scenerender/deform.py:1,50-52 (softBody warped by physics.soft_world via mesh_map, piecewise-affine)
rows.notes: [added by review] Overlaps the simulation area; listed here because it shares the deform pipeline. Mapping (piecewise affine on lattice triangles vs Rust mesh warp) not compared pixel-wise.

rows.capability: Itemised shaping with OpenType features and variation axes
rows.description: Text is split into runs by style, face and bidi level and shaped with rustybuzz: kerning, ligatures, the style's `features` list (liga=0, smcp, ...) and `variation` axes (wght=700, wdth 80).
rows.notes: Pango uses HarfBuzz, the same shaper family as rustybuzz, so shaping is equivalent in principle. Glyph positions differ at sub-pixel level because Pango lays out in its own units.

rows.capability: Bidi reordering and UAX #14 line-break opportunities
rows.description: Paragraphs are split by Unicode bidi level (unicode-bidi), reordered per line, and broken at UAX #14 opportunities (unicode-linebreak). Thai and Khmer break between characters.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/text.py:746 build_layout (set_base_dir, set_auto_dir, Pango line breaking)
rows.notes: Pango implements UAX #9 via fribidi and UAX #14 with its own tailoring. Break choices can differ in corner cases. Thai/Khmer dictionary breaking in Pango depends on how libthai was built, so it may differ from Rust's per-character break. Unverified.

rows.capability: Knuth-Liang hyphenation (`hyphenate`)
rows.description: A word wider than the line is hyphenated at Knuth-Liang pattern points (English only) when `hyphenate` is set. Otherwise it is broken between characters.
rows.notes: Python is a superset: any pyphen language chosen by @language (Rust is English only). It inserts soft hyphens on words of 5+ letters with limits 2/2 and lets Pango break at them. Rust hyphenates only the word that overflows. The en_US dictionaries (pyphen/Hunspell vs the Rust `hyphenation` crate patterns) may not be identical, so break points can differ for some words. Unverified.

rows.capability: Wrap modes: word, character, none, balance
rows.description: `wrap=balance` searches for the narrowest width that keeps the greedy line count. `character` breaks anywhere and `none` never wraps.
rows.notes: Same rule on both sides. The search width resolution differs, so the chosen balanced width can differ by under 1 px.

rows.capability: autoFit (shrink/grow/fit with minSize/maxSize)
rows.description: Searches one scale factor for all run sizes (tracking, letterSpacing and lineHeight scale with it) so the text fits the box and maxLines, within minSize..maxSize.
rows.notes: Both are bisections, so the final factor can differ by a few thousandths.

rows.capability: maxLines and overflow (visible/clip/ellipsis)
rows.description: maxLines and box overflow drop lines. The last remaining line ends with an ellipsis, or the drawing is clipped to the box.
rows.notes: Pango decides where the ellipsis lands and which glyph is used, so the truncated last line can differ slightly from Rust.

rows.capability: Alignment: start/center/end/justify, direction, verticalAlign
rows.description: Lines are aligned in the box (start/end follow direction). `justify` stretches spaces on every line except those ending a paragraph. verticalAlign places the block in the box height.
rows.notes: Pango justification is applied by Pango's own rules. The last-line exclusion is the same, but per-space widths can differ by sub-pixel amounts.

rows.capability: Vertical writing (vertical-rl / vertical-lr)
rows.description: Glyphs are stacked top-to-bottom in columns (right-to-left for rl, left-to-right for lr). Every glyph is set upright and centred on the column, advancing by vertical metrics or by ascender minus descender.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/text.py:746 build_layout (base gravity EAST, NATURAL hint)
rows.divergence: Rust sets every character upright, with no sideways rotation and no 'vert' substitution. Python follows CSS text-orientation: mixed (UTR #50): CJK and fullwidth glyphs upright using 'vert' forms, Latin and digits rotated 90 degrees clockwise. Latin text in a vertical box therefore lays out differently. Python also cannot apply tracking or line-height the same way inside columns. Unverified.
rows.notes: If Rust semantics are canonical, Python needs a text-orientation: upright switch (Pango gravity hint STRONG) for all scripts.

rows.capability: Style resolution: textStyle basedOn chain, spans, roles, brand-kit colour tokens, case transforms
rows.description: Spans inherit the asset style and apply their own `style` (a textStyle with its basedOn chain) plus attributes. Colour tokens resolve through the brand kit. Per-style attributes: size, colour, lineHeight, tracking (1/1000 em), letterSpacing, baselineShift, textTransform (upper/lower/capitalize/small-caps).

items.name: span > span@style > asset attrs > asset@style precedence
tracking in 1/1000 em, letterSpacing in px
textTransform small-caps
items.note: Rust flags Transform::SmallCaps in its own run handling. Python asks Pango for font variant SMALL_CAPS, which gives smcp if the font has it, otherwise synthesised caps. Appearance can differ.

items.name: lineHeight multiple of each run's size

rows.notes: Python docstring pins the precedence. Whether Rust applies the identical tallest-run line-box rule is unverified.

rows.capability: Font resolution: document fonts, font/fallback families, CSS matching, generic family mapping
rows.description: fontFile and fontAsset load files into the font database first. `font` and `fallback` name families with CSS weight/style/stretch matching through fontdb. Generic families map to the first installed of DejaVu, Liberation and Noto. Output depends on installed fonts.
rust_evidence: README 'Fonts come from the document first'
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/text.py:389 families (fontAsset, fontFile, font, fallback order)
rows.divergence: Python registers font files with fontconfig and gives Pango the family list [fontAsset, fontFile, font, fallback..., 'DejaVu Sans']. Matching and generic aliases (sans-serif, serif, monospace) come from fontconfig. Rust uses fontdb queries. If a fontFile/fontAsset loads it wins outright (fontAsset beats fontFile), and the generic list is DejaVu, Liberation, Noto. Python always appends DejaVu Sans as last fallback. When the document ships its fonts (assets) both agree on faces; with system fonts the chosen faces can differ.
rows.notes: Collection-index selection of font assets is covered on both sides.

rows.capability: Per-character fallback and emoji colour fonts / presentation
rows.description: Characters a face lacks fall back through the style's other families, then to any installed face with them, preferring colour faces for emoji. `emoji=text` disables colour faces.
rows.notes: Python is a superset: full TR51 variation-selector handling, text-presentation silhouettes. The fallback order is Pango/fontconfig's, not Rust's explicit order.

rows.capability: Colour glyph formats: COLR v0/v1 vector glyphs and CBDT/sbix bitmaps
rows.description: COLR v0/v1 glyphs paint as vectors (layers, clips, transforms, linear/radial/sweep gradients). CBDT and sbix PNG bitmaps are decoded once and drawn as textured quads with the glyph transform. Scales cleanly under any transform.
rows.searched: grep -i colr|cbdt|sbix over scenerender, tests, docs: only a comment in text.py and unrelated hits
rows.notes: Colour glyph painting is delegated entirely to Pango/cairo (1.52 / 1.18) and FreeType. Only a CBDT font (Noto Color Emoji) is installed here and only one emoji-render test exists. No code or test exercises COLR gradients, clips or sweep gradients. Bitmaps are drawn by cairo at device resolution rather than as scaled textured quads. Whether COLRv1 paints correctly through this Pango/cairo build is unverified.

rows.capability: Stroke positions inside / centre / outside
rows.description: Strokes sit inside, centred on, or outside the glyph outline. Outside strokes are drawn behind the fill at twice the width; inside strokes are clipped to the glyph. Per-glyph stroke colour/width/position.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-text/src/glyph.rs::draw_glyphs (outside under fill, Inside via mask)
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/text.py:1442 _Draw._strokes (2x width outside, clip for inside)
rows.notes: Same construction on both sides. Joins are round in both; only AA/precision differs.

rows.capability: Text shadows (offset, colour, blur)
rows.description: The glyph silhouette is drawn offset in shadowColor. Blur is produced by averaging nine offset copies (the centre at 0.4 weight and eight ring copies at 0.075, ring radius = blur/2).
rows.divergence: Rust approximates blur with 9 offset copies (centre 0.4, eight at radius blur/2 with 0.075 each). Python renders the shadow to its own tile and applies a true Gaussian with sigma = blur/2. Edge falloff, extent and peak opacity differ visibly for blur > 0.5 px. With blur 0 both draw one plain offset copy.
rows.notes: To reach pixel parity Python can switch the shadow tile to the 9-tap kernel.

rows.capability: Decorations, highlight boxes and backgrounds (block/line/word)
rows.description: Underline, line-through and overline use the font's metrics (overline = ascender). Highlights are per style run. `background` draws block, line or word boxes with padding and radius.

items.name: overline
items.note: Rust puts the line at the face ascender with underline thickness. Pango places it by its own overline metric.

items.name: background block/line/word with padding and radius

rows.notes: Decoration position and thickness come from Pango's font metrics, not from ttf-parser's underline/strikeout records, so there may be sub-pixel differences. Rust skips decorations on colour glyphs.

rows.capability: Animator range selector: shapes, falloff, ease, order, units
rows.description: A range selector with start/end/offset in percent or index, shapes square/ramp-up/ramp-down/triangle/round/smooth, smoothness, easeHigh/easeLow, and order forward/reverse/center-out/edges-in/random (seeded D24 permutation). Units: char, char-no-space, word, line, span (optionally filtered by role).

items.name: shape square (coverage, smoothness)
items.note: Hard rule: Rust coverage >= 0.5, Python unit centre in [s0, s1). Equivalent except at exact ties.

items.name: easeHigh / easeLow
items.note: Rust: one blend v + (smoothstep(v) - v) * clamp((eh+el)/200). Python: easeHigh bends toward 1-(1-v)^2 and easeLow toward v^2 separately.

items.name: order random (D24 permutation)
items.note: Both use the D24 Fisher-Yates over channel 0. Identical output with the same seed derivation is unverified.

rows.divergence: The only measured difference is the ease curve: Rust blends toward smoothstep by the mean of the two ease values; Python applies easeHigh and easeLow independently with quadratic curves.
rows.notes: Python also treats unknown shapes as square with a warning. [review] The ease difference is confirmed. Rust animate.rs:369 computes ease=clamp((eh+el)/200) and v += (smooth(v)-v)*ease, with smooth = smoothstep. Python _ease_hl (text_animators.py:206) takes eh as a 0..1 weight toward 1-(1-v)^2 and el as a 0..1 weight toward v^2. It also does not divide by 100. The unit scale of easeHigh/easeLow may therefore differ (percent in Rust, fraction or percent in Python); check how ev.num feeds eh and el.

rows.capability: Wiggly selector
rows.description: Selection is D24 noise N(seed, 0, t*rate + 7.31*i) scaled by amount, evaluated per unit.
rows.divergence: Rust returns noise * amount, independent of the range. Python multiplies the range selection (which depends on start/end/shape) by noise N(seed & 0xFFFF, 0, t*rate + 7.31*i), with a default wiggleRate of 2.0 and its own seed masking. With the default full range the two agree only if the seed derivation matches (unverified), and a non-default range makes them differ.
rows.notes: Both use the D24 noise function (scenerender/noise.py::noise1 vs sr_vector::d24::noise). [review] Wiggly confirmed DIVERGENT. Rust Selector::Wiggly (animate.rs:327-330) returns noise(seed,0,t*rate+7.31*i)*amount/100 and ignores the range. Python (text_animators.py:433-435) multiplies the range selection by _noise1(seed_for(an,'wiggly')&0xFFFF, t*rate+7.31*i) and defaults wiggleRate to 2.0. The noise phase formula is identical.

rows.capability: Expression selector with textIndex / textTotal
rows.description: The animator's `amount` expression runs once per unit with textIndex and textTotal.
rows.notes: Python is a superset: it also evaluates <expression> children on offset properties per unit and exposes `value` (the range amount). textIndex is 1-based in the Python docstring; Rust 1-based-ness is unverified.

rows.capability: Per-unit properties and combination rules
rows.description: Selected units move, scale, rotate, skew, fade, blur, recolour fill and stroke, track, shift baseline or offset characters. scale/scaleX/scaleY are factors, tracking is in thousandths of an em. Combine rules: add (offsets add, factors multiply by 1+(v-1)s), multiply, replace.

items.name: fill / stroke colour mix and strokeWidth

rows.notes: The formulas match line by line. Rust additionally handles tracking by keeping each line's alignment; Python re-aligns the line, same effect.

rows.capability: Blurred glyphs in radius buckets
rows.description: Glyphs with blur >= 0.5 are drawn apart in radius buckets a half-octave wide (steps of sqrt 2) and blurred with the effects blur kernel.
rows.divergence: Rust quantises blur to half-octave buckets and uses the compositor's effects blur kernel. Python blurs every piece individually with a Gaussian of sigma = blur/2 and no quantisation. A bucket can differ from the exact radius by up to about 19 percent.
rows.notes: Bucketing is a performance optimisation in Rust; the visual result matches only approximately.

rows.capability: Variable-font axis animation (`variation` property)
rows.description: Animated `variation` moves variable-font axes from the style's value (or the font default) toward the target by the selector's share. Advances are kept from the static layout.
rows.divergence: Rust re-outlines each glyph at the mixed axis value but keeps the static layout's advances and positions. Python reshapes the line with per-range Pango font variations, so each glyph takes the advance its axes give it and following glyphs move (continuous advances). Base values differ too: Python seeds wght from weight, wdth 100 and opsz from size, while Rust uses the style's value or the font's own axis default.
rows.notes: A line animated in Python changes width; in Rust it does not.

rows.capability: The 24 text animator presets and their timing formula
rows.description: Each preset fixes a unit, timing mode, em-relative offsets, ease and overlap. With M unit slots, duration D and overlap o a unit lasts D/(1+(M-1)(1-o)) and starts (1-o) of that after the previous one (`stagger` sets the step). 'in' presets rest in the offset state until their window. Typewriter and word-by-word step without fade, wave runs a sine, karaoke fills words, highlight wipes a box behind words, scramble resolves seeded letters, counter counts numbers, mask-reveal clips each line.

items.name: pop
items.note: The opacity eases cubic-out and the scale eases back-out, in both.

items.name: wave
items.note: y = -0.25em*sin(2pi(1.5t - p/8)) with a 10 percent envelope, in both.

items.name: scramble
items.note: 20 ticks per second, pool[floor(U(seed, ci, tick)*|pool|)]. The seed source (a.seed vs rc.ev.seed_for) is unverified for identical output.

items.name: counter
items.note: See TEXT-23.

items.name: karaoke
items.note: Default fill #FFD400 in both.

items.name: highlight
items.note: Default box #FFD40059 in both.

rows.notes: The preset table in the Python docstring matches the Rust table row for row. The Python registry labels all 24 as FULL, and this was verified against the code.

rows.capability: counter preset and character-substitution (scramble, characterOffset)
rows.description: `counter` rewrites every number in the text (cubic-out from 0, keeping decimals and thousands commas) before layout. Scramble and characterOffset substitute characters before layout.
rows.notes: The number regex and formatting are equivalent. Python applies `span` role filtering to counter runs.

rows.capability: textPath (text on a path)
rows.description: Glyph centres are placed along a path by arc length, rotated to the tangent when `perpendicular`, spread over the path with `forceAlignment`.
rows.divergence: Python is a superset. It honours align=center/end against path length minus margins, wraps closed paths, and extrapolates past the ends along the end tangents. Reverse adds 180 degrees to the angle and perpendicular defaults to true. Rust positions only from startOffset + firstMargin (or forceAlignment) and clamps to the ends. Rust ignores `align` and does not wrap closed paths. For start-aligned text inside the path length the two agree.
rows.notes: Python warns that vertical writing modes place glyphs horizontally.

rows.capability: Per-unit 3D animator properties (zDepth, rotationX, rotationY)
rows.description: zDepth, rotationX and rotationY on animators are approximated as 2.5D by scaling each glyph.
rows.divergence: Rust approximates depth by scaling the glyph. Python builds a true plane per unit, projects it through the active camera with an exact homography (raster.warp_projective), culls at the near plane and sorts back to front. The two differ visibly under rotation or strong perspective.
rows.notes: Python is closer to a real 3D result. If Rust is canonical, Python's exact path would need an approximate-2.5D mode.

rows.capability: Caption input formats: inline cues, SRT, WebVTT, ASS, TTML/ITT, SCC
rows.description: Tracks read inline cues, SRT, WebVTT (voice tags become speakers, inline timestamps become word timing), ASS (\k karaoke becomes word timing), TTML and ITT (clock, offset, frame and tick times), SCC (CEA-608 pop-on, roll-up, paint-on, special characters).
rust_evidence: crates/sr-text/src/captions.rs::parse, parse_srt, parse_vtt, parse_ass, parse_ttml, parse_scc
python_evidence: scenerender/captions.py:332 parse_srt, 347 parse_vtt, 428 parse_ass, 823 parse_ttml, 1315 parse_scc

items.name: WebVTT incl. <v> speaker and <hh:mm:ss.mmm> word timing
items.note: Python also reads cue settings (position, align, line, size).

items.name: ASS/SSA with \k karaoke word timing
items.note: Python reads far more (styles, positions, tags). See TEXT-27 for rendering.

items.name: TTML / ITT / DFXP (clock, offset, frame, tick times)
items.note: Python adds timeContainer seq/par, drop-frame SMPTE and intermediate synchronic documents.

rows.notes: Python is a superset on parsing depth. Error handling differs: Rust returns a CaptionError with line number and fails the track, while Python warns once and skips the cue or track.

rows.capability: Rendering of styled caption sources (ASS, TTML, SCC)
rows.description: All sources become plain cues. The track's `preset`, `style`, `activeStyle`, paging and placement apply to every cue, whatever the source format.
python_evidence: scenerender/captions.py:35-40 docstring ('Styled sources carry their own presentation')
rows.divergence: Rust ignores the source's own styling and draws every cue with the track's preset and style. Python renders ASS, TTML/ITT and SCC cues with the source's fonts, colours, regions, positions, effects and the 608 grid, and ignores preset, style, activeStyle, x, y, width and the pagination limits for them. The same document renders differently: for example an ASS file with preset=karaoke is a karaoke page in Rust and a native ASS render in Python.
rows.notes: To follow Rust semantics Python needs a mode, or default, that routes styled cues through the plain-cue path (rich=None); the parsers already produce Cue objects with words.

rows.capability: Transcription cache
rows.description: A transcription cache verified by cacheSha256 (Whisper-style `segments` or a flat `words` list) supplies cues. Word lists are chunked into cues of 12 words.
rows.divergence: Python is a superset in shapes: Whisper, OpenAI, Deepgram, AWS, Google STT, Rev.ai, AssemblyAI, subtitle files as cache. It verifies cacheSha256 at read time and skips the track on mismatch. It reads @cache without requiring @transcribe. It groups word lists into cues at sentence ends, speaker changes and pauses over 1 s. Rust reads only segments/words, requires @transcribe with @cache, does not hash-check at render time (the check is in sr-resolve), and chunks word lists into fixed 12-word cues. The same words-only cache therefore yields different cue boundaries and pages.
rows.notes: Python's grouping is richer, but byte-identical pages with Rust need the 12-word chunk rule for the `words` shape.

rows.capability: captionTrack transcription provider attributes (prompt, provider, model) and `resolve` cache filling
rows.description: captionTrack carries prompt/provider/model. `scene-render resolve` fills the cache through providers (whisper.cpp, cloud services with --allow-cloud, or scene-render-provider-NAME programs) and rewrites cacheSha256.
rows.searched: grep -rn -i 'provider|prompt|resolve|whisper' scenerender/captions.py scenerender/cli.py scenerender/schema; the captions docstring says running a recogniser is not the renderer's job.
rows.notes: Python can only consume a pre-made cache. The transcribe attribute names the audio track but nothing triggers recognition. The schema lacks prompt/provider/model. Also see the area covering `resolve` for generated media.

rows.capability: Caption paging (maxWordsPerLine, maxCharsPerLine, maxLines, one-word)
rows.description: Cues split into pages by maxWordsPerLine, maxCharsPerLine and maxLines. Pages start with their first word and last until the next page (the last until the cue ends). Cues with no word timing share the cue duration by length.
rows.notes: Same greedy line-filling rule. Python also supports cue/@position, safeArea clamping and z ordering that Rust does not apply.

rows.capability: captionTrack lineBreaks (greedy | source)
rows.description:
`lineBreaks="source"` ends a line at a cue newline (
). The limits still wrap long source lines and page them. Blank lines add no rows. Multiword timing spans are split by word length; untimed words share the cue by length. `one-word` still pages each word. Greedy (default) treats newlines as spaces.
rows.searched: grep -rn -i 'lineBreaks|line_breaks|source_words' scenerender; the schema has no such attribute.
rows.notes: Python's paginate always uses whitespace words (Word.text split) and ignores newlines inside cue text for plain cues, which is the greedy behaviour.

rows.capability: profanityFilter
rows.description: `profanityFilter` masks common profanity: the first letter is kept and further letters become asterisks. The built-in list is 12 words and matching is exact on the word's letters.
rows.divergence: Different word lists: Python has its own built-in list plus prefix entries ('fuck*') and an SCENERENDER_PROFANITY_LIST file (extend, remove, replace), and masks letters and digits after the first character. Rust has a fixed 12-word exact list and masks alphabetic characters only. Neither list is configurable in Rust. Words that one side masks and the other doesn't will differ.
rows.notes: Python applies the filter to every source including styled ones.

rows.capability: Burn-in caption layout and defaults
rows.description: Tracks with mode burn or both (or the one named by output burnCaptions) draw over every layer. `x` is the centre and `y` the top of the block, `width` its box, with lines breaking only where the pagination puts them. Default style is 4.4 percent of frame height, white DejaVu Sans, line height 1.2. The active word is the last that has started.
python_evidence: scenerender/captions.py:1835 _page_spec (4.4 percent, DejaVu Sans, lineHeight 1.2, wrap=none)
rows.divergence: The core rules and defaults are identical. Two differences: (1) Rust draws burned-in captions with emoji in text presentation (emoji_color=false); Python uses emoji="color". (2) Python additionally applies cue @position/WebVTT settings, safeArea clamping and track @z ordering; Rust parses `position` but caption_scene does not use it.
rows.notes: Layouts differ only at the pixel level because of Pango vs rustybuzz.

rows.capability: The 13 caption presets
rows.description: classic adds a soft shadow to a style with neither shadow nor stroke. boxed-line puts a #000000B3 box behind each line, boxed-word an activeColor box behind the active word. one-word shows one word per page. karaoke cross-fades whole words to activeColor over their duration. highlight, pop, enlarge, bounce, typewriter, fade and slide animate words or pages. none draws the text as styled.

items.name: classic
items.note: Shadow #000000CC, blur 0.12 size, offsetY 0.04 size, in both. Shadow blur is rendered differently per TEXT-14.

items.name: boxed-word
items.note: Padding 0.12 em, radius 0.18 em, in both.

items.name: pop
items.note: Scale 1+0.15 sin(pi u) over 0.25 s in both.

rows.notes: The motion constants match line by line. A Python-only presentation difference is that boxed-line adds extra block height of size*0.5 when positioning.

rows.capability: Caption sidecar writing (VTT/SRT)
rows.description: Tracks an output lists in `captions`, and tracks with mode sidecar or both, are written next to the output as <stem>.<track>.<language>.vtt (or .srt when the source is SRT), with cues cut to the rendered range and times rebased to it.
rows.divergence: Naming: Rust always writes <stem>.<track-id>.<language>.<ext>; Python writes <stem>.<language>.<ext> and uses the track id only when two tracks share a language (captions.py:1819). Range: Rust drops cues outside start..end, clips and rebases (pipeline.rs:1519-1531); Python has no range handling. Content: Rust writes the track's raw cues (track_cues); Python's sidecar_cues (captions.py:1785) writes the PAGINATED pages from track_pages, so maxWordsPerLine/maxCharsPerLine/maxLines split cues in the sidecar, and styled (rich) cues are written as plain text with no words. Python also writes every track whose mode is sidecar/both or listed in job.captions.
rows.notes: Python also handles styled cues by writing their plain text.

rows.capability: Output-time captions: caption tracks mapped through output segments, output-level captionTrack children, burnCaptions per output
rows.description: With segments the composition's tracks are mapped through them: each cue appears in every output interval showing its composition span (repeats and holds included), with word times clipped. Transcribed tracks follow their audio selection and mute. Cues shown under 0.7 s warn. Output captionTrack children are in output time already.
rows.searched: grep -rn -i 'segment' scenerender/captions.py scenerender/output.py (only Matroska hits); output children list in the 1.1 schema; burnCaptions IS supported (output.py:331, captions.py:2305).
rows.notes: The Python schema has no `segment` or output captionTrack elements.

rows.capability: Chart kinds and data input
rows.description: Nine kinds read `series` children or a CSV or JSON `src`, draw axes and value labels, and draw on with the animatable `progress`.

items.name: bar (horizontal)
items.note: Python adds gridlines, nice ticks, a legend, rotated labels and axis titles from data files. The Rust value axis is skipped for bars.

items.name: column
items.note: Same family: Python has grid, legend and a staggered grow-in; Rust has a plain axis.

items.name: line
items.note: Python overlays series and marks points; Rust strokes a trimmed polyline.

items.name: area
items.note: Python stacks series cumulatively at 75 percent opacity; Rust overlays series at 45 percent alpha.

items.name: pie
items.note: Python puts labels outside with leader lines and shows percentages inside slices; Rust prints the formatted value inside. Palette differs.

items.name: donut
items.note: Python shows the total in the hole with a hole ratio of 0.6 (same as Rust); Rust leaves the hole empty.

items.name: scatter
items.note: Python draws x and y nice-tick axes with grid and legend; Rust scales each axis to nice_max of the data with plain circles.

items.name: counter
items.note: Same semantics (one value counts from 0, two from the first to the second); Python sizes the number to fit and adds a caption label.

items.name: progress
items.note: Python draws a pill bar or a ring (squarish box) and stacks several series; Rust draws only a pill track and fill at 35 percent of height.

rows.divergence: Inputs and kinds are the same and `progress` animates every kind in both, but the pixel layout is wholly different. Python uses its own pinned layout (gridlines, nice ticks, legend, rotated labels, stacked area, rings, a different 8-colour palette #3DD6D0, #FFC23D, ...) and Rust uses a simpler layout with its 8-colour palette (0.26,0.52,0.96 ...). A document drawn by Rust will not match the Python layout.
rows.notes: Chart text is drawn through the text engine in both. Python reads CSV with a header row and JSON with labels/series/categoryTitle; Rust reads CSV and JSON with its own ChartData loader (not compared field by field).

rows.capability: Chart number formats
rows.description: Value labels and ticks use `0.0`, `#,##0`, `0%`, `$#,##0.00` and printf `%.2f` patterns. Without a format, integers print plainly and other values print with 2 decimals trimmed.
rows.divergence: All five documented patterns work in Python, plus `{:,.1f}`, '%' scaling and quoted literals. The default differs when @format is absent: Rust prints integers as-is and others with up to 2 decimals trimmed. Python prints a thousands separator and the data's decimal places (ticks: the tick step's decimals), so 1234 is '1,234' in Python and '1234' in Rust.
rows.notes: Python's printf branch rounds %d via int(round(v)); Rust's `%` prefix only reads the decimals.

rows.capability: Audiogram styles (bars, line, wave, circle, spectrum)
rows.description: Five styles draw the source's analysis envelopes: bars rising from the bottom, a line, a mirrored wave, a radial circle, or a three-band spectrum.

items.name: bars
items.note: Bars are the last `bars` envelope samples (history, newest right) in Rust. They are `bars` log-spaced FFT bands in Python.

items.name: line
items.note: Rust: smoothed history polyline stroked. Python: spectrum polyline across FFT bands.

items.name: wave
items.note: Rust: mirrored filled wave of the level history. Python: oscilloscope stroke of the raw waveform over one frame.

items.name: circle
items.note: Radial bars, r0 = 0.25 min(w,h), same construction.

items.name: spectrum
items.note: Rust: three bars interpolated from the low/mid/high band levels. Python: a mirrored filled area over all FFT bands.

rows.divergence: The style names map to different visuals. Rust drives bars/line/wave/circle from a time history of full-band envelope levels, with exponential smoothing along the history and slot*0.7 bar width, and spectrum from three band levels. Python drives all styles except wave from an FFT of the source at the frame time, with `bars` log-spaced bands (40 Hz to 16 kHz), dB mapping and a stateless smoothing window of 12 frames.
rows.notes: Rust unknown style names draw bars; Python warns and draws nothing.

rows.capability: Audiogram audio analysis source
rows.description: Audiograms read the audio pipeline's analysis envelopes. Rendering without audio draws them flat and reports it.
rows.divergence: Python decodes the source audio and runs its own 2048-sample Hann FFT inside the renderer, so it needs no delivery pipeline and is deterministic per frame. Rust needs the delivery pipeline's envelopes, and `render` without audio draws flat. Quantitative levels (dB window -60..0, band edges) are therefore not comparable.
rows.notes: Python does not need audio to be rendered first; Rust levels would need to be fed from sr-audio's analysis to be matched.

rows.capability: Machine-readable codes: six kinds
rows.description: QR (with error-correction level), Data Matrix, PDF417, EAN-13, UPC-A and Code 128 are encoded and drawn as merged module rectangles over a background box.

items.name: qr
items.note: Rust: rxing. Python: segno with the same L/M/Q/H levels. Module matrices are the same unless mask or version selection differs. Unverified.

items.name: datamatrix
items.note: Rust: rxing. Python: zxing-cpp, forced square ECC 200. Symbol size selection may differ. Unverified.

items.name: pdf417
items.note: errorCorrection to security-level mapping differs: Rust L->2, M->4, Q->6, H->8; Python L->2, M->4, Q->5, H->6.

items.name: ean13
items.note: Rust passes digits to rxing. Python accepts 12 or 13 digits and recomputes a wrong check digit with a warning; the behaviour on a wrong check digit may differ.

items.name: upc-a
items.note: Python maps 11 or 12 digits to EAN-13 with a leading 0.

items.name: code128
items.note: Python's own encoder uses set B, switching to C for 4+ digit runs. rxing selects sets by its own optimiser, so the module string can differ for mixed data.

rows.divergence: Besides the PDF417 ecc mapping, the encoders are different libraries (segno / zxing-cpp / built-in vs rxing), so equal inputs can give different module patterns for Code 128 mixed content, QR mask choice and Data Matrix size. 1D codes carry no human-readable digits in either engine.
rows.notes: segno and zxing-cpp are optional dependencies in Python; the registry lowers `code` to PARTIAL if either is missing. [review] The PDF417 ecc mapping is confirmed. Rust code.rs maps L->2, M->4, Q->6, anything else (H)->8. Python code.py:140 maps L->2, M->4, Q->5, H->6. PDF417 is also built by zxing-cpp in Python and rxing in Rust, so row heights and module patterns can differ. Both are optional deps in Python.

rows.capability: Code quiet zone and module drawing
rows.description: Codes are drawn inside a quiet zone of `quietZone` modules. 2D codes keep square modules, centred and as large as fits. Linear codes stretch to the width and fill the height. Runs of dark modules merge into rectangles.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/code.py:181-240 render_code (qz modules, is2d square, 1D stretch, run merging)
rows.notes: Same geometry. Python centres the matrix without adding the quiet zone to the offset, which is the same layout because the quiet zone is symmetric. PDF417 row height handling may differ because rxing and zxing-cpp return different matrix row heights. Unverified.

rows.capability: Formulas: TeX math subset typeset with an OpenType MATH font
rows.description: A built-in TeX subset is laid out with the installed OpenType MATH font: math italic letters, Greek, operators and relations with TeX spacing, fractions, roots with index, scripts, big operators with limits in display style, \left/\right stretched delimiters, text and function names, matrix environments, accents and infix \over. The formula is centred and scaled down to fit. Unknown commands and malformed environments report errors.

items.name: math italic letters, Greek, operators, relations, spacing
items.note: With LaTeX or mathtext. The glyph shapes are Computer Modern, not the installed MATH font.

items.name: \frac / \dfrac / \tfrac and infix \over
items.note: The mathtext fallback rewrites \frac to \dfrac. \over support in mathtext is unverified.

items.name: sub/superscripts and big operators with limits
\text, \mathrm, \operatorname, function names
items.note: The mathtext fallback rewrites \text and \operatorname to \mathrm.

items.name: matrix environments (matrix, pmatrix, bmatrix, vmatrix, Vmatrix, cases)
items.note: LaTeX engine only. The mathtext fallback has no environments. A machine without pdflatex and pdftocairo drops to a Pango-markup approximation.

items.name: centre in box and shrink to fit
unknown command / malformed environment is an error
items.note: Rust reports an error and draws nothing. Python warns and falls through to the next engine, so a document renders something instead.

rows.divergence: Python delegates typesetting to a real LaTeX (pdflatex + pdftocairo; present on this machine), or matplotlib mathtext, or Pango markup. Rust has its own layout engine on the system's OpenType MATH font. Python therefore accepts far more TeX than Rust, but glyph shapes, spacing and metrics differ (Computer Modern vs the installed MATH font), and Python results depend on the machine's TeX installation. Rust's source of math metrics is the font's MATH table; a pinned font is needed for repeatable output.
rows.notes: A Rust-style built-in engine would remove the pdflatex dependency. Implementing it means a new layout engine over a MATH font, hence size L.

rows.capability: 3D text glyph outlines for solid extrusion
rows.description: Glyph outlines of a text laid out in a family at a size are flattened to polygons (y down, baseline 0) for object3D text extrusion.
rows.notes: Python lays the text out in Pango and extracts the path outlines, so the outline vertices differ in flattening and in line layout. This row only confirms that the capability exists; the geometry itself belongs to the 3D area.

rows.capability: Scene space, default 2.5D camera, physical lens, camera pose and target
rows.description: Scene space is composition pixel space extended into depth (x right, y down, z away, 100 units per metre). The default camera sits at (w/2)/tan(fov/2) with 60 deg horizontal fov so z=0 maps 1:1; a <camera> uses fov or focalLength/sensorWidth, absolute x/y/z, yaw turning toward +x, positive pitch looking up, roll about the axis, target look-at (roll still applies), orthographic with orthoHeight, near/far.
python_evidence: scenerender/camera.py:3-60 (normative conventions docstring, A.E engine-space boundary)
scenerender/camera.py:576 default_fpx, :637-679 build_camera (fov clamp 0.1-179, focalLength -> 2 atan(sw/2f))
rows.notes: Python works internally in a GL engine space (origin at frame centre, +Y up, +Z toward viewer) and converts once at the boundary; numerically equivalent to Rust's scene-axis matrices. Verified by reading both and the Python tests; Rust not executed.

rows.capability: Camera/light parenting, 3D transform constraints, 2.5D layers registered to the 3D camera
rows.description: A camera or light with transformConstraint type=parent (or @parent) has x/y/z/yaw/pitch/roll in the parent's frame (blended by influence); an object3D whose parent is a camera/light takes its full 3D pose; 2.5D threeD layers project through the same camera (position and rotation) so they stay registered with 3D objects.
rows.notes: Python applies the full constraint set to object3D, cameras and lights; Rust render_three applies parent plus look-at, copy-position/transform, distance and follow-path to lights and parent to cameras/objects (rest through sr-eval rig). Python is a superset or equal.

rows.capability: Layer model: all object3D under one parent render as one pass/layer at the first one's paint position
rows.description: Every object3D under one parent shares one depth buffer, one light set and one shadow-map set, and composites as a single normal-blend layer at the paint position of the first of them; opacity, blend, masks and effects come from the enclosing group. The same pass also hosts particles3D, ocean, fracture and volume draws.
python_evidence: scenerender/three/renderer.py:1-40 (frame model docstring: each object3D renders its own layer)
scenerender/three/scene.py:692 render_node_layer, :602 frame3d (shared world: lights/shadows/env), :550 world3d_at
rows.divergence: Rust: one merged pass per parent, depth-sorted together, composited once at the first object's position, group opacity/blend apply to the whole set. Python: lights, shadows and the environment are shared per frame, but each object3D is its own layer composited in its own stacking slot, with other opaque objects pre-drawn into the depth buffer only to occlude it; translucent/transmissive objects do not occlude other layers and are ordered by document order, and an object's own opacity/blend/effects apply per object.
rows.notes: Pixel results differ for interleaved 2D and 3D layers, translucent objects overlapping each other, and per-object blend modes. depends on nothing; a fix lets 3D-04 refract uniformly.

rows.capability: Transmission refracts the 2D layers already drawn behind the 3D layer

rows.capability: Lens distortion (radial k1)
rows.description: lensDistortion is a radial k1 applied to the 3D render. Rust's post pass samples the source at p*(1 + k1*|p|^2) where p is the output position centred, in units of frame height (x scaled by aspect).

rows.divergence: Sign: Python treats k<0 as barrel and k>0 as pincushion (x_d = x_u(1+k r_u^2), output pixel is the distorted one, inverted by Newton); Rust samples source at r(1+k r^2) for each output radius r, which makes k>0 pull content inward (barrel), the opposite sign. Normalisation: Rust radius unit is the frame height, Python the half diagonal. Python also applies it to threeD 2.5D layers via camera_post, Rust only to the 3D pass. (From code reading; not executed.)
rows.notes: Python overscans the render so barrel distortion has content at the edges.

rows.capability: Gaussian splat loading (.splat and 3DGS PLY, DC colour)
rows.description: Splat files use COLMAP axes (y-down, z-forward) matching scene space, scaled 100 per unit; .splat carries base colour only (32-byte records); a PLY with f_dc_* and scale_* imports as splats: positions, exp scales, rotations (w,x,y,z), sigmoid opacity, DC colour 0.5 + C0*f_dc sRGB-decoded; opacity attribute on the object.
rows.notes: Python supports ascii and big-endian PLY too. Python never reads f_rest_* (see 3D-37).

rows.capability: Gaussian splat spherical harmonics (degree 1-3), view-dependent colour
rows.description: A PLY with f_rest_* (channel-major) carries SH degree 1-3 evaluated per splat for the direction from the camera in the capture's own frame (colour = 0.5 + sum Y_k(d) c_k), so highlights stay put while the object turns; 192 bytes per splat on the GPU.
rows.searched: grep -i for f_rest, sh_degree, harmonic, spherical harmonic across scenerender/ and tests/: only audio ambisonics hits; _load_ply_splats uses only f_dc_0..2 and clamps 0.5+C0*f_dc.
rows.notes: Needs loader changes (parse f_rest, 48 floats per splat), a per-splat SH uniform/storage buffer, and the shader evaluation in the capture frame via the inverse model matrix. Python's splat vertex shaders would gain a camera-position uniform in model space.

rows.capability: Gaussian splat rendering: projected covariance quads, depth sort, depth blending, opacity
rows.description: Each frame splats sort back to front by view depth (Rust: GPU radix sort in four 8-bit passes) and each draws as a quad sized to three standard deviations of its projected covariance (EWA, +0.3 low-pass, guard-band culling), blended over the opaque scene with depth testing; object opacity scales alpha; splats are not relit and cast no shadows.
python_evidence: scenerender/three/shaders.py:859-895 SPLAT_VS (3 sigma, +0.3, 1.3x guard), :933 SPLAT_SORT_CS (bitonic double-precision sort), :912 SPLAT_KEYS_CS
scenerender/three/renderer.py:877-1023 (_sorted_splats CPU path, _gpu_sorted_splats GL 4.3 path, draw_splats, depth_mask off)
rows.divergence: Sort algorithm differs (Python: bitonic on fp64 keys at GL 4.3, CPU stable sort otherwise, reused until the camera moves 0.5%; Rust: radix every frame) and Python draws each splat object as its own layer, so splats in different objects are depth-composited per layer, not per splat. Same visual model otherwise.
rows.notes: Rust also composites splats in its path tracer (other area).

rows.capability: 360 video: six cube faces per eye from the viewport camera, full-compositor content
rows.description: With <scene360>, every frame renders six 90 deg faces from the viewport camera's eye (viewportCamera else the active camera) turned relative to that camera, running the whole compositor per face so plain 2D layers outside isolated groups are placed in space as 2.5D layers at their depth (a title card floats in front of the viewer); a reprojection pass writes the layout; delivery renders at scene360 size unless the output sets its own.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-gpu/src/render_three.rs:2050-2243 (360 pass: ViewOverride, face_rotations, per-face render_with, SpherePipe)
rows.divergence: Python renders only the 3D participants (object3D, threeD layers, collapsed groups, visible dome) into the six faces and renders the 2D composition as one flat frame placed on the front face spanning 90 degrees, composited over it. Rust renders the whole compositor per face, so 2D layers sit at their z in space and appear on whichever face they face, with 2.5D perspective, effects and masks applied per face.
rows.notes: Python's camera_override and pass360 flags already allow re-rendering at another camera; extending to the full compositor reuses them.

rows.capability: 360 stereo: top-bottom and left-right with interpupillary
rows.description: top-bottom and left-right stereo split the output frame between eyes (each eye gets half) offset by +/- interpupillary/2 (metres) along the viewport camera's right axis; the eye shift is one constant per eye for all six faces.

rows.divergence: Python renders omni-directional stereo (ODS) with per-strip eye offsets so parallax is correct all around; Rust shifts the whole eye by +/- ipd/2 along the camera right axis for every face, so parallax is only correct looking forward and vanishes or inverts toward the sides and back. rows.description: Probe runs ffprobe and yields duration, video stream (size, fps, codec, pix_fmt, depth, chroma shifts, alpha/rgb, colour matrix/transfer/primaries tags, full-range, display rotation) and each audio stream (rate, channels, layout, codec). Executables are overridable by env; ffmpeg crash cannot take the renderer down.

rows.divergence: Rust uses ffprobe structured output and has duration, codec, channel layout, chroma shifts, rotation from the display matrix, per-audio-stream info, and SR_FFMPEG/SR_FFPROBE overrides. Python scrapes ffmpeg's banner text, has no ffprobe use, no duration/codec/channels/layout/rotation from the file, and always uses the imageio-ffmpeg binary (no general override env var).

rows.capability: Frame-accurate video decode at constant frame rate with accurate seek
rows.description: Each video layer has its own ffmpeg decoder process; frame n is the image displayed at n/fps. Decode seeks with -ss, resamples to the asset frame rate (CFR) and indexes frames by integer; a backward or far-forward request restarts the decoder; past the last frame the last frame holds.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/video.py:84-175 _Decoder (-ss restart on jump<0 or > max(8,2*fps), fps filter to asset @fps, EOF holds last frame, LRU of 6 frames)
rows.notes: Same indexing rule. Python decode downsizes by powers of two when drawn small (video.py:669 level) which Rust does not (README limitation: no mipmaps).

rows.capability: Decoder look-ahead ring, damaged-media reporting, end-of-stream bracketing
rows.description: A background thread keeps up to four decoded frames ahead of the last request so decode overlaps rendering; decoders that stop early or complain mark the media as damaged (reported once, later frames hold the last good frame); a seek past the end brackets the real last frame via a few container-duration seeks instead of stepping back.
python_evidence: scenerender/assets/video.py:84-175 (synchronous sequential reader on the render thread; eof_at holds last frame; no thread, no stderr capture - stderr=DEVNULL)
rows.divergence: Python reads frames synchronously in the render path (no look-ahead thread/ring), discards ffmpeg's stderr so truncated/corrupt media is not reported, and finds the end only by reading to EOF. Hold-last-frame semantics match.
rows.notes: Performance and diagnostics only; pixels are identical for healthy files.

rows.capability: Time controls: clipIn/clipOut/loop/reverse/speed/timeStretch/freezeAt/timeRemap to source time
rows.description: A layer's local time maps to source seconds: timeRemap channel overrides everything; else freezeAt holds one local time; rate = |speed|/timeStretch, negative speed plays backwards, loop repeats whole clip lengths and holds the end, reverse mirrors within the clip, clipIn offsets; non-remapped, non-frozen layers end when media runs out.

items.name: loop (extra plays)
items.note: Python also accepts negative loop as infinite and animated loop

items.name: speed / timeStretch
items.note: rate = speed/timeStretch in both

items.name: negative speed plays backwards
items.note: Rust flips reverse for rate<0; Python core.py:208 keeps the sign so u<0 and the source time falls before clipIn

items.name: timeRemap
items.note: both return the channel value unmodified by clipIn

rows.divergence: Core mapping is equivalent; Python lacks negative-speed reversal and, past clipOut without loop, returns None (layer disappears) where Rust ends the node at start + len*(loops+1)/rate (same visible effect). Python additionally supports animated loop/speed (re-solved windows), which Rust takes statically.
rows.notes: [review] The Rust side of the negative-speed item is wrong as cited. MediaClock::map (program.rs:100-145) does not flip anything for rate<0. It is layer_clock (program.rs:~1495) that sets rate=|rate| and reverse = l.reverse != (rate<0). Python's media_time (nodes/core.py:208) keeps the sign, so u<0, the `u >= span` and `min(u,span)` branches both pass it through, and the result is clip_in+u, before clipIn. The MISSING status for negative speed stands. Rust also ends the node at start+len*(loops+1)/|rate|.

rows.capability: Constant-power panning between speaker pairs
rows.description: Mono sources pan across the front arc (+-30 deg stereo) by constant-power sin/cos between the two nearest horizontal speakers (centre = -3 dB per channel); stereo pan is a constant-power balance; ambisonic encode with SN3D.
python_evidence: scenerender/audio/dsp.py:229 pan_gains (gL=sqrt2*cos, so unity at centre / +3 dB hard-pan)
rows.divergence: Rust point_gains/route: stereo pan is th=(1-x)*pi/4 with g=(cos th, sin th), so centre mono is 0.707 per channel. A stereo source's balance leaves the unattenuated side at 1.0 and attenuates the other with cos(pan*pi/2). Python dsp.pan_gains is sqrt2*cos/sin, so 1.0 per channel at centre and +3 dB at hard pan. Python's centre mono is therefore +3 dB louder than Rust. The 3 dB difference was verified for the mono-to-stereo pan law only. Surround VBAP vs pairwise sin/cos was not compared line by line.
rows.notes: A 3 dB level difference on every centred mono track changes loudness-normalised results only slightly (normalisation compensates) but not un-normalised masters.

rows.capability: Analysis table: per-frame four-band envelopes for audioAmplitude()/audio links
rows.description: Before the video pass the mix produces per-frame envelopes of every track and audio layer in four bands (full, <250 Hz, 250 Hz-4 kHz, >4 kHz), RMS per video frame mapped linearly from -60 dBFS (0) to 0 dBFS (1); audioAmplitude() and audio links read it.

Serial for two-pass/maxFileSize, sequences, GIF/APNG/WebP, audio-only, simulations. Flash/contrast findings judged in frame order over the whole output.

Python has no per-segment encoder or concat join, and does not default to parallel.
