rows.capability: Flash analysis (WCAG 2.3.1 / BT.1702) on a 48x27 luminance grid with 1/3-frame windows
rows.description: Rust access.rs: each delivered frame is reduced to a 48x27 grid of display-linear sRGB. Per cell, general transitions (delta Y >= 0.1, darker state < 0.8) and red transitions are counted with hysteresis. A cell flashes with 8 or more opposing transitions in 1 s. A frame fails when flashing cells cover more than 25 % of any window one third of the frame wide and tall. The detector streams in frame order across parallel chunks.
python_evidence: scenerender/qa.py:101 FlashDetector (same thresholds 0.1/0.8/red 320/20, sat>=0.8, hysteresis, >3 flashes per second, 25 % windows of 341/1024 x 256/768 of the frame)
scenerender/qa.py:140 _reduce (box-reduces to at most 192 px wide, not a 48x27 grid)
rows.divergence: Same rule set, different spatial resolution. Python analyses up to 192 px wide and sizes the window from the 1024x768 reference geometry; Rust uses a fixed 48x27 cell grid with 16x9-cell windows. Python weights luminance by the output colour space's primaries and decodes the output transfer, Rust assumes display-linear sRGB. Verdict reporting differs: Python emits time ranges and a flashes-per-second count, Rust emits a frame count and first failing time. Borderline content can be judged differently.
rows.notes: [added by review] Probably belongs to the accessibility area; listed here because access.rs is in this area's file list. Not a gap in capability.

rows.capability: Fixed-step timeline from physics@start with periodic checkpoints and seek-order bit-identity (physics)
rows.description: Physics and particles step at a fixed dt from their start time and keep a state copy every simulated second. Seeking reuses the nearest checkpoint, and the result equals a straight run whatever the request order. Checkpoints are thinned (every other one dropped, spacing doubled) when they exceed a 256 MB budget.
python_evidence: scenerender/physics.py:175-206 Seekable (checkpoint dict, deepcopy, resume from last state)
scenerender/physics.py:873-917 PhysicsSim (Seekable every=120 steps, fixedStep default 1/120)
rows.divergence: Same mechanism. Python's spacing is 120 steps (equals 1 s only at the default fixedStep), keeps no memory budget or thinning (checkpoints grow unbounded up to max_steps 10M), and the step lookup tolerance is 1e-6 vs Rust 1e-9. Bit-identity holds only within Python, not against Rust numbers.
rows.notes: Optional work: add the thinning budget for long, large-lattice documents.

rows.capability: Rigid-body 2D world model and solver (Rapier 2D f64, enhanced determinism; metres, y up, pixelsPerMeter, gravity default -9.80665)
rows.description: The world is in metres with y up. physics@pixelsPerMeter (default 100) maps it to document pixels with y down. Gravity defaults to -9.80665 m/s2. Rapier 2D in f64 with enhanced determinism does the solving, with physics@solverIterations, friction and restitution combined with the Max rule, and a body's own friction/restitution on bound walls.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-sim/src/physics.rs World::new (Max combine rules lines ~347-349, IntegrationParameters, num_solver_iterations)
rows.divergence: Units and defaults match. Rust: Rapier 2D f64 solver, friction combine Max, restitution Max. Python: its own sequential-impulse solver (Baumgarte 0.2, 5 mm slop, speculative contacts 4 slops), friction sqrt(fa*fb), restitution max(ea, eb). Trajectories (stacking, bounce heights, resting jitter) will not match Rust numerically. Python has no Rapier or Rust binding.
rows.notes: Matching Rust exactly would mean binding rapier2d (pyo3), which is a different dependency decision (no installs allowed in the Python tree as of now). Behaviour-class parity already exists.

rows.capability: Collision filtering and sensors: collisionGroup, collidesWith, sensor
rows.description: collisionGroup and collidesWith filter contacts (symmetric AND). sensor bodies detect overlaps without colliding.

rows.divergence: Rust folds groups above 31 onto bit 31 (physics.rs 317-321). Python accepts any group id. Python's sensor_overlaps accessor (physics.py:1970) has no caller in scenerender, so sensor pairs are recorded but unused. Rust has no pair list either.

rows.capability: Initial velocity units: velocityX/velocityY, angularVelocity
rows.description: velocityX/Y are pixels per second in document axes (y down). angularVelocity is degrees per second, clockwise on screen. Applied at activation.
rust_evidence: README rigid-bodies paragraph ('velocityX/velocityY are pixels per second')
crates/sr-sim/src/physics.rs World::new set_linvel(v(b.velocity[0]/ppm, -b.velocity[1]/ppm)) with BodySpec.velocity 'px/s (y down)'
python_evidence: scenerender/physics.py:1122 b.v0 = (velocityX, velocityY, angularVelocity) and 1313 b.vel = np.array(b.v0[:2]) with no ppm scaling or y flip, so values are metres per second with y up; Rust physics.rs:273 set_linvel(vx/ppm, -vy/ppm).
rows.divergence: Rust: px/s, y down (velocityY>0 moves down). Python: m/s, y up (velocityY>0 moves up). The same document launches a body at 1/ppm of the speed and with the vertical sign flipped. angularVelocity agrees (deg/s clockwise). The fix is a unit/sign change plus updating Python tests that assume m/s.
rows.notes: Verify against the canonical schema documentation owner before flipping, since Python tests (velocityX=400 bullet) encode m/s.

rows.capability: Bounds: floor and frame walls
rows.description: bounds="floor" adds a ground at the frame's bottom edge, "frame" adds walls around the frame. Walls take each body's own friction and restitution.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-sim/src/physics.rs enum Bounds {None, Frame, Floor}; wall colliders use body friction/restitution (README)
python_evidence: scenerender/physics.py:908-914 planes (floor = bottom; frame = four edges)
scenerender/physics.py:21 doc ('frame = all four frame edges (friction 0.6, restitution 0)')
rows.divergence: Rust wall colliders are built with friction 0 and restitution 0 under the Max combine rule (physics.rs 344-349), so a contact takes the body's own friction and restitution. Python walls use friction sqrt(f_body*0.6) (physics.py 1410-1411) and restitution max(e_body, 0) = e_body. Restitution therefore agrees. Friction diverges: Rust uses f_body, Python uses sqrt(0.6*f_body). Real divergence is friction only, and it is minor.
rows.notes: Python restitution rule max(ea, eb) with wall e=0 gives the body's own value, so restitution probably agrees. Friction does not (sqrt(f*0.6) vs Rust Max(f, body)). Mark as friction-only divergence.

rows.capability: Body-to-node transform: simulated pose replaces node world transform; children and @parent descendants follow; child bodies keep own pose
rows.description: The simulated pose replaces the node's world transform, and its children follow, including explicit parent links and their descendants. A child with its own rigid body keeps its simulated pose regardless of paint order. Cycles mixing containment and @parent are rejected as E11 (validation: see schema parity work).
rust_evidence: crates/sr-eval/src/sim.rs apply_bodies (sorted by transform_parent depth), set_world (descendants via transform_parent)
rows.divergence: Python converts the simulated pose into the node's parent (XML-containment) space, so contained children follow. keyed_pose/world_doc walk getparent() only and ignore @parent, so a body whose pose depends on a @parent link starts from the wrong world pose. No handling of parent-link descendants of a body or of child-body ordering; no E11-style cycle detection for physics (grep E11/cycle: only include cycles in document.py:164).
rows.notes: Python behaviour of explicit @parent on descendants was not exercised by a test; unverified. Rust README Limitation: descendants reached only through @parent do not follow a motion-blurred body.

A joint whose impulse exceeds breakForce is removed.

rows.capability: 3D rigid bodies on Rapier 3D: rigidBody inside object3D, stepped beside the 2D world
rows.description: A rigidBody inside an object3D makes the object a body of a second world with the same step, checkpoints, gravity and bounds. It starts at the object's 3D pose, in its 3D parent's frame or its 2D container's. The simulated pose replaces the object's transform, so objects parented to it follow and cameras and lights can target it. Velocities are px/s and deg/s in scene axes (y down, z away). Needs version="1.2".
rows.searched: grep -i rigidBody|gravityZ|forceZ|rapier|trimesh|vhacd|"ball" across scenerender/ and docs/; physics.py has no object3D/scene3d reference; XSD 1.1 rigidBody only in rigidBodyType for 2D nodes (xsd:1293). 'trimesh' hits are the unrelated mesh loader (three/loaders.py).
rows.notes: Needs a 3D rigid-body engine (new solver or rapier3d binding), mesh access from the 3D scene graph and a 3D pose hook into three/ rendering.

rows.notes: Python's tangent-follow (forceX on attractor-path) is an extra not in Rust.

rows.capability: Force-field radius/falloff weighting, start/end windows, animation, and affects
rows.description: radius (metres) bounds a field with weight (1 - d/r)^falloff, otherwise the weight falls as (d/100 px)^-falloff beyond 100 px. start, end and animated values apply. affects restricts a field to bodies or particles. Bodies receive mass*acceleration.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-eval/src/sim.rs FieldSrc::at/at_step/named (start/end filter, animated props), build_fields (affects)
rows.divergence: With radius: both use (1-d/r)^falloff inside r and nothing outside (Rust treats falloff<=0 as exponent 0, i.e. weight 1; Python the same). Without radius: Rust weight = 1/max(d/100px, 1)^falloff (flat inside 100 px); Python weight = 1/(1+d_m)^falloff with d in metres (so strength is already attenuated at distance 0 for falloff>0 only at d>0, and decays from 0). Different attenuation curves for unbounded fields with falloff>0. Rust 100 px is fixed, Python uses ppm. Start/end and animated attributes: both supported (Python via evaluator node_ctx).

rows.capability: 3D force fields: z / forceZ
rows.description: z places a radial field's centre in depth and forceZ pushes toward the camera, acting on 3D bodies (and 3D particles).
rows.searched: grep -i 'forceZ|"z"' in physics.py and field_accel; XSD 1.1 forceField lacks z/forceZ
rows.notes: Only meaningful after 3D bodies or 3D particles exist.

Jelly springs all have the body's stiffness. Cloth shear springs 0.15 and bend 0.02 of it. rope is a chain of cols points along the centre line. stiffness is N/m, damping a fraction of critical damping, mass the total mass.

rows.capability: Soft-body integrator and substep rule (P01)
rows.description: Symplectic Euler in substeps of about 1/omega with omega = sqrt(8k/m) per point. Validation rejects a body needing more than 4096 substeps per fixedStep (P01); past the cap, stiffness is softened to remain stable.
python_evidence: scenerender/physics.py:810-815 soft_substeps (omega*h <= 0.25 plus damping criterion; spn 9 for rigid-anchored)
rows.divergence: Rust: substeps = ceil(step*sqrt(8k/m)), i.e. omega*h <= 1. Python: ceil(omega*dt/0.25), i.e. 4x more substeps, plus a damping-based minimum. Both cap at 4096 (P01 validation: see schema parity work). Rust clamps the effective stiffness past the cap; Python behaviour past the cap is not documented in the code read. Different integration error, so soft motion differs.

rows.capability: Soft-body collisions with rigid bodies and bounds, and coupling direction
rows.description: Soft points collide one way with rigid bodies and the bounds: they are pushed out and lose normal velocity (Rust damps tangential+normal by 0.9). Soft bodies do not push rigid bodies.
python_evidence: scenerender/physics.py:1779-1828 _soft_collide/_respond (restitution 0.2, friction 0.5, 1 cm skin; two-way impulse on the rigid body)
rows.divergence: Python is two-way (rigid bodies receive the opposite impulse), with restitution 0.2 and friction 0.5. Rust is one-way, restitution-free with a flat 0.9 velocity damping. A soft body resting on a dynamic box moves the box in Python, not in Rust.
rows.notes: Python also supports a node with both rigidBody and softBody (grid anchored to the rigid pose); Rust has no such mode (extra).

rows.capability: Soft-body drawing: node stays at start transform and lattice deforms its drawing through the vector mesh warp
rows.description: The soft node keeps its start transform; its lattice warps the layer or shape drawing through the mesh warp, so layers and shapes deform alike.
rows.divergence: Python warps the rendered tile through deform.mesh_map with smooth lattice upsampling; Rust uses the vector mesh warp (geometry-level for shapes). Pixel output differs in tessellation/AA.
rows.notes: Rope in Python is drawn as a ribbon of box thickness.

rows.capability: Particles: deterministic rate and burst emission with counter-based RNG
rows.description: rate particles per second (animatable, fractional carry) with birth times spread within each step, plus burst children (time on the emitter's clock, count, repeat, interval). Each particle's variances come from a counter-based hash of the emitter seed and its index (SplitMix64 finaliser). Emission step is the physics fixedStep (default 1/120).
rust_evidence: crates/sr-sim/src/particles.rs Emitter::step_once, spawn, EmitterSpec; crates/sr-sim/src/rng.rs hash/unit/signed
crates/sr-eval/src/sim.rs build_emitter (burst, seed = hash_str(id) ^ project seed)
rows.divergence: Mechanism matches (carry accumulator, bursts with repeat/interval, hash-per-index, determinism). Streams differ: different hash function, seed derivation, channel numbering and variance mapping, so a given seed does not give the same particles. Python steps at a fixed 1/60 s regardless of physics@fixedStep (Rust uses fixedStep, default 1/120). In-step birth spread: Rust (i+0.5)/n; Python (j+1)/(n+1).
rows.notes: Exact equality with Rust would need porting rng.rs and the channel layout (small) and the Rust per-step integration order (medium), at the cost of changing existing Python goldens.

rows.capability: Particle motion model: gravity, drag, turbulence (curl noise) and coordinate space
rows.description: Particles move under gravityX/Y, drag, curl-noise turbulence and the force fields. They are born turned by the emitter's world transform and live in frame space once born. drag is applied as velocity *= max(0, 1 - drag*dt) per step.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-sim/src/particles.rs step_once motion (damp = 1 - drag*dt; curl2 turbulence *2.0, scale px, t*0.2)
python_evidence: scenerender/nodes/particles.py:488 damp = math.exp(-max(0, drag)*DT); DT = 1/60 (line 75) is a module constant and ignores physics@fixedStep
rows.divergence: Drag: Rust linear (1-drag*dt, clamped at 0), Python exp(-drag*dt). Turbulence: Rust curl-of-value-noise, acceleration 2*turbulence; Python independent fbm per axis, acceleration 3*turbulence, different time rates. Space: Rust particles live in frame space and are not carried by the emitter's parent; Python particles live in the emitter's parent space (moving the parent moves them) and gravity/turbulence act in parent space.
rows.notes: Python's parent-space inheritance is documented and heavily tested (test_particle_transforms.py, 36 cases); changing it would break those.

rows.capability: Flash check: ITU-R BT.1702 / WCAG 2.3.1 general and red flash algorithm
rows.description: Each frame reduces on the GPU to a 48 x 27 grid (8 x 8 lattice per cell) in display-referred linear light. General transition: relative luminance change >= 0.1 with the darker state below 0.8. Red transition: saturated red (R/(R+G+B) >= 0.8) with a change in (R-G-B)*320 above 20. A cell flashes with eight or more opposing transitions (more than three flashes) in one second. A frame fails when flashing cells cover more than a quarter of any window one third of the frame wide and tall (10 deg field at 1024x768).

items.note: Python records, per frame, whether transition pixels covering >=25% of a window occurred, then counts frame-events in a 1 s window and requires n//2 > 3; transitions are not tied to the same cells over time (Rust is per-cell)

items.note: Rust uses > 25% (limit = WIN_W*WIN_H/4 cells), Python >= 25%

items.note: Python decodes PQ/HLG with output primaries luminance weights; Rust luma 0.2126/0.7152/0.0722 on display-linear sRGB

rows.capability: Contrast check: measurement of burned-in text and captions against the real backdrop
rows.description: The compositor copies the target just before each text layer or caption burn-in; after the frame the changed pixels give the text luminance from the frame and the background luminance from the copy; ratio = (L1+0.05)/(L2+0.05). The lowest ratio per text, taken at its maximum accumulated opacity over the whole encode, below minContrast is reported.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-deliver/src/access.rs Judge::contrast (lowest ratio at max opacity)
rows.divergence: Python measures once per text at the midpoint of its longest visible run (_sample_time), rendering the node alone for alpha>=0.5 glyph pixels, then the frame with and without the node (rc.exclude) and takes the MEDIAN per-pixel ratio from 8-bit sRGB. Rust measures in every frame during delivery from an inline backdrop copy and reports the lowest ratio at maximum opacity, using mean foreground and mean background luminance (display-linear floats), over the pixels the text changed. Python therefore misses fades, animated text and text that is visible only briefly in the sampled run.
rows.notes: Python runs only at the render stage before encoding (static_checks); a streaming per-frame probe would need compositor snapshot hooks.

rows.capability: Contrast probes for isolated groups, masks, mattes and effects; ink-replacement coverage probes
rows.description: Text drawn inside an isolated group, mask, matte or effect is listed by the renderer and, after the pass, delivery renders every frame at that text's maximum accumulated opacity twice, with and without the layer, and measures the changed pixels. If text changes no colours, two additional renders replace its ink with black and white while preserving alpha, masks, transforms and covering layers; their difference establishes visible coverage (identical colours report 1:1; transparent, fully covered, offscreen and empty text produce no measurement).

rows.capability: FBX units: scene converted to metres (target_unit_meters = 1)
rows.description: Rust asks ufbx for target_unit_meters = 1.0 with SpaceConversion::ModifyGeometry, so a centimetre-unit FBX (the usual Maya/Blender export) lands at the right size.
rows.divergence: Rust converts FBX units to metres, then applies the 100 px/m basis. Python sets target_axes only, keeps the file's units and treats them as metres, so a cm-unit FBX renders 100x too large. Python also uses TRANSFORM_ROOT (scale and rotation on a root node) where Rust uses ModifyGeometry (baked into geometry). The visible result should match, but the node hierarchy differs.
rows.notes: A one-line ufbx option change plus a regression test. Not verified with a cm-unit fixture. [review] Confirmed: _load_fbx L1531-1536 passes only target_axes, space_conversion=TRANSFORM_ROOT, HELPER_NODES for geometry and inherit modes, and no target_unit_meters. The module docstring (L8-9, L80) says file units are kept. A one-line fix is target_unit_meters=1.0. Rust (import.rs L1003) sets it, with ModifyGeometry.

rows.capability: OpenColorIO display pipeline: working space through looks to display/view
rows.description: colorManagement/@ocioConfig loads a config (file, ocio:// URI or builtin name) and builds working space to looks to DisplayViewTransform. The OCIO view replaces toneMapping. Exposure applies first. The display is chosen from the first output's colour space and transfer.
rows.divergence: Python is more exact. It evaluates through PyOpenColorIO's own CPU processors with no lattice approximation (Rust's baked table has about 0.011 trilinear error). It handles scene-referred outputs (acescg, camera log) by leaving OCIO at the working space and taking the built-in encoding. Python then bakes a 65^3 log-shaped LUT per context for speed (color_lut.py), with an exact per-pixel mode available. Rust requires ociobakelut on PATH. Python requires the opencolorio wheel, a core dependency in pyproject.toml.

rows.capability: OCIO bake lattice: 129^3 indexed by ACEScct, ACEScg fast path, 65,536-entry log shaper path
rows.description: Rust bakes the transform onto a 129^3 lattice indexed by the ACEScct curve of each working channel (scene-linear up to about 222). For an ACEScg working space whose config ACEScct matches (checked with a 17^3 bake), the table comes straight from the config. Otherwise it goes through the config's log space (compositing_log, color_timing, ...) with a 65,536-entry shaper and is resampled.
rows.searched: grep -rn -i 'ociobakelut|bakelut|129|acescct lattice' scenerender. Only color_lut.py (65^3 log-shaped LUT of the whole finish plan, a different mechanism) and PyOpenColorIO CPU processors exist.
rows.notes: Implementation artifact of Rust's no-library design, not a user-facing capability. Python's in-process OCIO makes it unnecessary. Mark as not required unless a GPU-only path with an OCIO lattice is wanted. [review] Not a gap: an implementation artifact of Rust shelling out to ociobakelut. Python evaluates PyOpenColorIO in-process (opencolorio is a core dependency, pyproject.toml L7). Recommend treating this row as N/A.

rows.capability: Seekable fixed-step sim timeline (1/60 s steps, checkpoint every simulated second, order-independent seeking)
rows.description: Timeline<S> steps a state at a fixed dt from the node's start, keeps a clone every simulated second, and serves any time by restoring the nearest earlier checkpoint and replaying. A frame requested out of order equals a straight run. The state at t is the one after floor((t-start)/dt) steps.
python_evidence: scenerender/physics.py:175-205 Seekable.at(n): the checkpoint dict keyed by step, with step(state, i) called per step. It has a last_n fast path and max_steps. Used from nodes/particles.py:64 (import). Rust Timeline::at takes a float t and passes the step's start time t0 to the callback, while Python passes only the integer step i.
rows.divergence: Python Seekable is integer-step addressed (at(n)) and is used by physics and particles, so the mechanism exists. No sim node uses it for flock, fluid, slime or erosion. Rust keys on a float time with a floor(+1e-9) rule and a node-local clock from the composition graph (local_time, offset).
rows.notes: Reuse Seekable; add a float-time wrapper that matches the Rust step-index rule.

rows.capability: Checkpoint thinning to a 256 MB budget for large sim states
rows.description: When checkpoints times state bytes exceed 256 MB, Timeline doubles the checkpoint interval and drops every other checkpoint, so memory stays bounded and worst-case replay doubles. Each State reports its byte size (slime: trail*4 + agents*12; flock: n*32; erosion: height*4).
rows.searched: grep checkpoint/budget/thin/every in scenerender/physics.py and nodes/particles.py: Seekable.checkpoints grows without bound (one deepcopy per `every` steps, no byte accounting, no eviction).

Rust thin() runs only while more than 2 checkpoints remain. Python Seekable (physics.py:175-205) also has no byte accounting, and its max_steps cap of 10M differs from Rust.

rows.capability: Counter-based hash RNG (splitmix64 finaliser of seed, a, b) used by every sim
rows.description: rng::hash mixes seed, two counters with fixed odd multipliers and a SplitMix64 finaliser; unit() takes the top 53 bits. All spawning, droplets, slime coin flips and boundary re-headings are pure functions of (seed, index, step), so runs are reproducible and seekable.
python_evidence: scenerender/physics.py:135 hash01 -> noise.uniform(seed, channel, id) (D24 splitmix64 of seed, channel, id)
rows.divergence: Both are splitmix64-based counter hashes but built differently. Rust rng::hash: x = seed ^ a*0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 ^ b*0xC2B2AE3D27D4EB4F, then one splitmix finaliser. Python noise.hash64: splitmix64(seed ^ splitmix64(channel ^ splitmix64(index))), with the +INC step inside splitmix64 (nested, not packed). Same seed gives different streams. Rust lattice noise2 uses smoothstep 3-2x on (x,y) only. Python vnoise is 3D with a quintic fade and a channel argument.
rows.notes: Needed first by flock, slime and erosion for numeric parity. Value noise (noise2, 3-2x smoothstep) also differs from vnoise (quintic).

rows.capability: Flock: Reynolds boids rules (separation, alignment, cohesion) over a uniform neighbour grid
rows.description: Each agent steers by separation, alignment and cohesion within `perception`. Separation is the inverse-distance repulsion inside separationDistance. Steering is desired minus velocity, clamped to maxForce. Velocity is clamped to maxSpeed and floored at cruise `speed`. Neighbours come from a perception-sized cell grid in fixed (stable counting-sort) order and every agent updates from the previous state. Initial headings and positions are hashed from the seed.

rows.notes: Needs an opaque colour buffer. Python already keeps one for refraction (renderer.py:6 'opaque colour buffer').

rows.capability: Directional shadows as 4 cascades (practical split), each fitted to its view slice within the scene
rows.description: Under a perspective camera, directional lights render 4 cascaded shadow maps. Splits blend the logarithmic and uniform schemes (practical split), over the view frustum out to the scene's farthest point. Each cascade is fitted to its slice across the light, clamped to the scene. The split depths ride in the light record and the shader selects the cascade per pixel. An orthographic camera uses one view. A thin pole on a 20,000-unit floor casts a visible shadow at 512 texels.
python_evidence: scenerender/three/renderer.py:1133 render_shadow (kind 0: one orthographic map centred on casters, radius rad, near .01 far rad*4)
scenerender/three/lights.py:35-38 (PCSS soft shadows, shadowMapSize up to 8192, shadowBias)
rows.divergence: Python casts directional/dome shadows through ONE orthographic map fitted to all casters, with PCSS soft shadows (lights.py lines 34-37: softness in metres or degrees). Rust uses 4 camera-fitted cascades under a perspective camera (three.rs CASCADES=4) and filters with a fixed 3x3 PCF (three.wgsl lines 226-236, kernel scale li.spot.w, minimum 1 texel). Rust has no PCSS, so the 'unverified' note is resolved: Python has the softer shadow filter, Rust has the better cascade fit. Porting cascades must keep Python's PCSS, which means per-cascade blocker search.
rows.notes: No schema change: it changes the existing castShadow behaviour. Pixel-different results for any scene with a large extent, so it needs a golden-image policy decision.

rows.capability: Shadow memory budget (512 MB) with map-size reduction and caster-layer capping
rows.description: SHADOW_BUDGET = 512 MiB. map_size is halved until size^2*4*layers fits (floor 64). shadow_casters limits how many lights cast given max_texture_array_layers (4 layers per directional cascaded light, 6 per point, 1 per spot), and shadow_note reports the dropped casters.
rust_evidence: crates/sr-gpu/src/three.rs SHADOW_BUDGET:27, shadow_casters():176, shadow_note():198, budget loop ~L1624
python_evidence: renderer.py:654 'Shadow maps exceed GPU array capacity' (raises)
renderer.py:17-19 'GPU capacity errors are explicit, never truncation'
rows.divergence: Python never shrinks or drops casters: it raises on over-capacity, by design ('never truncation'). Rust degrades silently (halves the size, drops casters) and adds a diagnostic note. There is no memory byte budget on the Python side.
rows.notes: Policy conflict: Python's explicit-error stance vs Rust's degrade-with-note.

rows.capability: cacheSha256 verification on <generated> at render time: mismatch or missing file refused
rows.description: A cache is used only if its SHA-256 equals cacheSha256; wrong digest or missing file is an error (A02/A05) that names the file, expected and found digests and points at `scene-render resolve`.
rust_evidence: README line 'refuses it unless its SHA-256 equals cacheSha256'
rows.divergence: Rust reports A02/A05 as load-time/validation diagnostics for every generated/captionTrack/tiles element, whether or not it is drawn, with a help hint to run resolve. Python raises SceneError lazily only when an asset is actually drawn/mixed (frame_rgba/audio_source_path), so an unused generated asset with a wrong digest passes; the error has no resolve hint and uses a file-wide memoised hash (path,size,mtime).
rows.notes: A02-style eager verification belongs partly to the validation/schema parity work; row covers only the digest-refusal semantics.

rows.capability: captionTrack transcription cache: digest-verified, mismatch refused
rows.description: A captionTrack with transcribe/cache reads its cache JSON, verified against cacheSha256 at load (A02); a mismatch is an error, not a silent skip.
rows.divergence: Python logs an error and drops the whole track (cues=[]) on a digest mismatch (captions.py:1636-1638). A missing cacheSha256 skips the check in the reader (`if sha and ...`), but Schematron rule C32 (schema/scene-render-1.1.sch:114) already requires @cache and @cacheSha256 whenever @transcribe is set. So the missing-digest gap exists only when validation is bypassed. Rust refuses the document or render.
rows.notes: Python superset on formats is fine; the gap is strictness (and strict-mode behaviour).

rows.capability: SRVOL cache version 1 binary format (reader and canonical writer)
rows.description: Little-endian one-frame format: 8-byte magic 'SRVOL\0\r\n', u32 version 1, u32 grid count (0-64), per grid name (u16 length, 1-64 ASCII, unique, sorted), f32 finite background, 16 f64 column-major affine index-to-world matrix (invertible, finite inverse), u32 brick count, bricks as 3 x i32 key in [-2^28, 2^28-1] plus 512 f32 samples (8^3, x fastest). Keys unique and sorted, background-only bricks omitted, EOF required, budgets (256 MiB bytes, 100k bricks, 64 grids by default) enforced before allocation; deterministic serialization.

rows.notes: Rust: implemented. Truncation-at-every-boundary, duplicate grid/brick, non-finite and budget tests exist in Rust and should be mirrored. Pure numpy/struct implementation is straightforward.

rows.capability: Sparse brick grids with per-grid affine transforms and world-space trilinear sampling
rows.description: SparseGrid stores 8^3 bricks keyed by integer brick coordinates with Euclidean division for negatives, a background value for absent bricks, and trilinear sampling in index space that includes background from absent bricks. Each grid (density, temperature, velocity components) has its own transform (affine incl. reflection/shear), so linear/advect interpolation evaluates each frame in world space, no matching voxel arrays required. rows.capability: Fixed-step seekable simulation framework with budgeted checkpoints and atomic failure
rows.description: Common behaviour across pyro/particles3D/ocean/whitewater/rigid3D: fixed canonical dt, checkpoints thinned/evicted before cloning under independent hard byte budgets (workspace vs checkpoint), per-seek work and step budgets (e.g. 100M work units, 1M steps), forward/backward/fractional seeks give identical states, failed requests keep the published frame, and exhaustion errors instead of partial output; local clocks via ancestor-clock inversion; hidden/conditional nodes do not reset the simulation.
python_evidence: scenerender/physics.py:175-206 Seekable (checkpoints every N steps, max_steps cap, order independence)
rows.divergence: Python Seekable (physics.py:175) keeps unbounded deepcopy checkpoints every N steps (60 default; particles use 30 = 0.5 s). It has no byte budget, thinning or work-unit cap. at(n) silently clamps n to max_steps (10,000,000) instead of erroring, and a failed step can leave the shared 'last' state mutated (non-atomic). Rust enforces explicit MiB/work limits and returns errors.

corrections_applied.reason: physics.py Seekable (lines 175-206) is a plain deepcopy checkpoint dict with no byte accounting. It also silently clamps n to max_steps instead of erroring, and has no atomic-failure semantics. Adding byte budgets, thinning, work caps and atomic failure is a rewrite of the recurrence engine and every caller (physics, particles), not an S change.

corrections_applied.new: Python Seekable (physics.py:175) keeps unbounded deepcopy checkpoints every N steps (60 default; particles use 30 = 0.5 s). It has no byte budget, thinning or work-unit cap. at(n) silently clamps n to max_steps (10,000,000) instead of erroring, and a failed step can leave the shared 'last' state mutated (non-atomic). Rust enforces explicit MiB/work limits and returns errors.
corrections_applied.reason: Seekable.at() reads min(int(n), self.max_steps): the clamp is silent, and step() mutates s in place, so a mid-step exception leaves self.last stale. Both facts are absent from the original text.
